A SONG OF THE SEA.

One night a small girl came down to the rocks 13y the side of the great big sea: And she pulled off her shoes, and she pulled off ;her socks, And waded in tin to her knee. An old crab wondered with all his might . What the little girl's game could be, And why she was out so late at night; , So he climbed up the rocks to see. • Said the ' "I'm a fish in the big, salt sea; I'm a fish, and I live in the water 1" "That's odd," thought the crab, "as odd can be I'm sure it is*Mrs. Brown's daughter."

Then the girl jumped round and tried to behave Just as the fishes do, When suddenly up came a great big wave And soaked her through and through. The old crab laughed and laughed, till he cried, As the girl ran cripping away: Be laughed till he get a stitch in the side, And it served him right, I say.

Popular fiction: Lying. Chemistry: The cookery of science. The hasty match often starts a running fire. If brevity is the sole of wit, levity is the upper. Sickness is nature's way of saying: "I told you!so." The less head a man has the more frequently he loses it. • Rank and riches are chains of gold, but still they are chains. The debt of nature is one of the things we:must pay as we go. Advice to boys who wish to be sailors "A life on the ocean" waive! Many of our cares are but a morbid way'of looking at our privileges. When a clock strikes it is working, but:when a man strikes he isn't. Man is advised to net on the square and woman to keep in her sphere. When! they get married, the prob- lem is something like squaring the circle. "I have nothing but:my heart to give you," said a spinster to a lawyer, who gained a suit for her. "Well," said the lawyer, gruffly,:" go to my clerk, he takes the fees." Madame Hautry "You the singing master! But we do not want the singing master !" Herr Pumpernickel: " Bardon; de ladty next door toldt me you vented one badly—she sent me !" Fight hard against a hasty temper. Anger will come, but resist it stoutly. A spark may set a house on fire. A fit of passion may give you cause to mourn all the days of your life. He that bath pity on another man's sorrow shall be free from it himself; and he that delighteth in and scorneth the misery of another shall one time or other assuredly fall into it himself. A mole may set off beauty; but a poor piece of court plaster has the same effect, and may be easily removed. Pont despise temporary expedients because your mind is set on permanent principles. Parishioner "Well, doctor, I enjoyed your sermon very much." Dominie : "You pain me, deeply, sir. My sermons are written for instruction, not for the giving of pleasure on the holy Sabbath." The first step to self-knowledge is self-distrust. Nor can we attain to any kind of knowledge except by a like process. We must fall on our knees at the thresh- old or we shall not gain entrance into the temple. Miss Lenox : "Has your church closed for the summer yet?" Miss Murrayhill : "No, but I've stopped going, as, you know, pa refuses to leave town until July, and I can't afford to let religion interfere with my standing in society. Houston (of Texas): "I've finally *Wed that soa dollars I've owed Hank Jones for so long." Mrs. Houston: "I'm so glad ! But where did you get the money?" Houston: "Didn't have no money. I just shot Jones." Bobby: "Mamma, what do they mean when they say a thing is between the devil and the deep sea ?" Mamma (who has imbibed newspaper ideas of the city of the un- salted sea) : "Oh! they mean anyplace between Chicaey and the Atlantic." Mistress (to servant who is about to throw away an old lamp) "What is the matter with that lamp, Bridget? Does it smoke?' Bridget: "I don't know nothin"bout whither it. smokes or drinks; but it goes Out noights, mum!" "Why, Clara. you look radiant! What has happened?' " I've just received an invitation to a wedding." "Well there's nothing particular in that to go in raptures over.' " Yes, but it happens to be my own,"sand she showed. the new engagement ring. Mrs. Wickwire: "I could have married a dozen men before I met you." Mr. Wickwire: "You mean you could have married one out of a dozen, don't you?'" Mrs. Wickwire: "No ; I don't. You forget I lived aiehteen'months in Chicago." Paddy is often poetically polite. On picking up and: I returning a lady's parasol, which had been blown out of her hand, a gallant Irishman said, "Faith, Miss, an' if ye was as stlarong as yer handsome, be labors, a hurri- can couldn't have snatched it from ye." The importance of letting. the sunlight fall into all parts of our dwellings cannot be too highly estimated. Good health is dependent on sunlight and pure air. An eminent physician has said, "Sunlight should never be excluded except when so bright as to be uncomfortable to the eyes. Angry landlord: "See here, are you going to pay the Tent or anove r Tenant: "I've always heard it was cheaper to move." Angry landlord (sneeringly): " you ought to know: something about it by this time." Tenant "I'm not so sure about that. You see I have I never paid any rent." The conversation had turned on an old beau' "who by ; the aid of cosmetics and other artifices seemed te grow .a little younger every year. "You will see," said some .one, "now he will succeed in hiding ithe ravages of •time." "And finally die of extreme; youth," added another speaker. Miss de Smith: "Our engagement is broken from this moment, Mr. Roberts." Mr. Roberts: "Why, I've done nothing, have I?" Miss del Smith: "You havei :You promised to teach me lawn tennis, and the firstithing you do is to call me 'Thirty. love ? and I not a day•oYer seventeen, and you know it." "Do you ever ;receive contributions, written on both sides of the paper?" asked a gentleman entering a news- paper office. "No, sir; never," emphatically replied the editor. All right: I was going to endorse this cheque to your order, but I don't want to:break your rules." Then he Went out, leaving the editor in, a deep-green astudy. A coloured dude chanced to be among tha seated pas- ties in a Washington horse-car. A esoung woman of his own colour entered, and be hestreediately rose and offered her his seat. She gracefully e.emurred, and said, "I do not like to deprive you, sir, tif your seat." Oh, no depravity, Miss," was his reply; "no depravity at all • I prefer to stand." S'cene—.Mining village.. Minister (at miner's door): "Is James at home, M-. 5. Brown ?" Mrs. B.: "No, sir, he's siva to toon tbe day. AN APPROPRIATE JACEEP.—Mrs. Peterby is the terror of the Austin dry goods clerks. She will spend an entire afternoon looking over a counter full of goods, and go off without taking anything except her leave. All the establishment may get from her is a threat to call again next day. A few days since, Ike Silveston, Mose Schaum- burg's affectionate clerk, lost his patience. Mrs. Peterby was looking for some peculiar kind of jacket, but nothing in the store suited her. "It vas no use hunting dot shacket up for you any more. Ye don't keep 'em." "How do you know what sort I need ?" "I know very well. You need *trait shacket. Ye don't keep 'ern." That "walls have ears," and that hotel walls in par- ticular are apt to be of the slenderest texture, should be borne in mind by married women when they suffer themselves to lose their tempers with their husbands amid the discomforts of travelling. A certain bachelor in a foreign hotel was once kept awake for hours by the angry vituperations of an injured wife in the bedroom adjoining his OWII. Apparently the husband had the advantage in temper, for his manly voice was presently heard pleading for a reconciliation—" I am very sorry, Susan; so kiss me and let us go to sleep." The long- suffering bachelor seized his opportunity and took the ball at the hop. Rapping vigorously on the wall, he called out loudly and distinctly, "Kiss him directly, Susan, and let me go to sleep." Needless to say, he was nOt disturbed again that night.. Colonel Lebel, the inventor of the French maga- zine rifle, has retired from active service in conse- quence of bad health. . lie is fifty-two years of age, has served in the army thirty-five years, and has been through eight campaigns. .---

f f The great Almack's, formerly the rendezvous of connoisseurs, and now known as Willis's Rooms, King-st., St. James's, has been leased for a long time to a German syndicate, who intend to establish an elaborate system of German health baths of every description, including the latest developments of the science of massage. -- The most curious incident in connection with the going over of Newman to Rome is the fact that Mark Pattison would have gone over with him if he had not happened to miss a train, an accident which gave him time for further reflection, with the result that he presently drifted so far from his old moorings that he came within a quite measur- able distance of pure atheism.

The Dockers' Union are not content with demon- strating. They have a practical policy as well. They have sent a strong delegation to the Trades Congress, and they are giving their delegates a still stronger instruction. They propose (1) Union rates and an eight hours day for Government dockyards; (2) the organisation of the great field of " blackleg " labor—the agricultural laborers; (3) the boycott of unscrupulous employers.

There is no truth in the story published by the "Manchester Guardian" that John Burns intends to retire from his candidature for Battersea or from the County C3uncil. The story may have arisen from the fact that Burns is trying (at present with- out success) to get away for a few days' holiday as soon as the strikers will let him. Considering that he has now won three strikes in three weeks, he has fairly earned a rest.

By the way, General Booth's new schemes of social reform have excited the attention of very different types of character. Henry George, who called on the General the other day, was vastly in- terested, and described it as the greatest social movement he had ever witnessed. Lord Wolseley has also signified his desire to know more about the plans which are not developed as yet; and yet a third inquirer is Lord Rosebery.

-- The approaching Assemblies of the Baptist and Congregational Unions tit Cardiff and Swansea will be marked by an interesting exchange of courtesies, the former body having invited Mr. Albert Spicer to preside over one of its largest gatherings, while the Congregationalists have asked Mr. Alfred Thomas, M.P., late chairman of the Baptist Union of Wales, to render a similar service for them. Both gentlemen have consented.

, It was Cardinal's Day at the Crystal Palace on Monday. The League of the Cross festival is mainly a demonstration of the love and loyalty of London Catholics to Cardinal Manning. The Grand Old Man was everywhere—hie name was on every- body's tongue. lie spoke at the meeting; he lis- tened to the children's concert; he reviewed his guards. Everywhere he was accompanied by a knot of fathers, with whom he kept up a pretty lively conversation.

Mr. Bradlaugh intends next session to raise the question of regularly procuring, either through colonial governors or by independent local commis- sions sitting on the spot, accurate information as to the nature and results of colonial legislation similar to that which is mooted here. Sir Charles Dilke's recent work indicates that Australian legislatures have given a fair trial to the eight hours, free State education, local option, and early closing of shops, on the lines sometimes advocated here._

Mr. Gladstone's speeches at Midlothian are to be followed by a counter-blast from Lord Hartington, at theinvitation of the East and North of Scotland Liberal Unionist Association, who have asked him to visit Edinburgh and take part in a national demonstration to be held under the auspices of both sections of the "Unionist "-party in Scotland in November next. Lord Hartington will also be present at the annual meeting of the Association, 'which will be held in Edinburgh at that time.

Mr. George Charles llerhert, who was married on Thursday to the Hon. Violet Lane-PO:4 is nephew and heir-presureptive of the. Earl of Pbwis. Lord Powis is great-grandson of the illustrious Robert Clive-of Plessey, and represents in the, female line the iferberts, Earls of Powis, whose territory of 60,000- acres in Wales and Shropshire he has in- herited, and whose name he bears. The future Countess of Powis is sister of the Countess of Yar- borough, and theftwo young ladies are co-heiresses of their father's ancient barony of Conyers.

, It is noticed that vegetarian restaurants are in- creasing very rapidly, and this is accounted for by the excellence of the accommodation they provide visitors in the shape of reading, waiting, and smok- ing rooms. The tendency to greater comfort and elegance is, of course, not confined to this class of i public caterers, but I believe the success of the . vegetarians is likely to bring about a new departure 1 in general restaurants by toe provision of special 1 dishes, just as you. see in many public-house win- dews about Easter, a prominent announcement that "Kosher Rum "is on sale within,

O'Donovan Ressa's term of banishment will, says an American authority, expire next New Year's Day. In America it is proposed to raise an annu- ity which may enable him to spend the rest of his days in Ireland. O'Donovan Rossa was Mr. Davitt's fellow-convict. The cruel hardships he endured in prison affected his mind, and this accounts for the violence of his speech and action against the Gov- ernment during his American career. In his evi- dence before the Parnell Commission, Mr. Davitt described how O'Donovan R9ssa, with his hands tied behind his back, was obliged to lap up his food like a dog.

Sir George Campbell, who has figured so promin- ently in the proceedings of the House of Commons this session, is a barrister as well as a baronet. He entered the Bengal Civil Service in 1842, and WAS for a time judge of the Supreme Court of Calcutta. He has also served with some distinction as Lieutenant- Governor of Bengal, and in the still higher capacity of a member of the Council of India, so that he has some claim to be ranked as an authority upon the affairs of that country. His "Modern India" and 66A Handy Book on the Eastern Question are among his published works. He 'first entered the House of Commons as member for Kirkcaldy in 1875, and still represents the Kirkcaldy District.

-- Well done, Theosophy! With a thousand pounds from a lady member of the Theosophical Society, Mrs. Besant has established a first-class girls' club in the East-end, where the poor female workers can obtain good cheap food and social comforts. It will give some happiness and enjoyment to a class who know only the black side of life. Some people may wonder what this has got to do with Theosophy. But while awaiting the day which will inaugurate the happiness of their astral bodies in the human hinterland, theosophists, during the period, of their terrestial existence, do their best to promote uni- versal brotherhood. And in opening this oasis in the East-end they deserve the best thanks of all.

The health of the youthful King of Spain has con- siderably improved since he went to St. Sebastin, although the course of sea-bathing prescribed for him has been countermanded. The life led by the. Queen Regent and her children is of the simplest. They leave the Ayete Palace every morning at ten for a rustic pavilion erected on the sea-shore, where the King and his sisters spend some hours in digging trenches in the sand. A few days ago he presided at a children's fête given on the Plaza de Toros, and seemed thoroughly to enjoy the fun , , which raged around him. After his siesta lie is driven in the cool of the evening along the shady avenues of the Ayete Park, accompanied by his mother, his governess (Countess Peralta), and General Cordova, who has become his Sovereign's prime favourite and inseparable companion.

Ministers hare flown, and are flying from the dreary scene of their failures and humiliations. The Prime Minister and Mr. W. 11. Smith are seek- ing "the cure" at La Bourboule. The Chancellor of the Exchequer went home to Seacox Heath on Monday, to prepare for a journey to the Tyrol ; the Lord Chancellor hies away to Cornwall; Mr. Balfour has left for his Haddingtonshire home, but is bent on a golfing season at North Berwick in September. Lord George Hamilton is away to Selkirkshire. Mr. Matthews has retired to Hampshire, and Sir M. Hicks-Beach to Wilts. Lord Cross ismaking himself happy in his home at Eccle Riggs. Mr. Gladstone is speaking through the phono- graph every night to delighted audiences in the Athezueum Hall, Melbourne. The message he sem', through the instrument to Lord Carrington, Gover- nor of New South Wales, is faithfully and success- fully repeated every evening. The Melbourne papers say that Mr. Gladstone's voice is sonorous, and that it is characterised by an oratorical swing that is highly impressive. But this phonographic entertainment is of a decidedly mixed description, and the G.O.M. may reasonably object to his little oration being bracketed with J. L. Toole's " 'Orrible Tale," cornet solos by Arthur Smith, of the Covent Garden Opera, a banjo duet by the Bohee Minstrels, London, &c., &c. It is certain that Mr. Gladstone never contemplated this use of his voice when he graciously consented to send a message to Lord Car- rington through the phonograph.

A novel use has been found for the instantaneous detective camera. It seems that at one of the large punlic schools the rule is that when a form master is under the necessity of caning a boy he must not lift the cane higher than his own shoulder. Last term complaints were made that one of the masters habitually disregarded the rule ; but as this was invariably denied by the castigator him- self one of the young rascals determined to bring him to book. Accordingly a detective camera was produced at the moment of punishment, the mas- ter's attention being otherwise occupied, and a proof struck off exhibiting, without possibility of doubt, the cane elevated beyond regulation point. The head master, to whom the photograph was shown, with a strict sense of justice condemned his subordinate, but at the same time promptly gave the scholar 400 lines for " playing in class."

We had expected the sea-serpent,. as usual,. on the prorogation of Parliament, but a correspondmit in Kirkwall provides us, with an amusing variant on the perennial theme. Here is the story : " What is said to be a mermaid has been seen for aome weeks at stated times at Southside, Deerness, Orkney. It is about six to seven feet in length, has a little black head, white neckrsnow-white body, and two arms, and in swimming it just appears like a hu- man being. At times it will,come very closa in shore and appears to be sitting on a sunken rock, and will wave and work its hands. It has never been seen entirely out of water.". The first comment that will occur to readers of this story will naturally be "very like a seal," and it seems the people in, the neighbourhood have themselves arrived at that conclusion, but slow to admit that they have seen nothing out of the common they say that, if -only a seal, it is, at least, a deformed example of! that species.

The report on the naval matunuvres which have just concluded will be awaited with a considerable amount of interest, if only for the reason that the lay mind is unable at present to gather what have been the precise objects of opposing fleets, and cer- tainly to calculate the amount of success which has attended the evolutions. The secrecy which has been observed with reference-to the manceuxAres this year is a part of the Admiralty plan, and it is probable that many important facts which have been ascertained will never be made public in any form. The authorities felt that it was inadvisable to put foreign Governments in possession of inforrua- tion we might acquire, and hence the unusually severe restrictions on newspaper correspondent.s and the expulsion of one of their nomber. A certmr London daily has heard nothing of its correspon- dents with the enemy's fleet for nearly a fortnight; In actual war this might be necessary, but it woullfl be tantalising.

div.p: STORY OF CASSRM,

OR AVARICE PROPERLY REWARDED: -- There dwelt at Bagdad an old merchant, nained Abou Cassem, noted for his,avarice. Although he was very rich, his clothes were nothing but patches and rags; his turban was of the coarsest cloth, and so dirty that it was difficult to distinguish the colour. But of his whole dress, his papoosheß [slippers] were what merited most the attention of the curious; the soles were armed with large nails, and the upper leathers were an assemblage of botches; the famous ship Argo had not so many pieces in it; and ever since they had been papooshe9, which was about ten years, the most skilful cobblers in all Bagdad had exhausted their ingenuity to keep them together. They were even become so heavy that they passed into a proverb; and when any one wanted to express a thing that was remarkably clumsy, Cassem's papooshes were always the object of comparison. - - -

One day this merchant was walking in the bazaar, when an offer was made him of a large quantity of crystal, of which he made an advantageous pur- chase; and hearing some days after that a per- fumer, whose affairs were in a ruinous state, had some excellent rose-water to sell, which was his last resource, he instantly took advantage -of the poor man's misfortunes, and bought his rose-water for half the value. This new bargain put him into good humour; however, instead of giving an entertain- ment to his neighbours, according to the custom of the merchants of the East, when they have made a fortunate purchase, he found it more convenient to go to the public baths, where he had not been for a long time. As he was undressing, a person whom he took to be his friend, for the covetous rarely have any real ones, told him that his papooshes were the ridicule of the whole city, and that he ought to buy a new pair. "I have thought of it a long time," replied Cassem; "however, they are not yet so bad but they may serve a little longer." During this conversation he was quite undressed, and eetired to the bath. While he was bathing, the Kazee of Bagdad came likewise to bathe. Cassem, coming out before the judge, passed first into the dressing-room, and having put on his clothes, he sought in vain for his papoosies, in the room of which he discovered a new pair. Our avaricious merchant, persuaded, because he wished it so, that the person who had just re- buked him about his old slippers had made him a present a the new pair, put them on his feet with- out hesitation, and quitted the place, overjoyed at the thought of being saved the expense of buying. When the Kazee had done bathing, the slaves looked about for their master's papeashes, instead of which they could only find a vile old pair, which were readily known to be Cassem's ; the Kaeee's officers went directly in search of the suspected thief, and finding him with the stolen effects upon him, after exchanging papooolies, the Kazee sent him to. prison; and as he was reputed to be as. rich as he was cevetous, he was obliged to compromise the matter with the Kazee, by the payment of a considerable- sum of money. Otehis return home, the afflicted Cassem, fee-very spits threw his slippers into the Tigris, which ran Mader his windows, Some, days afterwards, a fisherman, pulling up his net, found it heavier than usual, which, was owing to the weight of the papceslaes, the nails of which' had caught' hold of his net, and broke several of the meshes. The poor fisherman, enraged at Cassem and his slipperee took It into his head to flag them in at the windows; and he threw them with such force that he overset the crystal vases- which decoraMd the cornices and mantlepiece of the room, and one of them likewise struck the beetle curtaining, the nese-watere and dashed it to pieces,. Figure to younself, Et you can, the- agonies cf Case sem, on beholding this scene of devastation. "Cereal papooges!" exclaimed the covetous wretch, tearing his heard,. "you shall not do me mu farther, mis- chief." So sayhtg,, he took up, a spade, repaired to his garden, and dug a hole to. bury them. One of his neighbours, who for a tonsid)srable time had owed him an ill office, seeing hima turning up the ground, ran to the governor and aequaintsd hams that Cassem had just dug up a hidden treasure in his garden. This was sufficient to arouse the cupidity of the commandane„and our miser invoke remonstrated, assuring him that he had not die- covered any gold, but was only butying his- cursed slippers.; the governor had, made sure of money, and the unfortunate Caseem ceuld not obtain his liberty without. giving alhandsome present.. The-distraeted old man gave his papouflimmnst heartily, to the devil, and' went and threw them Into an aqueduct at a great; distance frone the city, Imagining that he should, bean no more off them; but thedevil, who had not done playing his tricks with him, directed them. to the conduit of the aqueduct, by which means; they intercepted the current of the waters, and caused an inandathen in the adjoining gardens. 'The owners, on diseovering the cause, took' the slippers. to the Kazee„ and demanded satisfaction or the damages- they had occasioned. The unhappy master of them was once more committed to prison,, and condemned to pay a fine which amounted to a larger sum than the two former ones together;, after which, the Kazee, who would by no means detain his property,, restored to him his choice papeerhea Cassem, that he might: he finally delivered from all farther harm from the suppers, now :determined to burn them; but as they had imbibetha peat deal, of water he set them en the terrace at the top of his, house to dry by the son. But fortune had not yet exhausted her quiver against the nnleeky- mean, andi she now dealt him a more cruel stroke then all the, ' rest. A young dog in the next Imam, perceiving the slippers, leapt from his master's tezzaee over to, Cassem's, seized one of them in his mouth, and played his gambols with, it, till at lest he let it fall over the parapet, each uahappily, it/lighted on the head of a woman with child, who was paesing along. the street before Casseet's door. Fear, added to the violence of the blow, made the poor-woman mis- carry. Her husband: carried his complaint to the Kazee, and Cassemmae condemned to make him a recompense proptetioeed to the injury' he had dave his wife. Upon this freelemiefortune, cateraleer ran home, and, taking his papooohes in his hand, he once-more repaired to the Name. "Behold! ray 10re1,7 said he, with an impetuosity which diverted the judge, "the instruments-of all my sufferings; thesefoursed papooshes haen.recheced me to poverty; , deign, therefore, to publish a decree,. that I maesnot he made responsible for the ills they will doubtless occasion hereafter." The Karen could not:refuse this reasonable petition; and Cassem at length, by dear-bought experience, learned the fatal &Zees of avarice.

SIX PERSONS SHOT DEAD. Terrible scenes were enacted in a well-filled excursion train about fitteen miles west of Cincinnati maSunclay. Some drunken labourers boarded it, and from sdmetause or other began disputing among themselves. Ilevolvers were drawn, and the quarrel terminated itt a five fight, the shooting being close and rapid. When it ceased, and the smoke cleared away sufficiently for the terrified passengers to see about them, six persons were found lying dead on the floor, including two passengers. 'The following-is from a work on Llandudno and , Great Onme's Heed, written by Mr. Tracy Tur- nerellisand printed for private circulation:— And now, friend, reader, before we spart, I must , make ,yousequainteda with one more " marvel" connected with the great Orme's Heads which came won Me by surprise—indeed, the factsof my learns ing,about it all was as curious a bit of " wonder- ,ment Many Ihave told you of. But judge for ' yourself. 'The day after ,rayanalk round the -mountain, I was chatting with, olstKendrick—the quaint primi- tive-looking Welsh lapidezy I introduced to you at ' the commeneementof this narrative, and who is certainly one of the ", lions " of the spot. k. We were talking retrospectivelysaf•things and people we had both seen on this reeky. promontory. . Among other ' matters our conversation,terned on the old miner. Isaac .Jones, the owner of Ss Gogarth Cave aGottage " and ,of Keturab,, his daughter. " A nice, ensible saidl to aKendriek.—" Yes! indeed. I suppose you know. she, was horn in a cave."--" Born in cave!l" I.repeated ,with some astonishment,— " Yes !.and soroefifteen little brothers andssisters with her."--," Do esaplain ,w,last you mean,"-acid I more andmore bewildered. s Thereupon, liendricki told me what he knewJor whet he had heardabout Isaac alonege history_ ,Whether from limited, , very limited:means, or the want ,cf a dwelling Islam or an innate love for sutterranean caverns, which ,his smining ,ocenpaticns had probably inspired him .withalsaac Jones, having no •heme of his ,evan—he .seems always to have hmen an odd, .ecoentric. unsettled kind of being invariakly poor—took it into his head, some fifstss years age, to live, 'hertaitslikea in a cave not 'far from Gogarth nins. In this cave, the wife e his bosom, good Mrs. MiriascsJenes,iived with herdetas, and spouse from the date of her asmarriage, conten- tedly and happily, and in this , cave also, on two different mammon.% ehegasse birth tz twins—Beturah - was one of them—and several other "units," male ,and female, iikewiee. In. facts Isaac Jones's mister-, ,mnean lime-stone ,cave saaon became, humanly -speaking, a well-stocked and populcus habitations so many were the little rlsaac;Joneses running wild', on the mountain side around it—pure children of . the mountain, a lon fadjauwiz. In this antediluvian ' ,cave Isaac Jones would probably have lived to the; ,endof his days, had note good or eviletroke of fore! tune—l am puzzled toatly which it ;was—suddenly eent,in his way a very extraordinary ,God-send— nothieg less than the petrified, iossilized—possibly pre-hietoric—body of a linmaniaeing, certainly two thousand years old and for aught we know, twenty tbsousand. I dare say you think, reader. lam jo- king,but the fact is neverbiaelesaautrueseehat Isaac Josses. the miner, lived in a ,cave,—a ,portion of which ,cave, you can see, if you wish it—Land had a prolific family of young bantlingin it—sse equally undosabtedfact likewise. This is &ow the thing happened. One day, deanc Jones, and his cave family being hungry—,they were very often iso if (Deport, Apeaks true—lsaac started in quest et wild rabbit, up, high up, onthe mountain. This was a favourite and cheap .obgect of food with the wild young Joneses. Al about 400 feet from the level of the sea, Jones cams Across a regular colony ,oi the rabbit species, and set out in pursuit of them. 'They were quick-footed, but Sio was Isaac. Isaac tlaought ;he had nearly got one of them, when, bounce, in they went into a small aperture in the mountain side—a kind of cave-hole or entrance, which even Law the miner had never yet atioticed. Isaac determined not to be baulked. Besides, his cave-children were , hungry—and their mother also—so he made his way, tooth and nail, to the precipitous rather inac- cessible spot where these succulent and intended living materials of his cavedinner had taken refege, The entrance to the cave was narrow, and Isaac Jones had to crawl into it serpent-like—flat on his hands and belly. This was the way he advanced for about 20 yards. When he bad got beyond that distance, dark as it was, Isaac'e expeiienced eye eould clearly discern that there was a larger cave, Of probably several caves, before him. IS'aac, how- ever, having neither matches, lampasor candle with him, did not think it wise to proceed further—on that day at least—so leaving the rabbits to make their escape, out crawled Isaac Jones just as he had entered, as flat as any crawling reptile in the Creation ever crawled. But Isaac Jones, though he had lost his rabbits, thought he had at least found a mysterious place worth looking at —a place of which neither he nor any human being around him knew anything. So, next day, stealthily armed with a torch, matches, and sundry useful implements, off starts Isaac Jones again to the spot of his previous day's scramble. Into the cave once more crawls Isaac. Now he lights his torch, and proceeds onwards. Gracious Providence! whose will it is, from time to time, to rake up objects that have been buried for ages. Can it possibly be? Isaac sees before him —partly imbedded in the solid lime-stone and partly in stet- actitic and stalagmitic matter—how shall I have courage to say it? Isaac sees the petrified body of a human being—nothing less? There was the skull projecting from the rock, with a perfect row of large white teeth, glittering in the torch light—not a single tooth missing. The thing was grim enough to terrify the boldest, and Isaac was at first, they tell us, dumbfounded, panic-stricken and half petri- fied himself at the sight of it, But Isaac soon recovered and fond as he was of gathering queer stones and fossils, he knew full-well, this time, be had found "a queer stone" and no mistake—one well worth hammering at. We cannot suppose that Isaac knew he had discovered a possible "pre-historic man !" whieh some of the learned assert it to be—a relic which ought to have immortalised the finder, and would have done so, had the finder been a Roderick Mur- chisan, a Dr. Lyon Playfair, or a Charles Lyall, instead of a poor, simple, hungry Welsh miner, the inhabitant of a mere Gogarth cave. Isaac Jones went home again, then returned to the cavern, tak- ing his mining tools with him and began his work keeping the matter meanwhile secret. Isaac was wise and Welshman enough for that. But Isaac did his work clumsily and rudely. He got it is true, by aid of hammering and cutting, a large fragmsnt of the lime stone with the skull intact and part of the clavicles, arm-bones, thigh-bones, ribs, etc., with its—but he shattered, oh ! the Vandal! most unques- tionably, various other parts and portions of this petrified treasure, little imagining the amount of injury he was doing. To Isaac, the discovery was a petrified skeleton—nothing more. He, unlearned fellow as he was, had no notion of the l'al,ronie period or the rest. However, what he could take and get, he did, and in order to remove and carry home even that—for the block broken from the solid rock was of tolerable magnitude—he had to widen the entrance to the cave, which took him some days likewise and cost him no end of trouble and labour. At last, however, out came the huge stone, with the fossilized skull and part of the body in it. "Nobody Knows Who " was the quaint name Isaac gave it—and down, down the moun- tain side, Isaac rolled "Mr. Nobody Knows Who" from "The Dead Man's Cave," as he called it, to the entrance of his own cave—the Gogarth Cave, where he and his cave-children were living, and while their father was engaged excavating petrified skeletons—still, I fear, hungering. There this treasure of treasures remained a considerable time, till some wide-awake person saw it, bargained for it, and finally gave thirty golden sovereigns for it. Issac was now a rich man, but somehow his riches soon vanished, and before long he was no better off than he had been when he had probably never touched a golden sovereign in his life or dreamt he would possess one. However, out of that treasure trove, he managed to buy materials to build the shed on the mountain .side--where his wife and daughter now sell the refreshing beverages I have before alluded to. He also constructed a kind of primitive museum, where he kept some of the wonders he has excavated from time to time, and ' which if it still exists, I recommend you, reader, should you ever go to Llandudno, to visit. It has (or had) its curiesities—but the greatest curiosity— the Cave hermit and eight of his Cave children— have left this earth; the remaining few, those who are still living, you may see for nothing.

A ROMANTIC SA_ tliss Frith, the daughter of the distinguished sends to the Toronto " Week" an interesting incident in the early career of Mr. Millais. It is re- lated by her father, and runs thus:—" At the Artists' Benevolent Fund dinner, the other day, where Millais was in the chair, he told us something that had happened to him when he was a boy,which I don't think has ever been in print. When Millais wasl ainting the 'Ferdinand and Ariel,' a dealer who -saw it said if, when it was finished. he liked it as much as he did then, he would buy it for .ElOO. Millais was jubilant, lie was living with his father , and mother, and as they were badly off, the money which, they made up their minds was quite secure, they anticipated, and the greater part was spent. At last IFerdinand was finished—do you recollect ; it? It, was painted when Millais was twenty, in '49, in 'hie pre-Raphaelite days, and was exhibited with 'ale!, of his others some years ago in Bond-st. —and the dealer was asked to come. But it was no good. promised when I was here before to have the picture if I liked it,' he said. But I don't like it, and I won't buy it,' and off he went. When the anxious Old, people were told in the other room you can imagine their distress. There was nothirg to be done 'bet to retrench. So 'Furnished Apart- ments' was-written out on a card and wafered to the front parlour window, and the family sat down • to wait fore? lodger who was to mend their broken fortunes by helping with the rent. A week or two after thie another dealer dropped into the painting room, bringing with him an old gentleman in a blue coat and brase-buttons. Millais showed them what he was doing, ,sod the strange old gentleman listened to the story.of the disappointment, looked atten- tively at the '-Ferdinand' on the easel, and seemed , to know a good deal about pictures, and to care for them. To Millais he gave some kindly advice and finished by pulliog a book out of his pocket, a book he particuiariprecommended to young artists. Pll give you this (copy,' he said' if you wilt promise to read it. And if you will fetch me pen and ink t'll write yottralaraei in it.' So the old gentleman xi the blue coat amblrass buttons took the volume r,to a side-table in -the kpainting-room, wrote in it, ,ftad brought it back•to_Millais. "Mind you read it, now; mind you -read it; it will do you good,' he kept on repeating. As Milieu; was letting them out of the front door the dealer contrived to whisper that his eompanion was Mr. Ellison—the Mr. Ellison, by tbe way, who afterwards left pie- tures to the Fitzwilliamlituseum in Cambridge. So Mitiais on returningrto•hisswork opened the book which had been so ihighly recommended by this judge of art, whose name of.course he knew, and as he opened the covert there fell out a cheque for I 1.50 guineas, signed by TElliscn, for the' Ferdinand! There's a delightful surprising way of selling a pic- ture. !Do you know wthat MiKais declares was the firetthing he did after telling his people? From the window he unwafered that 'Furnished Apart- metrta',card and tore it e:;-and since that day he has never had occasion -to ,call in the help of lodgers.

div.p: TETE EX k NTINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 23, 1890.
IREITAS.

A daottardly attempt was mactle early on Wednesday morning to wreck a train on tbe Dublin and Wicklow Railway, near Dalkey. The misweant had fastened a chair to a rail, nnut the engine cut ttiii.e obstruction in two, and went on in.safety. THE ARKLOW HARBOUR SCHEME.

The Atlilow— Town Commissioners.on Tuesday accepted the offer of Mr. Jackson. secretary to the Treasury, of a free grant of £3.,U0 for the completion of Arklow Her- our, provided the Commissioners will guarantee a like amount.

AN ORfiNGE RIOT IN TYRONE. Serious rioting is reported at Stewartstown, ,county Tyrone. An Grange drumming band visited the town and *necked the Cattsctlic school and houses of Catholic inhabitants. There Malt renewal of rioting at night, when missiles were freely thrown. Several Caltholic houses were wrecked, and the town kept hi an uproar for an hour. Several persons were sentenced to a month's Imprison- ment each at Arklow, onTlaursday, for taking part in " religious " riots in that town. In the police court one of the defendants tried to assault a Protestant clergyman., and for a time the greatest excitement prevailed, with every prospect of a serious general disturbance. MURDER IN 1886. At Tralee, on Monday, after a private inquiry lasting over several weeks, Bartholomew Sullivan and Patrick Hackett were committed for trial at the Assizes, on a charge of having murdered Patrick Flahive, at Heirhill. Ballyheicue, in August, 1886. Flahive was returning from cutting corn on an evicted farm, whcn he was way- laid and shot.

SAD DROWNING CASES ON THE IRISH COAST. Drowning accidents are reported from parts of the north of Ireland. On Monday a young French lady, who was governess in the family Of Mr. J. Blakiston Houston, was drowned at Ballywater. A sailor named Scott was drowned in Dundrum Bay, on the county Down coast. Four young ladies, who were bathing at Portrush, county Antrim, were caught by the current, An excit- ing scene ensued, and eventually the ladies were rescued by the exertions of Mr. Wm. M'Alister. "BRUSHING" A POLICEMAN.

Lord Chief Justice O'Brien, sitting in the Four Courts, Dublin, on Thursday, granted an absolute order for a mandamus to compel Messrs. Shannon and Erwin,R.M,'s, to state a ease for the opinion of the Exchequer Division concerning the sentence of fourteen days' imprisonment passed on Mr. Gill, civil engineer' Tipperary, for an alleged assault on a policeman by "brushing" hi in with his shoulder as they passed each other in the street. The Crown did not oppose, and it was stated that Mr. Gill would be immediately discharged from custody.

We have had three of these visita- tions in eleven years—in 1879, in 1885, and now in 1890. The present attack on the crop promises to be even more destructive -than that of t 1879. Mr. Davitt writes suggesting that something should be done at once towards replacing the blighted potato by such other vegetables as will make some sort of food between now and March. Surely (he says) there are eatable and nourishing roots, such as broccoli and cab- bage, that could be at once planted and made to pro- duce some kind of nourishment by the spring of 1891. He advises local consultation between priests, Protestant ministers, and others.

ANOTHER NEW CROSS MYSTEBY. Details are given of another New Cross mystery in con- nection with which the names of Dr. Townsend and his wife—the latter of whom was found dead the other week in company with Dr. De la Motte—are given in some of the London papers. A gentleman named Hart died sud- denly in June last, the cause of depth being believed to be a fall downstairs. Re was frequently visited by Dr. Townsend, and was also acquainted with Mrs. Townsend, and owing to several anonymous communications re- ceived by the coroner, it has been deemed desirable to obtain from the Home Office an order for the exhumation of the body.

div.head: BRUNNER, MOND, AND CO.
div.p: BRUNNER, MOND, AND CO.
HALF YEARLY MEETING.

The nineteenth half-yearly meeting of the share- holders of Messrs. Brunner, Mond, and Co., Limited, alkali manufacturers, Winnington, was held at the Law Association Rooms, Liverpool, on Monday. Mr. John Crosfield, the Chairman of the Board of Direc- tors, presided, and there were amongst others pre- sent—Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., Mr. E. Milner, Dr. Hewitt, Messrs. IL Brunner,J. P. Brunner, C. M. Holland, C. J. Galloway, Jones, L. B. Walls, W. Anderson, Barclay, A. Fletcher, T. W. Read, C. Griffiths, White, T. H. Forgan (secretary), Sze. The Secretary having read the notice convening the meeting, The Chairman said that the directors had much plea- sure in presenting to the shareholders another satisfac- tory balance sheet, lie moved the following resolution : —" That the directors' report and statement of accounts be adopted, and that a dividend be paid the holders of the preference shares at the rate of seven per cent. per annum on the amount paid up on such shares-; and that a dividend be paid to the holders of the ordinary shares attire rate of thirty per cent. per annum on the amount paid up on such shares, free of income tax, for the half year ended 30th June, 1890." This was seconded by Mr. Galloway, and unanimously carried. The directors' report, which was taken as read,appeared in the " Examiner" last week. The balance sheet and profit and loss account show a balance to the credit of profit and loss account on the working ef the half-year of £129,691 111 s. lid., which, with the amount of £13,305 16s. lid., brought forward from the previous half-year, makes a total of £142,997 16s. The directors propose to deal with the above balance as follows :—Dividesd on the preference capital, at 7 per cent, per annum, £12,035 6s. ed.; dividend on the ordinary capital, at 30 I per cent, per annum, £88,125; amount to be written off patents account, £2,500; amount to be placed to sus- pense account, £20,000; balance to be carried forward, £20,337 9s. 3.; total : £142,997 16s. The directors propose again to place to suspense ac- count a sum of £'20,000. Mr. J. T. Brunner, 11. P., moved "That Mr. Thomas ETungerford Forgan be and is hereby elected a director of the company." He proposed this resolution with very great pleasure—a pleasure upon which he need not dilate in the presence of gentlemen to whom Mr. Forgan was so well known. He heartily congratulated, not only his colleagues on the Board, but every share- holder in the company upon the motion he now made to the meeting. Mr. Milner, in seconding the resolution, assured the meeting that it was a pleasuee to the directors to know that Mr. Forgan was about to become a member of the Board. . .
The Chairman said he had much pleasure in putting the resolution. _ . _

The meeting adopted: the resolution unanimously, amid applause. Mr. J. T. Brunner then submitted for approval a reso- lution with regard to the mode and amount of the re- muneration to be paid to Mr. Edward Milner, Dr. David Basil Hewett, Mr. Gustav Jarmay, and Mr. T. H. For- gan, who are directors of the company, for services other than those of ordinary directors. He remarked that the shareholders had, at the many pleasant meet- ings they had attended, both by their action and by their silence, eloquently expressed their satisfaction with the management of the affairs of the company, and, he thought that, in view of that fact, he need not say any- , thing to recommend the resolution to their acceptance. Mr. Galloway seconded. He had been on the Board for several years, and he could say that there was no company withwhich he was acquainted that was so well and so energetically served by the officers as Brunner, Mond, and Co. (Hear, hear.) The resolution was unanimously carried. On the motion of Mr. J. T. Brunner, seconded by Mr. Anderson, Messrs. T. W. Read and Co., chartered accountants, j4iverpool, were re-appointed auditors for the current half-yeai, A vote of thanks havieg, on the proposition of Mr. Jones, seconded by Mr. Darcy, been given to the Chair- man, the meeting terminated. The directors in their report intimated that in the event of Mr. Forgan being elected a director, it was their intention to appoint Mr. Frederick William Brock as secretary of the company,

GREAT FIRES. TWELVE MONKS BURNED TO DEATH. A " Times " Vienna telegram states that a large ilre broke out a few days ago in the immense aggregation of buildings forming the monastry of Mount Athos. Several of the conventual houses, four churches, and two gran- ilries were destroyed, and about a dozen monks lost their lives. FIRE IN LONDON.--DAMAGE £27,000. A destructive fire broke out early on Saturday morning at the premises of Messrs. Thorley, cattle food makers, King's-cross London. The inflammable contents of the warehouses burnt fiercely, and floor after floor was at- tacked, the flames shooting up to a great height. The work of putting them out was very difficult, and it was 'early seen that the premises were doomed. The horses were safely got out of the stables, but no property was saved. It was some hours before the conflagration was subdued, and then the entire place was gutted. The 'loss which was insured against, is estimated at £27,000.

A' MANCHESTER TTIEATRE BURNED DOWN. The Queen's Theatre, Manchester, an old and well- known playhouse, was on Sanday destroyed by fire. Shortly after four o'clock in the afternoon some cleaners were at work in the theatre, when they discovered that some old property at the rear of the theatre was in flames. This consisted of a side block, not connected with the main building, but used by the theatre man- agement. Some effort was made to extinguish the fire by the people about the place, but without avail, and the fire brigade were apprised of the outbreak. They were at the time, unfortunately, chiefly engaged at another fire at a mill some distance away. Superintendent Toter, however, was on the spot, and everything possible was .lone to save the building. The roof fell in, and the centre part of the theatre was completely destroyed ' before the fire was extinguished. The stage portion was saved by the lowering of an asbestos curtain. Happily there was no loss of life. Mr. Pitt Hardacre, lessee of the theatre, was absent at Blackpool. The building was insured. MILL FIRE AT MILES PLATTING : DAMAGES £120,000. On Sunday morning the Manchester fire brigade were for many hours engaged in suppressing a most disastrous fire at Miles Platting. The cotton mills of Messrs. William Holland and Sons were the scene of the struggle, and before the contest could be decided damage was sustained to the extent, it is believed, of not less than £120,000. Messrs. Holland and Sons' mills—which bear the name of the Victoria Mills, and in which the business of cotton and worsted spinning is carried on—are situated at Miles Flatting. They form a long block of buildings, some 100 ft. or seven storeys in height. At the front is Varley-st., and immediately in the rear is the Rochdale Canal. There are also a number of sheds, used for weaving and other purposes, in close proximity to the main block of buildings. It appears that shortly after midnight of Saturday, as some engineers were at work in the engine-house, a lighted oil lamp was accidentally !icielc-id over. The flame came in contact with 'me fat and very rapidly spread, in spite of every 'effort the men could make to overcome it. An ifarm was raised, and pending the arrival of the isity fire brigades, the workmen on the spot, who have been trained to the use of the fire apparatus, attached jets to the mains and exerted themselves to the utmost. Ii was found impossible to beat down the flames. Owing td the high wind which prevailed, the jets of water were very much sprayed"; indeed, they were almost 'educed to vapour. The men were not altogether !successful in keeping the fire from the left half of the mill; the roof became ignited, but the flames did not spread beyond the top storey. During the entire day the jets and steamers were kept In use, and at a late hour on Sunday several of the firemen were still there. As already stated the damage is . estimated at £120,000. One-half the mill is entirely gutted. A considerable number of persons will be thrown out of employment in consequence. The property is insured in the London, Liverpool. and other offices. The mills were burnt down 17 years ago, and were then rebuilt on the most modern, and on what are known as fireproof principles.

div.head: LAEOUR AND CAPITAL
div.p: LAEOUR AND CAPITAL

THE PONTYPRIDD STRIKE. The strike at the Great Western Colliery, Pontypridd, concluded on Monday, when the 1,400 workmen returned to work. STRIKE OF RIVET MAKERS. The rivet makers in the Rowley, Blackheath, and Cradley Heath districts in Staffordshire have struck against a deduction in wages of from 5 to 10 per cent. SHIPPING STRIKE AT MELBOURNE. MELBOURNE, WEDNESDAY.—The wharf labourers have joined the strike of the marine officers and seamen at Sidney.. The number of men on strike. has reached 5,000. The despatch of the homeward mails is not interfered with. THE TILBURY DOCKS STRIKE. The representatives of the men who struck work at Tilbury Docks and Mr. Coton, acting superintendent of the docks, met on Wednesday evening to arrange a settlement of the dispute. An arranvment was arrived at whereby the company recognised the union men, and would employ them in preference to others, the discus- sion of Mr. Adam'sschetne to be left open. This arrange- ment was verbal only, and the men required a written agreement, which was refused. On Thursday morning a meeting was held outside the docks, and the arrange- ment arrived at was announced to the men, who were strongly advised to return to work. The men appeared to think that the dock officials were insincere, and alleged that on previous occasions they had broken faith. A show of hands far and against returning to work was made, and the great majority elected to stop out, and demand a definite arrangement. DOCK STRIKE ANNIVERSARY. On Sunday afternoon, a great demonstration of the organized labour trades, under the auspices of the Lon- don Trades Council, -took place in Hyde Park, to celebrate the first anniversary of the great dock strike in London last year. There were five platforms, the speakers in- cluding Mews. lalan Burns, Ben Tillett, and Tom Mann. The resolution which was adopted at all platforms ex- , pressed unbounded satisfaction at the solid advantages 'which had been derived from last year's strike, and ex- pressed the opinion that the strike failures sustained dur- ing the past year -were due to the supply of "blacklegs" obtained from the ranks of the unorganized and lowest paid. To cut off this source of supply, the resolution advocated the limitation of the hours of labour to a maximum of 48 per week. On Monday, the Dockers' Union sent in demands to the employers of unskilled labour at Southampton for a material rise in wages, the demand being for sixpence an hour and eightpence for , overtime. They have fixed Saturday next for the re- ceipt of replies. Mr. Sprow, on behalf of the London Dockers' Union, is conducting the agitation, and meet- ings are being organized. THE GREAT WELSH STRIKE. Traffic was resumed on all the Welsh railways on Sat- urday morning, and all the railway men, dockers, miners, and iron workers, numbering about 40,000 men, who were affected by the strike, have returned to work. , Thousands of tons of coal which were stocked along the colliery sidings in the Rhondda and Rhymney Valley were being carried off by the mineral trains. The mails which have been delivered by coach throughout the dis- turbed districts during the past week, were on Saturday conveyed by rail. The hitch in the construction of the agreement, which caused considerable excitement and anxiety is now adjusted. Both Mr. Inskip and Mr. Ilarford state that it was distinctly understood that 60 hours should form a week's work. The terms of the jaint agreement are briefly The The railway companies pay for at least a week's work of sixty hours. 2. The piloting and shunting day to he eleven hours, but six hours per week to be allowed each man. 3. Each signalman's day to Ze twelve hours, but twelve hours in each seven days to be allowed off. The railway men have received their strike pay from the amalgamated union r—Twelve shillings per week was given to klnion men, and is. per child, and half these amounts granted to non-union men and their families. A BRILLIANT Idea, try what' SUNLIGHT SOAP " will do next washing day.--Adtt. The Bank rate of discount has been reduced from 5 to 4 per cent. Mrs. Collins, wife of a dock labourer, living at Ber- mondsey, has been confined of three children, all of whom are doing well. Lord Tredegar has announced his intention of grant- ing a rent remission of 15 per cent, 0 the tenants of his Welsh estates for another year , SUPPOSED WRECK AND LOSS OF 25 LIV., The ship Assa,ye of Greenock, left London early M rebruarV for Nevi:Zealand. She made the run to the Equator in twenty three days, but as she has not since been heard of it is feared she has foundered with her crew of twenty-five. The Assaye was owned by Messrs. J. and IV. Stewart, Greenock, and was an iron vessel built in 1868. Vessels which left Great Britain about the same time report a terrific hurricane in June, and it is feared she then foundered. div.head: DESPERATE FIGHT IN A _ MENAGERIE
div.p: DESPERATE FIGHT IN A _ MENAGERIE

• WITH WOLVES. An exciting scene was witnessed on Monday evening at a menagerie at Ashton-under-Lyne fair ground. A lion-tamer named Lorenzo was going through a perform- ance with a pack of six wolves, when one of them sprang upon him and proceeded to worry him. Attend- ants outside the cage beat back the other five, and Porenzo had a desperate battle with his foe. Although badly bitten about the hands he succeeded in beating it off, and finished the performance.

div.head: FOUR YEAR OLD HOMICIDE.
div.p: A FOUR YEAR OLD HOMICIDE.

At an inquest held on a boy named Potter, at Stoke- on-Trent, on Tuesday, it transpired that on Saturday laat, Potter was playing near the canal, when a coin. panioni John Noakes, aged four years and a half, deliberately pushed him into the water and then went to Potter's mother, and told her what he had done. The Coroner stated that Noakes had pushed at least two other toys into the water previously, although neither of these were drowned. On the jury's recommendation the Coroner promised to write to the Home Secretary for special powers to control Noakes.

div.head: SHOEBURYNESS MEETING.
div.p: SHOEBURYNESS MEETING.

At the Shoeburyness meeting the Bth Lancashire, third and'fourth detachments, under Sergeant Smyth, Liverpool, have been awarded National Artillery badges for the highest score in the repository competition-195 points, time 24 mins. 34 secs. At the artillery volunteer meeting at Shoeburyness, on Thursday, in the Royal Artillery competition with the ten-inch gun, the first prize was won by the Royal Marine Artillery, and the second prize by the School of Gunnery. In the volunteer competition with 16-pounders for both weeks, the first prize of £2O is taken by the First Detachment 2nd Kent Plumstead), with 51 points; the second prize by the Third Detachment 2nd Durham (Sea- ham), with 48 points ; and third prize by the Seventh Detachment lst.Susses (Brighton), with 47 points.

div.head: ACCIDENT TO A ritRA.CHITTIST.
div.p: ACCIDENT TO A ritRA.CHITTIST.

EXCITING SCENE AT CREWE. On Wednesday evening Professor Higgins and Miss Devoy attempted a balloon ascent at Crewe, which some 50,000 people had assembled to witness. The moment the word was given to "let go" a strong wind drove the balloon with much force against some palisadings, and a great sensation was manifested as the laay was seen to fall, while Higgins was struggling to disentangle the netting. By some means the balloon got away with Higgins alone, leaving Miss Devoy lying upon the ground. The spectators were reassuren on finding that the lady parachutist had fortunately escaped with nothing more serious than a few cuts and bruises. The balloon ascended at a great rate to an altitude of nearly 10,000 ft: Higgins then let go, and came safely down in Lord Crewe!! Park, and received a perfect ovation on returning.

div.head: SUPPOSED DEATH_THROUGH EATING
div.p: SUPPOSED DEATH_THROUGH EATING

TOFFY. An inquest was held on Wednesday, by Mr. W. T. husband, at the Warrington Police Station, regard- ing the death of a girl named Susannah Flynn, six years of age, which took place last Sunday. Dr. Peacock, who was the first witness Called, said that on Saturday evening about six o'clock he was called to see the deceased, and found that she was apparently suffering from gastro-enteritis. Ile asked what she had been eating, And he was told that she had been eating toffy. On the 19th he made a post-mortem examination, when he found inflammatory Patches on the coating of the stomach, the duodenum being also somewhat inflamed. He took away the stomach, the duodenum, the liver and kidney, for examination, and they were now sealed up in the jars produced. He did not find anv trace of the irritant, but he knew that arsenic was used extensively in colouring sweets. The Coroner: Was ' there anything you saw while the child was alive that would give you any cause of suspicion? Dr. Peacock: Not. the slightest; the parents appeared to be very anxious about the child. It was possible that the irritation might have come on naturally, but it was more likely to have been caused by something the child had eaten. He had not been able to find any of the toffy that it was said the girl had eaten. Mary Flynn, the mother of the deceased, said she lived at 24, Cockhedge-lane, and her husband was a general labourer. She saw the child eating some toffy on Friday evening. It was white toffy, and the child told her she had bought a half-penny packet. Witness told her not to eat it, and the child came in afterwards and said she had given it to another child. The rear she told her to throw the toffy away was that it ' gave her the toothache. The deceased began tobe ill mariday evening. The child was insured by witness in the Prudential,and she expected to get 1.0. She had been insured ever since she was a fortnight old. She had another child which would be nine in November. Catherine Corbett, mother of the last witness, and living next door to her, said she had also told the child to throw away the toffy that she was eating on Friday night. This was all the evidence called, and the deputy Coroner suggested that an open verdict should be re- turned. The police could take any further action they liked, and they could have the stomach analysed. A verdict was then returned to the effect that the child had died from gastro-enteritis, but how, that was set up there was no evidence to show.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.

THURSDAY.— Before his Honour Judge Nonlkea+ THE CAUSE Mar contained two default sumo- monsea. eight adjourned plaints, 48 original plainta,--- and. 39 judgment summonses. I Cram AGAINST A CYCLIST.—The case -in which S. , Walton, cab proprietor, CroSs-lane, Earlestown, was the plaintiff and Henry Millar, cabinet makers' apprentice, 40, Bewsey-road, was the defendant, was resumed. The claim was for £1.2 damages for injuries to a horse, harness, wagonette, and for loss of ser- vices of a horse, occasioned by the alleged negligent riding of a bicycle by the defendant on the 26th May. Mr. H. J. Lougton, solicitor, appeared on behalf the plaintiff, and Mr. A. Browne represented the defendant. This claim arose out of an accident which took place at Preston Brook on the date named. Some I trippers from Earlestown were being conveyed in a I wagonette from Earlestown to Frodsham, and when at I the foot of the hill at Preston Brook thedefendant and a [ companion named Lawton rode down the hill on bicycles. In passing the vehicle defendant was thrown from his machine,which was then run into by one of the horses and the damage sued for thereby caused. The witnesses called for the plaintiff were Thomas Hughes, Frederick Boughton,the driver of the wagonette, John Taylor, shopkeeper, Ashton; John Mather, collier. Ashton; John Blinston, collier, Ashton; and Thomas Pope, blacksmith, Earlestown. It was alleged by these witnesses that although there was plenty of room to pass the wagonette on the right side of the road defendant attempted to pass on the left, and this was the cause of the accident.—Henry Millar, the defendant said he was a apprentice at Messrs. Garnett and Sons, cabi- net makers, and his wages under his indentures were 7s. a week. The bicycle he was riding on the occasion in question was a 521 n. ordinary. At the top of Preston _Brook hill he commencea to: go down slowly, but towards the liOffoin he viaii-joink rather-fast. He - was riding with his feet on the pedals, and not with his legs thrown over the handles of the bicycle as had been alleged; he was, in fact, not able to ride a machine in that fashion. At the bottom of the hilt he saw the wagonette at the right hand side of the road, and some of those with it were on the same side of the road drinking beer. He therefore passed the 'bus on the left hand side of the road, and had got about twenty yards past it when the bicycle caught the fla,g, and he was thrown off. The bicycle ran along the road about thirty yards and then -fell in the middle of the road, the horses running into it. Evidence for the de- - fence was given by Thomas Lawton,saddler, of Warring- ton ; James Wilkinson, Albert Webb, and other witnesses from Preston Brook, and ultimately his Honour returned a verdict for the defendant,on the ground that there had been contributory negligence on the part of the plaintiff. JUDGMENT AGAINST A Sr. HELENS SOLICITOR.—A. judgment summons was heard against Mr. H. L. Riley, solicitor, St. Helens, the plaintiff being James Henry Fos- ter, publican, who was represented by Mr. T. Gorse, agent. The claim was for money lent. In order had been made against defendant in December last, but there was still an unpaid balance of £6 12s. His Honour - made an order for the money to be paid in two months, defendant to be committed for 40 days in default.

div.head: BOATING DISASTER OFF CONWAY..
div.p: BOATING DISASTER OFF CONWAY..
LOSS OF EIGHT LIVES.

On Wednesday afternoon, two Norwegian timber vessels were towed out of Conway in ballast. The second of the two, the Maria, left about half-past two, and took _ on board William Jones, pilot, of Conway, aged about 50, married, with two children, and three of his assist- ants, viz., William Evans, married, no children; Robert • Evans, son of the harbourmaster, of Conway, single; and Edward Pullin, also of Conway, aged thirty-three; married, two children. - There were also on board Mr. C. Greene, attached to a dental hospital in Birmingham, and another medical gentleman, who had been staying In.• a little building on the Conway quay, belonging to • Captain Roberts, of Conway, which they had fitted up • as a residence. With the two doctors two young ladies • also went on board the Maria. The pilot boat was eas pected back at Conway on Wednesday afternoon., about four o'clock, but as she did not turn up great uneasiness began to be felt, especi— ally as there was a somewhat rough sea on, . and telegrams were at once despatched to Llandudno,. Beaurnans, and other likely places for intelligence of the • missing boat, but no news was received. About five o'clock on Thursday morning, the body of William Evans,. who when last seen was seated in the pilot boat, which, was towing after the barque, was found on the west side of the Great Ormes Head, together with his boat. Telegraphing later a correspondent says :—The body of Mr. C. Greene, of Birmingham, has just been brought ashore at Conway, having been found floating in thefl estuary about a mile and a half from the harbour. The- quay at Conway is crowded with people, among whorcs axe several weeping women and children. A later telegram says it is now believed to be beyond doubt that the whole of the eight persons were drowned. It appears they were seen leaving the barque when she was off Conway on Thursday morning. The ladies whe were in the boat, which was evidently swamped in the rough sea, were Fanny and Beatrice Varcoe, of Stafford. A third body has been brought ashore. STATEMENT OF AN EYE-WITNESS.

A correspondent telegraphs :—There is no hope now that any of the eight persons named above have been saved. The two ladies proved to be the Misses Varcoe. of Hanley, Staffordshire, who had been staying at Deganwy with their brother for the last two months, during which time it is presumed they made the acquaint- ance of Dr. Green and his friend. Mr. Charles Ellis, son of Major Ellis, said that about four o'clock on Wed- nesday afternoon while driving with his father over Penmaenlach Tunnel' he saw the boat full of people, and with two sails set. He turned round to reply to a ques- tion by Major Ellis, and when he looked again the boat was nowhere to be seen, but on looking more intently he could see a number of people in the water, and could distinguish what he took to be a pink dress of a lady. One of the ladies wore a pink dress. The barque and tug were then too far away to have been able to see the accident, and s 9 of course the struggling people were left to their fate. It is stated Dr. Green must have SWUM about two miles before he succumbed. Mr. Ellis stated that be thought at the time there was too much sail on the boat for such a sea, and with so many people in her. At about half-past eight on' Thursday night, by a pre-arranged signal, news was received at Conway that another body—that of one of the younshidies--had been found, and quite half the population of Conway crowded the beach to watch its arrival. About nine O'clock the boat touched the shore, where Police-constables John Griffiths and Parry were in readiness with a stretcher, and the body was conveyed to an out-building on the quay, where that of Mr. Greene had already been placed. Dr. Jones, of Conway, who was in attendance, examined the face of the young lady, and found that the two eyelids were much cut and bruised. Nothing was found in the pockets to establish identity, with the ex- ception of a letter dated from Shelton, February 22, and beginning "My dear niece, Folly." The young lady was dressed in white, with a blue jacket having brass but- tons. Her hair appeared to be jet black. The body was found by one of the search parties on the bar at the mouth of the river, close by where the body of Mr. Greene was picked up.

Seeing that disease germs are so prevalent in tha, body, aird'yet aa sprule absent from.the blood, the questions, for bacteriologists has been—How dece- it hamen that these organisms-. are, generallyi speaking, kept out of the blood?' The answer given—a, conclusion arrived at but recently—may be describodi as another fairy tale_of science. Sir- HENRYI saya:!-- Underthe eye and in the hands of a Russian physic., logist working in Pasteur's laboratory in Paris, the secret of:this impotence of the microbe to pene- trate into the blood has been divulged. For Metsc- hnikofffhas•proved that certain cells contained in the blood of all the higher animals, termed phagocp• tee, identical with the well-known white blood- corpuscles, being endowed with the power of inde- pendent motion, not only wander inside but even make their way outside the tissue, and, tnir.3bilt dietu, pursue,. devour, and digest any bacilli, whether poisonous or not, with which they come into contact..

Hitherto it has been a common observation that the reduction in the number of red blood-corpuacles was indicative of reduced vitality, and iron, in me form or another, is frequently prescribed as a means of remedying the defect: Little attention has,,comparatively speaking, been paid to the white bload-corpuscles; but it would now seem thaittheir oats is of the highest importance. They might be described as the standing army of the be ex- cept for the fact that they are never allowed La stand ; they are incessantly at war with the common enemy—the thousands of bacteria that are ever seeking to penetrate the blood and set up disease. The protective organisms (the white blood-corpuscles) are termed phagocytes,. and we are told that—

The medical journals contain vivid accounts of their doings, with drawings of photographs, showing ;the enclesed and in some cases the half-digested bacterium. The wandering cells are, however, not particular as to what they eat, for we find that they swallow particles of carbon or other mineral matter with which they come in contact. This accounts for the fact that the interior portions of the lungs of all adult persons, whether inhabitants of our smoky towns or not, are blackened by particles of carbon, whilst those of young children are free from such blackening.

It comes to this that, as our phagocytes are the fighting organisms for the defence of the body, they should be kept in good fighting condition. It is not too much to say that a war is constantly going on in the body of man between the armies

of health and the armies of disease; and that it is the duty of man to assist in keeping down and keeping out the invading hosts. In considering how this could best be done, we get on familiar ground again. The purer the air, the purer the water, and the purer the food, the smaller is the number of the disease germs which are taken into the body. A dnnk of polluted water may mean the introduction of such a horde of vil- lainous bacilli as will completely overcome the guardian phagocytes, and the result is impure blood, disease, and perhaps death. The same thing may happen through eating bad food, or breathing foul air. Hence the need of fresh air in living rooms, for the oxygen of the atmosphere is a destroyer of a certain class of disease germs. Hence the recuperative influence of a sea voy- age, or of residence at the seaside, where the

air is less contaminated; and hence, above all, the need of cleanliness; for dirt is simply another name for piled-up disease germs. Dl9 ease and dirt thus become convertible terms. Crowded dwellings, stifling courts, narrow streets, and unpaved yards are nurseries of disease ; and the result is seen in the fact that, while children of the poor are as a rule as strong at. birth , as the children of the rich, they die at ther rate of two to one as compared with children whose parents can commandgood food,wide streets,roomY' dwellings, paved yasds, and well-flushed drains.
