div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

The members of the Wirral Farmers' Club are disposed to consider themselves ill-used, because objection is taken to cattle " only slightly affected" by tuberculosis. But where is the line to be drawn, and who is to draw it? There should be no traffic in diseased meat •it should be destroyed. Nobody wants to be "only slightly" poisoned.

A case of Asiatic cholera has been discovered in the East End of London; but prompt measures have been taken to prevent the spread of the disease. The victim is a coal-trimmer, and has recently arrived from Calcutta. The ravages of the dread malady have been something terrible in Spain, as many as sixteen hundred deaths being recorded in one week.

It would seem that the outbreak in Spain is traceable to excavations on the spot where t?",?,Ple were buried who died of cholera in 046 -L5. Disease spores retain their vitality, in , certain circumstances, for long periods. There are cases on record of sr ores found in the chalk formation developing into living bac- teria on being placed in suitable media. It iS not sufficient, therefore, to bury subjects of contagion after death. They should, for the benefit of the living, be cremated.

A month in gaol is little enough for the young savage of the name of Wynne who, on finding his advances unwelcome, proceeded to thump the -object of his attentions on the neck, and "knock her into the street in a senseless condition." Wynne has missed his way in Warrington; he should leave the country, and join the Indian braves who, when they want a wife, knock their lady love on the head with a club, and carry her off whilst she is senseless.

A little girl of six, living in Warrington, has lost her life presumably through eating toffy. The doctor's statement was that death was due to some irritant poison, and it is supposed that the poison Was taken into the system by means of the "sweets" he had been eating. "Sweets to the sweet" by all raeans—except when they are poisonous. it is a good rule to avoid coloured confectionery; but children will be children, and they like to have the eye tickled as well as the palate.

"Truth" thus girds at the Liberal-Unionists---- "Whenever a Liberal-Unionist M.P. is prepared to return to the fold, he ought not to be accepted " a candidate in the constituency where he has Wrought so much harm, but he should be required to come forward against a Ministerialist in some Tory stronghold, and to return with the scalp of that Ministerialist as a peace-offering." This is " Labby's " fun; we don't think, when the time tomee, he will be hard on the prodigals.

"The Welsh newspapers estimate the loss occa- sioned to the various industries in the principality through the strike to about half a million sterling." Just so ; but Ls a set-off against this, will some- body try to estimate the gain in shorter hours of work to the Welsh miners and railway men of this and of succeeding generations. It will have to be reckoned not by half millions, but by tens of millions Strike a balance of the result of the atrike, and it will be soon seen that it was worth striking for.

--- Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, expressed himself strongly, on Thursday, on the dangerous stairs which had resulted in more than one death stt Warrington. He said it was the duty of the Corporation to condemn such houses, if the owners Would not make them habitable; and we quite agree with him. . The law is found weak at times : but it often happens that the weakness is in those *who have to administer it. There is plenty of l'oom for enforcement of the precept that " pro- perty has its duties as well as its rights."

Secretary Blaine is making himself ridiculous in setting up a special claim on behalf of the United States for the fishery rights of Behring's Sea. When Russia set up a similar claim the then Secretary of the United States made short work of it, and his despatch on the subject is a weapon in the hands of the British Government. It is satisfactory to see that Lord Salisbury has ex- Pressed himself as willing to refer the dispute to arbitration. His lordship in this respect is follow- rig the precedent made by Mr. Gladstone in deal- ing with the Alabama claims.

The ideas about hell would appear to be as 11 timorous as the notions of heaven. In "The iiineteenth Century" Mr. James Mew describes the Hebrew hell. It is very like what Shakespeare calls the "prison house," with an average term of "twelve months." There is suspension of punish- ment "at prayer times, on the Sabbath, and the new moon." It is something to learn that " charity to the poor, by feeding them and otherwise, opens the doors of escape from hell." The charity must be shown on this side of the grave; so please to begin, you well-to-do sinners.

Shelley, in his parody of Wordsworth's "Peter 13ellr says : Hell is a city much like London— A populous and a smoky city; There are all sorts of people undone, And there is little or no fun done; Small justice shown and still less pity. tint the most stinging stanza runs as follows : And this is hell; and in this smother All are damnable and damned; Each one damning damns the other; They are damned by one another, By none other are they damned.

Too much tribute cannot be paid to the Character of the late Cardinal Newman • but it cannot be said that his theological subtleties have influenced thb views of the masses. He struggled Vith difficulties which do not seriously concern them; and which would not have seriously con- cerned him, if he had, in the first instance, been a curate with a small stipend and a large family. The Rev. John Yonao dealt with the life and work of the late Cardinal in a thoughtful and practical laanner in a discourse which he delivered, in Wycliffe church, on Sunday evening. We give a isununary of the sermon in another column.

4, The instances are numerous of miners who lose reir lives through breach of regulations which ;arye been framed for their special protection. 'nexnas Toft, aged forty-three, was killed at Edge- Peen Collieries the other night through proceeding prepare a second shot when the first shot ap- Deared to have failed. The first shot finally ex- ploded, with the result that Toft lost his life. It le stated that he had been warned against this practice a few hours before the fatal accident. It a mistaken kindness simply to warn him. He 'mould have been suspended for breaking the rule„.

The Rev. C. F. Aked, who has been pastor alike ' or the Baptists of St. Helens and Earlestown, is Rciug to Liverpool. Ho is noted for his plain BPeaking ; and keeps it up to the last. He said, °o Monday night, that there might be a splendid church at Earlestown "if two or three people sup- to be lc viers in the Church were hanged, drawn, and quartered." This was meant only, of course, in a Pickwickian sense. It would be in- terestina to know what the " supposed leaders ~ d'o with the pastor, if they could have their I'VEI37 With him. If they did not roast him, they !night make it hot for him. Well, well ; let brotherly love continue.
RUNCORN CO-OPERATIVE S3CIETY'S TRIP.

The annual exclusion in connection with the Runcorn Co-operative Society took place on Monday, when about 800 persons travelled by special train to Southport, where a 'pleasant day was spent. The arrangements had been admirably made by Mr. Thomas Riley.
HAYSTACK ON FIRE AT RUNCORN.

On Thursday a haystack belonging to Mr. E. Tuckey, boat owner, &c., Runcorn, was destroyed by fire on the farm of Mr. Ackerley, Higher Runcorn. The damage, which is estimated at about £6o,is covered by insurance. The stack is one of last years and it is a mystery how the hay became ignited.

RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH. The children attending the Sunday School had their annual treat on Wednesday, when about 500 were con- veyed by special train to Frodsham, and spent a plea- sant afternoon on Overton Hills. A capital tea was provided at Mersey View and the general arrangements were well carried out by Mr. John Littler.
SUCCESS OP A. WIDNES ATHLETE.

At Rochdale Cricket Club athletic sports on Wednes- day, Samuel Morris of Widnes, won the Northern Coun- ties Athletic Association's Championship in the quarter mile hurdle race in the quick time of 5945 sec., which forms a new record for the race. Shaw, of New Zealand, who started favourite for the race was two yards behind, second. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notlee.—J. &W. DUTTON'S Sankey. st., Warrington.—Advt. SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A NAVVY AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, before Mr. Chas. Reynolds, Leyland Haynes, a Ship Canal navvy, was brought up on remand, charged with having on the 17th inst., indecently assaulted Maud Popple, 10 years of age, on Runcorn Marsh. After hearing the girl's state- ment, the magistrate said he could not send the case for trial and the prisoner was discharged.
DEE- HORSE AMBI7LANCE-FOR WIDNES.

The com—mit—tet- appointed to expend the funds raised by the cricket match,Tradesmen v. Police, in the purchase of a horse ambulance for the town, have given the con- tract for the construction of the machine to Mr. Tyrer, of Tuebrook. The price fixed upon is £7O, and the com- mittee will thus have left remaining £3O, which, it is suggested, should be utilised in obtaining a number of hand ambulances, to be placed in convenient positions in the town. Probably this idea will be carried out. UMBRELLAS BE-COVERED at the shortest notice.-4. & W. DUTTON's Sankey-st., Warrington.-:Advt.

The German Emperor is "going it" as the father of his people. It is stated that In all the large towns where there are manufactories belonging to the Government, and; of course, especially in the capital itself, there is to be a careful examination of children employed by the State. And where these are found to be delicate, or not up to the mark, they are to be sent to the shores of the North Sea for a fortnight's sea air. Journey, board, and lodgings are to be defrayed by the Government and the necessary steps are to be taken without further delay." The dry-as-dust political economists will have some objection to take to this new way of spending the nation's money; but it is surely better to employ it in this manner than in big guns and enormous armies.

div.head: DROPPED DEAD AT RUNCORN.
div.p: DROPPED DEAD AT RUNCORN.

On Tuesday evening while a fight was taking place between a drunken tnan and woman in Cooper-st., a woman named Ann Kennedy, who was watching, was seen to stagger and fall to the ground. She was imme- diately attended to but life was found to be extinct. Mr. R. Dobson, the deputy coroner, held an inquest on the body on Wednesday night. Dr. Robinson,who had made a post mortem, informed the jury that death was the result of fatty degeneration of the heart, and a verdict accordingly was returned.

div.head: SUCCESS OF LOCAL PIGEON FANCIERS.
div.p: SUCCESS OF LOCAL PIGEON FANCIERS.

At the usual meeting of the Liverpool Homing Society, held at the club rooms, Great Charlotte-st., on Thurs- day evening, the secretary, Mr. A. Malins, reported par- ticulars concerning the young bird race, which had taken place from Gloucester the previous day. It appeared that 330 birds competed. The weather being unfavour- able, the rate of speed was nothing out of the common. The first six prize winners were :-1, Orme, Runcorn ; 2, Woods, Ditton ; 3, Cotsworth, Ditton ; 4, Wilkinson, Ditton ; 5, Bower, Southport; 6, Orme, Runcorn. MAIL CARTS for children.—Garland, Ironmonger, Warring- ton and Earlestown.—Advt. MAINTENANCE OF A WIFE IN RAINHILL ASYLUM.

Before Messrs. Gossage and Deacon, at Widnas Petty Sessions on Thursday, Charles Ray, was summoned by the Prescot Guardians for £2 19s. 6d., the arrears of an order made by the Court. The relieving officer, (Mr. Treacy)said some time ago the defendant was ordered to pay 3s. 6d. per week towards the maintenance of his wife Mary, who is an inmate of Rainhill asylum. The defendant was earning 265. per week. The defendant said he could not pay 3s. 6d. as he had a lot of debts, which were contracted during his wife's illness to pay.— The Bench ordered him to clear off the arrears and costs in three months or he would be sent to gaol.

RUNCORN WESLEYAN BOYS' SCHOOL. The friends of education will be pleased to find that Brunswick Day School still stands to the front, the result of the recent examinations being highly satisfactory. From the drawing report of the above school which is just to hand, we are pleased to notice that the excellent grant has again been awarded. This must be very grati- fying to the managers, particularly as this is the only school in the town, which has up to the present, obtained this distinction. The importance of drawing as a subject of training, will be seen from the fact that under the new code it has been made compulsory, it having hitherto been optional. At the same examination, Mr. W. Epps obtained a first-class in second grade geometrical draw- ing, while Messrs. W. Cook and J. 0. Dobson passed in second grade perspective. Mr. Benjamin Crosby, the headmaster, is to be congratulated on this satisfactory state of things, as it is to his unremitting attention that this desirable object has been attained. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.--J. & W. DUTTON'S Bankey-st., Warrington.—Adet.
EXTRAORDINARY CLAIM AGAINST A WIDNES CAR PROPRIETOR. _ .

Yesterday at Widnes-dOUnii-dmirt, before his honour Judge Shand, • Peter Boggino, tobacco merchant, of Liverpool, who resides at Gateacre, sued J. H. Lee, cab proprietor of Widnes, for the sum of £4 the value of a coat alleged to have been damaged through the defend- ant's neglect. Mr. A. E. Smith, jun., appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Knowles defended. It appeared that on the 6th May, the plaintiff was walking along Water- loo-road, when ram began to fall and he hailed one of Mr. Lee's cabs which was passing at the time. The plaintiff opened the cab door himself and jumped in. The window strap button was broken, and this caught the plaintiff's coat and tore it.—The defence was that the vehicle was a superior cab, used chiefly for Mr. Gossage and Mr. Timmins, and that the button was all right when turned out of the yard.. Dr. Hutchinson deposed that he had used the cab .just prior to the plaintiff, and he did not notice anything wrong with the button. The contention was that the plaintiff must have broken it himself .—His Honour held that there had been no proof of neglect, and gave judgment for the defendant with costs. CRITCHLEY'S Tailoring meets the times.— Advt.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, AUGUST 23, 1890.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, AUGUST 23, 1890.

BRUTAL ASSAULT ON AN OLD MAN AT BOLD. At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Joseph and Ellen Bather, husband and wife, of Bold, were sum- moned for assaulting James Clare, a farm labourer, in their employ. Mr. Knowles prosecuted. On the morn- ing of the 12th inst., Clare,' who is an old man, com- plained that no:one had helped him to milk the cows,and as Mrs. Bather cursed him very much, he left the house. In the afternoon he called at the house, and demanded a fortnight's wages, which were due to him ; but Mrs. Bather refused to, pay him, and following him outside,she pushed him about, and attempted to throw him to the ground. The male defendant came to her aid,and knock- ing Clare down, bumped his head several times on the stories, while Mrs. Bather kicked him on the legs and ribs. The old man was unable to work for several days in consequence of the ill-usage he received. It was stated that Mrs. Bat her was a very violent person, harr ing knocked her husband's eye out some time ago. The defence was a denial of the charge, but the Bench tined the defendants 20s. and costs, in all £3 2s. 6d. UMBRELLAS ItE..COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. ,t W. DUTTON'S Sankey-at.. Warrington.—Advt.

ASSAULT ON A HALTON PUBLICAN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. G. L. Davies and Mr. G. L. Wig?, a young man named Fred Johnson, labourer, of Fralsham, was summoned for having,on Bank Holiday,assaulted Thomas Higginson Wolstencroft, landlord of the Castle Hotel, Halton,—Mr. Percy Davies (Warrington), prosecuted, and stated that on the day in question Mrs. Jackson, who was in charge of a bar on the bowling green, complained that a num- ber of youths were misbehaving themselves and using bad language. • Mr. Wolstencroft went there and asked them to use better language, when the defendant struck him a blow on the side of the face and jaw, which swelled considerably, and caused him much pain. His ! nose bled very much. The force of the blow sent him to the ground. This statement was corroborated by witnesses.—The defendant said he and another young fellow called for two bottles of pop, and the complain- ant, who was drunk, fell all his length on the ground as he was bringing it. They put 4d. on the counter, and the plaintiff said he wanted more money, and said he would take the pop back. The defendant turned round, and then the complainant struck him, and he struck back in self-defence. He called William Dean, who cor- roborated.—The defendant was fined £l, and costs 12s. ed., or a month's hard labour. The sufferers from subsidences in the Cheshire salt district having failed to obtain the appoint- ment of a Royal Commission, to inquire into their grievances, a meeting was held at Northwich, on Wednesday to consider what further steps could be taken in the case. It was resolved to ask Mr. Brun- ner to introduce a bill into Parliament next session, which shall deal adequately with the question. Now OPEN FOR THE ScAsox.--Smart and Co.'s private Writhig and Commercial Academy for ladles and gentlemen, at Mr. Chantry's. 13 Sankey-it., Warrington. Open every Friday from 3 to 9 p.m. Writing : Gentlemen are taught a fine, bold, rapid business hand, and ladies an elegant and Sowing style. Terms for the complete course, One Guinea. Book-keeping : Pupils are taught how to open, keep, balance, and close a complete set of 'books by double entry • and our certificate for profieency is given to each pupil. Arithmetic and mental calculation taught practically. Shorthand. Pit- man's system. Pupils will Be received on Friday next, at any hour from 3to 9 p.m. No classes, the instruction is individual. Card of terms and full particulars may be had at Mr. Chantry's 13, Sankey-st.. Warrington, or post free from our Head Academy, 2, Brewn-st.. the Market, Man- ehester.—Advt.

- THE RECORDER OF PRESTON FINED. The new Recorder of Pteston, Mr. W. H. Higgin, Q.C., who resides at Timperley, Cheshire, has fallen a victim to the vigilance nf the Cheshire police. He was, on Monday, summoned at Sale Petty Sessions for not having his dog muzzled in accordance with the present order. Superintendent Leighton in- formed the bench that Mr.lliggin called at the police office and pleaded guilty to the charge, but owing to another engagement he could not attend that day. He was fined Is. and costs. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice—J. & W. DUTTON'S SaLlkey-St., Warrington.—Advt. SINGULAR RAILWAY ACCIDENT.

A singular accident occurred near St. Helens rail- way station, on Tuesday afternoon. A goods train approached from the direction of St. Helens Junction, and, whilst passing under Raven-st. Bridge at a fair speed, a large empty plate glass box reared on end struck the iron girders of the bridge. The box was smashed to splinters, which were scattered for some distance on each side of the lines. The waggon was also considerably damaged,and the force of the blow was such that the followiug truck was thrown off the Metals. The train was immedi- ately stopped, and a gang of men who were set to work, had soon replaced the waggon on the lines. Fortunately, the accident happened at a quiet part of the day, and there was no interruption of the passenger traffic. ELECTRO PLATED GOODS.—Garland's oldest established Ironmonger, Warrington.—Ads. Tint HOME IRON TRADE.

There is stillia-s-t-rO;i ;,..,-,;(1-uWaici- tendency in the English iron market, and the outlook is more encouraging in most departments of the trade. The demand for pig iron is fairly active, but it is not full enough to warrant the rise in prices which has taken place, and which must be attributed rather to speculative influences. Scotch warrants are quite Is. higher on the week, and up to Is. 6d. more per ton is quoted for Scotch makers' iron. Middles- brough iron has gained Is. 6d. a ton in value, warrants being about 9d. higher than the makers' price for No. 3, which is 465. There has been considerable business done in Lancashire pig-iron by merchants, who are evidently buy- ing for a further rise on present advanced rates In Staffordshire and the Midlands generally higher prices are stiffly quoted. Manufactured iron, under a better enquiry, has advanced about ss. per ton in the north of England and Scotland, but is un- changed at present in Staffordshire dad Lancashire. There has been a good business in tinplates. In the steel trade, although the demand is not over-active, better terms are quoted and obtained by the makers, who refuse to sell at the 'old prices. There is a slight revival in the shipbuilding trade, more orders having been placed this week. Engineers report themselves somewhat slacker as regards fresh work, but continue fairly well emploved.—lron. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.---7. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st.. Warrington.—Advt. WIDNES IRISH NATIONALISTS AND INCORPORATION.

The ordinary weekly meeting of the T. P. O'Con- nor (Widnes Branch) of the Irish National League, was held in St. Paul's Chambers, on Sunday after- noon, presided over by Mr. John Williamson. There was a good attendance. Mr. Delaney acknowledged receipt of £l3 ss. 4d. subscribed by the people of Widnes in aid of the "James Ryan County Wexford monument fund," for which he expressed the thanks of the Committee. A resolution regretting the un- timely death of John Boyle O'Riley, and expressing deep sympathy with his wife and children, was passed unanimously, Mr. Delaney said he had received a letter from Mr. J. T. Allen, clerk to the Widnes Local Board, notifying that the question of Widnes being incorporated was brought forward at the monthly meeting of the Board, held on Tuesday, the 12th inst. Mr. Delaney said, as members of the Widnes National League, the particular object of which was to help the Irish people to gain their own rights, they were called upon to endeavour to improve, as far as possible, the representation of Widnes. The reason why Widnes had not been incorporated before was owing to the fact that a large number of the gentlemen who sat on the Local Board were opposed to it, and were inclined to do all they possibly could, by overaround opposition and underground wirepulling, to defeat the chance that Widnes now had of obtaining a charter of incorporation. He appealed to the ratepayers present, and through them to the ratepayers of Widnes, to express during the present month their opinion on the subject, in order that the members of the Local Board need not be in the dark as to their opinion at the next meeting. In the event of an unanimous opinion in favour of incorporation I being expressed by the ratepayers, and being ignored by the members of the Local Board, then they ought I to take the earliest opportunity of unseating them, and electing members in their places more in sympathy with the wishes of the ratepayers. Mr. John Howling also spoke in favour of the incorporation movement, which, he said, if carried into effect, would be a great improvement to Widnes. The Chairman re- marked that as a ratepayer he wolqd do all he possibly could to support the movement. Ile had always been of opinion that Widnes was justified more than other towns in England to have the honour of be- ing incorporated, and being governed by a Mayor, aldermen and the town council. With regard to the belief prevalent that incorporation meant an increase in the present rates, he distinctly denied it, as it was optional with them whether they took the control of the police or not ; but even if this had to be done, their rates would not be increased. Extra police, he said, would not be required only in case of a riot or emergency,

and they should bear in mind that Widnes was at the present time contributing a fair share toward the main- tenance of the county police. If Widnes was incorporated they would only be called upon to support their own men. A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the proce,xlings.
RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE. ANNUAL REPORT. _ .

_ The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday, at the Town Hall. The Rev. Canon Wood presided, and there were present Messrs. S. Taylor, T. Riley, W. Hankinson, W. Handley, and J. D. Jones (Libra- rian). The Librarian presented the Bth annual re- port, which stated that the institution continued to exercise a beneficial influence in the town. This was strikingly illustrated during the winter months, when two courses of lectures were held under the auspices of the Oxford University Exten- sion movement. The lectures were a great suc- cess, towards which the Free Library Committee con- tributed in no small degree by purchasing special works bearing on the subjects of the lectures, which, together with the works already in the Library, were placed at the disposal of the students and were found to be of great assistance. It was pleasing to note that the help this afforded was gratefully acknow- ledged both by the Committee of the Runcorn centre and the lecturers, the Rev. W. Hudson Shaw and Mr. H. J. Mackinder. But what was more gratifying still was the influence of the lectures on the reading of the gen- eral public using the Library by creating a taste for a higher class of literature as was shown by the fact that in the classes containing books bearing on the lectures, viz., philosophy, science, history, biography, and miscellaneous literature, the number of issues was 5,196, being an increase over last year of 808. The Library had been open for the issue of books 148 days, and the number of issues was 24,143, a decrease of 273 as compared with last year, or an average daily issue of 164. The decrease was in the novels, consequent upon the demand for more serious works just referred to. The number of borrowers tickets issued during the year was 818, two less than last year. The number of sub- scribing members was six, two more than last year. During the year 340 vols. have been added to the Library, 290 by purchase, and 50 by gift; in addition to which 15 vols. have been purchased to replace worn out copies. The total stock is 5,425 vols. One of Cotgroave's indica- tors has been procured for the novels,and gives great satis- faction. The reading rooms continue to attract large numbers of visitors, who greatly appreciate the various newspapers and periodicals which are supplied. The Committee again thankfully acknowle,ged the numerous gifts of money, books, periodicals and newspapers, which tended to the greater efficiency. of the Library. The finan- cial statement showed that the Committee commenced the year with a balance in hand of £4 7s. 6d. ; the Free Library rate produced £lB6 18s.; fines £ll 155. 4d. : borrowers' tickets £7 2s. 2d. ; catalogues £2 4s. ; papers and waste paper sold £1 175.; subscriptions from non- residents £1 9s. ; donations £l5; total £230 16s. The expenditure amounted to £223 17s. 6d., and included the following items: Salary of librarian and secretary £5O; new books £55 10s. Bd.; magazines and news- papers £32 19s. lid.; bookbinding £2l 4s. 3d.; printing and stationery £ll 7s. 10d. ; fittings £l5 125.; sundries £1 2s. 10d. : rent, lighting, heating and cleaning £36. There was a balance in hand of £6 18s. 6d. Amongst the gifts to the Library were the sum of £l5 from Mr. .1. T. Brunner, M.P.—The report was considered highly satis- factory,and was adopted and ordered to be printed. On the motion of Mr. Handley, seconded by Mr. Taylor, a vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman .for his services during the year.

but it was not clear by whom and the pri- soner would be discharged. A young man named Michael Fitzsimons, of Grenfell, was charged on remand with having on the 9th inst., wounded a man named Thomas Fisher Butler, a joiner, of Lacey-st., with intent to do him grievous bodily harm. Mr. Knowles defended. On Saturday night Butler went into his sister's refresh- ment room in Victoria-road. He was very drunk at tilt time, and he remembered having some words with a per- son, and then being struck, but he could not tell who the person was. Ho fell to the ground, and aid not re- member anything further, until he found himself at ' home with his eye injured. By the orders of Dr. Hutch- inson he went to the Eye Infirmary at Liverpool, but he had lost the sight of his right eye. Several witnesses were called and proved that the prisoner was Butler's as- sailant. Dr. Hutchinson said there were small hopes that the man would ever recover his sight again. A blow from a man's fist might have caused the injury, but the blow must have been a very violent one. Mr. Knowles suggested that the injury had been caused by the man falling on a piece of macadam, as both men were more or less drunk at the time. The magistrates thought there was a strong case, and committed the prisoner to the Quarter Sessions for trial. Bail was allowed. Yester- day, at Widnes Police Court, Thomas Potter, a labourer, of 74 Pear-st., was brought up on remand charged with having on the 11th August unlawfully wounded his wife Mary, with intent to do her grievous bodily harm. It appeared that the woman returned home from gaol on the morning in question, and started a quarrel with the prisoner. Then peace was restored and the prisoner gave his wife 2s. to purchase some breakfast. In about two hours she returned in a state of drunkenness, and without breakfast. She used some annoying language, and the prisoner kicked her under the chin with his clog, inflicting a serious wound 2i inches in length and 2 inches deep.—The prisoner was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial, bail being allowed.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. BY AN "OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT."

The annual election of five members of the Run- corn Board of Commissioners takes place on Thurs- day, Sept. 4th,and before that day arrives consider- able interest will have been excited in the event. The retiring members are Messrs. Samuel Taylor (the respected chairman of the Board), W. Whittaker, W. Fisher, P. Smith, and It. Morris. The business engagements of Mr. Morris will not, permit him to pay that attention to the interests of the ratepayers which a seat on the Board demands, and he has therefore decided to withdraw from the contest. Mr. Whittaker has expressed a similar intention,but he will no doubt be prevailed upon to again represent the ratepayers, and his familiar form will be again seen at the council table. The return of Messrs. Taylor, Whittaker and Fisher is assured, and for the remaining two seats there will be four aspirants in the persons of Mr. P. Smith, Mr. E. Wynne Ilumphreys,Mr. S. Yarwood. and Mr. R. Abel. There is a rumour that Mr. James Kirk- ham will seek the suffrages of the voters, but this statement needs confirmation. Since Sir James Picton opened Runcorn Free Library, just over seven years ago, the institution has prospered more and more each year, and the report presented by the Librarian,at the meeting on Wednesday, was a very interesting one. The in- crease in the number of books issued to borrowers was no less than 808 over the previous year, an in- crease which was due not to novel reading, but to the study of works of an intellectual character. The Librarian ascribes this gratifying state of affairs to the influence of the lectures given under the University Extension Movement, and at the same time the Library Committee are to be credit- ed with having provided a number of valuable books bearing upon the subjects dealt with by Mr. Hudson Shaw and Mr. Mackinder. Finding their labour of providing a higher education for the townspeople has borne such good fruit, the Exten- sion Committee will be encouraged to proceed with greater energy and zeal in their preparations for the lectures of the coming season. . . . . .

Those travellers who are in the habit of walking three miles on a Sunday on purpose to be enabled to drink, and there are many such, would receive a severe shock on Monday. Two men who lived at Frodsham Bridge, had walked three miles to Halton Castle Hotel, and had been served with a pint of beer each, were summoned before the magistrates, and the Bench considered they were not bona-fide travellers, and they were each fined, as well as the landlord of the house. The formula of the publicans in future will have to be, not "Where do you come from ;" but " What's your business here."

lor some time tliere have been rumours that a local gentleman would cdntest the seat for the Widnes Division against Mr. T. C. Edwards Moss, at the next general election, and rumour has been busy with the names of several of the magnates. It has now transpired that the Executive Council of the Liberal Association have asked Mr. IL Wade- Deacon, J.P., a member of the firm of Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon,and Co., chemical manufacturers, to contest the constituency, and there is not the slight- est doubt that the district councils,when asked to do so, will ratify the action of the Executive. Mr. Deacon is a prominent Churchman, and on the School Board, and as secretary of the Traders' Association has done good work for the town. He is popular in all classes, and the party could not possibly have found a stronger man. Not only amongst Liberals, but also amongst Tories, his return is regarded as almost certain.

div.head: BONA FIDE TRAVELLER AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THE BONA FIDE TRAVELLER AT RUNCORN.
IMPORTANT DECISION.

Before Mr. G. L. Davies and Mr. G. L. Wigg, at the Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, Thomas Higginson Wolstencroft, landlord of the Castle Hotel, Halton, was summoned for having on Sun- day, the 3rd August, opened his premises at eleven o'clock in the forenoon, for the sale of liquor to per- sons net bona fide travellers. James Booth, Thomas Mercer, and Joseph Forster, labourers, Frodsham, were charged with being found on the premises during prohibited hours, on the ilame date. Mr. Cartwright (Chester) prosecuted on behalf of the police, and Mr. Percy Davies (Warrington) defended. Mr. Cartwright said this practice of serving drink during prohibited hours had caused some consider- able trouble to the police, and there were a certain number of persons in the habit of coming into Halton on a Sunday morning, and they went openly to this public-house and represented themselves as bona fide travellers. The allegation against the landlord was that he did not take all the care which he ought to do. The defendants were apparently there for the purpose of getting drink, and drink only, and were not bona fide travellers, and if their purpose was merely to get drink, it did not matter whether they lived three miles or under three miles away.—P.C. Fryer spoke to find- ing the men in the house about eleven o'clock, and took their names and addresses. They all stated that they had come three miles. He and P.S. Costello had measured the distance, and the distance to Forster's house, which was the furthest away, was two miles and a half and 579 yards, or 301 yards under three miles.—By Mr. Davies: Booth did not say he had slept that night at the Iron Dish, Helsby. They measured what they considered the nearest way. The men said they had come by Pickering's Boat—Mr. Cartwright said the Act of Parliament stated the three miles are to be measured by the nearest public thoroughfare, whether by land or water.—By Mr. Davies: If the men had walked from Frodsham Bridge by Pickering's boat, the distance would have been considerably over three miles. He and Costello measured the road at 11•30 p.m. P.C. Costello gave similar evidence, and said all the footpaths along which they measured were public thoroughfares.— After a speech by Mr. Davies, Thomas Gerrard,survevor, of Kingsley, said he had measured the highway from Halton Castle to the "double doors." Frodsham Bridge was three miles. Across the fields, the way the police had measured was 66 yards less than that distance. Forster lived 525 yards over three miles away, Mercer 60 yards over, and Booth 30 yards short of the three miles. In cross examination, it appeared that the witness had not measured along the footpaths from the hotel, past the corner and down the steps to the vil- lage, whereas the police had done so ; hence the discrep- ancy.—Booth deposed that he was a foreman at Weston Chemical works,and on Saturday night, the 2nd inst., he slept at the Iron Dish in a house that belonged to himself and his wife, and at half past nine on Sunday morning he had breakfast with his brother at Kingsley. He then walked on through Aston to Halton to give instructions to Alfred Retford, one of his workmen. He then went to the hotel for refreshment.—Alfred Retford, Fletcher's Buildings corroborated.—Wolstencroft said he always understood that Frodsham Bridge was three miles from 1 his house.—By Mr. Cartwright : On the Ist June, P.S. Costello told him he was doubtful whether the distance was three miles, and he must be careful.—The Bench retired, and after an absence of about a quarter of an hour the Chairman said they did not consider the case proved against Booth, and they dismissed it. Mercer and Foster would be each fined 10s., and costs 9s. 6d. With reference to Wolstencroft, as this was his first offence, he would only be fined 405., and costs 17s. 6d. They would not endorse the license.—Mr. Davies asked if he were to take it that the magistrates considered it was not three miles to Frodsham Bridge, and Mr. Davies replied that he did not consider the two defendants bona fide travellers.—Mr. Cartwright asked to have the advocate's fee allowed, but the magistrates refused the application.

WOUNDING AFFRAYS AT WIDNES.

Michael Donlan, of 3/, Charlotte-st., was brought tip at Widnes Police Court,on Monday,charged with wounding Miles Darcy, on the previous Saturday evening. From a statement by Superintendent Noblett, it appeared that the men were in the Crown Vaults, Ann-st., between eight and nine o'clock, when they had a dispute, during which the prisoner threw a tumbler at the prosecutor. The missle struck him on the • left cheek, causing a wound over the right eyebrow, and also a lacerated wound on the left cheek. The injured man was unable to appear in court and the prisoner was remanded for a week.—Felix McConville, Ann-st., West,was charged on remand with wounding Ann Morgan, wife of Peter Morgan, 8, Catherine-st.—Mr. Mearns defended. It was alleged that on Saturday afternoon, the 9th inst., the prisoner went to Morgan's house and after some " words " struck Morgan. Mrs. Morgan then pushed him out of the house, and he struck her. She struck him "back again" and then he kicked her about the legs and body. Some women came to her assistance and took her into the house. At ten o'clock at night the pri- soner again came to the house, and Morgan went into the street and a fight ensued. Mrs. Morgan went be- tween them and it was alleged the prisoner knocked her down with a blow from his fist, and also struck her while on the ground. When she was taken into the house she became unconscious. She had only been con- fined four weeks previously, and she had been very ill in consequence of her injuries.—Dr. O'Keaffe said the , woman had an incised wound penetrating to the bone ' at the angle of the left eye. The wound had undoubtedly ' been caused by a sharp instrument. The woman was also much cut about the legs.—ln cross-examination the prosecutrix said she did not think the prisoner deliber- ately knocked her down.—After hearing the evidence the Magistrate (Mr. F. 11. Gossage) said there was no doubt the woman had been brutally assaulted

div.head: DEATH UNDER CHLOROFORIL
div.p: DEATH UNDER CHLOROFORIL
EXTRAORDINARY CASE.

On Monday forinoon, Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy- coroner. held an inquest at the Griffin Hotel, Peasley Cross, near St. Helens, touching the death of Ellen Borrows, 60 years old, wife of John Borrows, a glassworks labourer, of 15, Gerard's-lane, Sutton, who died at the Cottage Hospital whilst under chloroform on the previous Thursday night. Evi- dence was given to the effect that about nine weeks ago deceased had a gathering on one of her fingers. Dr. Pennington, Of Liverpool and St. Helens, was called in, and the woman was removed to the hospital. ' On Wednesday week the doctor's assistant informed the woman's husband that it would be necessary to have the finger amputated, and that a specialist would be required to administer the chloroform. The fee for the specialist would be two guineas. The husband stated to the jury that he was under the impression the operation would not be performed unless he could raise the two guineas. On the Thursday the doctor did not visit his wife at the hospital, and at night he went for Dr. Casey, of Sutton, who went to the hospital. At Dr. Casey's request he went to Dr. Pennington's surgery and left word there that Dr. Casey had been called in. In reply to Dr. Pen- nington witness said the assistant did not say that the operation would not be performed unless the money was paid.—Miss Annie Stocks, matron, and Miss L. Rhodes, nurse at the hospital, gave evidence that according to Dr. Pennington's instructions on 'the Wednesday, prepara- tions were made on the Thursday for the deceased to undergo an operation. Dr. Pennington did not visit the hospital on the Thursday, and at night Dr. Casey at- tended. With the consent of the patient and her hus- band the deceased was chloroformed. but before the operation could be performed respiration had ceased and the woman died.—Mr. H. B. Bates, assistant to Dr. Pen- nington, gave evidence that he told the deceased's hus- band that the attendance of a specialist would ho necessary before the operation could be performed. He mentioned that the fee was two guineas, and the husband said be would try to get it. The husband left and did not return.—Dr. Pennington said he, did not perform the operation, as he had not got the husband's consent. If he had got the husband's consent he would have performed the operation, and paid the fee out of his pocket. He considered it was necessary to have assistance in such cases.—Dr. Casey (Sutton) was the next witness. He said the deceased's husband implored him to go and see his wife at the hospital. He advised the husband to go and tell Dr. Pennington. He then went to the hospital and saw the woman.—The Deputy- Coroner asked if it was not usual to go and see any other doctor who had been engaged in the case previously.— Witness : Yes : If it had been another doctor—an ordinary doctor—l should have done. He added that he found the woman suffering from great exhaustion, mental excitement, and severe blood-poisoning. He considered it necessary that the finger should be imme- diately amputated, as it was in a state of mortification and was rotten. Chloroform was accordingly adminis- tered, and respiration immediately ceased. Efforts were made to restore respiration, but they were unsuccessful. He had administered chloroform hundreds of times and never had an accident up to the present. He considered the circumstances and condition of the woman were desperate.—The Deputy Coroner, in summing up, remarked that he was always very reluctant to say any- thing about professional matters, but it was a pity to see gentlemen connected with the honourable medical profession carrying on their businssses in an unfriendly spirit and unable to agree amongst themselves. In regard to that case, he thought the medical gentlemen might have consulted in regard to the woman, and it was far better to act in a more friendly spirit in those matters, and not be so anxious to do such things inde- pendently of each other. He had often heard doctors say for their own sake It Was desirable for them to have assistance when performing such operations. In reply to a remark by a juror, he added that the doctors differed even in most important cases, and it was not for the jury to decide. Ile suggested that the only verdict they could return would be one of " Death from mis- adventure under the administration of chloroform," and the jury returned a verdict accordingly.

div.head: WELSH LIBERAL PROGRAMME
div.p: THE WELSH LIBERAL PROGRAMME

The following are the items of the very comprehensive Liberal pr.gramme accepted at the representative Liberal Welsh Conference held at Builth Wells : Disestablishment and disendowment ; federated Home Rule for the four nations ; free and unsectarian education : fixity of tenure, judicial rents, and free sale of tenant- right ; taxation of ground rents, royalties, and values; equal taxation of land and personal estate ; just division of rates between owner and occupier; abolition of tea duty; entire control of police by county councils; better housing of the working classes ; extension of the Factory Acts; triennial Parliaments ; payment of mem- bers ; one man, one vote; radical reform of the registra- tion laws; mending or ending of the House of Lords; and direct veto on the drink traffic.

div.head: RITMOURED RESIGNATION OF SIR RICHARD MOON.
div.p: RITMOURED RESIGNATION OF SIR RICHARD MOON.

It is stated that Sir Richard Moon, Bart., chairman of the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany, has, owing to ill-health, privately intimated his intention to resign his position. This report, which is given on professedly good authority, will be noted with very general regret, and especially by the shareholders whose interests he has so long and so effectively promoted. Sir Richard, who is seventy-six years of age, has been intimately associ- ated with the above great railway enterprise for more than forty years, and has held the posLion of chairman since May, 1861. To him is principally due the high position which the London and North- Western Company holds in the railway world, alike in regard to sound finances and substantial struc- ture. It is not likely that he will altogether with- draw himself from the management, with which he has been for so many years identified, but though directors and officers may still have the advantage of his counsel, his resignation of the chairmanship involves withdrawal from that active supervision which has done so much to place the company in its present proud position, and the announcement now made will be read with deep regret. Sir Richard Moon, whose seat is Copsewood Grange, near Stoke, was created a baronet in 1887. His wife is a daughter of the late Mr. John Brocklebank, of Hazeldine, Cumberland, and his eldest son, Mr. Edward Moon, married a daughter of Mr. Benjamin Darbyshire, of Claughton, Cheshire.

div.head: MYSTERIOUS TRAGEDY AT HALE.
div.p: MYSTERIOUS TRAGEDY AT HALE.

The body ora man unknown was found on Tuesday in a field in the occupation of Mr. J. Griffitlin, farmer, Bale. When an examination was made it was found that the deceased had in one hand a revolver, three barrels of which had been discharged. There was also a receipt for the weapon and twenty-five cartridges, which ap- peared to have been purchased at the shop of Mr. Crown- shaw, Dale-street, Liverpool, on July 4th, and on the back of the receipt was the name W. H. Burley. The deceased, who is described as about five feet five inches in height, and about fifty years of age, was dressed in a dark overcoat, an undress coat, grey vest and trousers, low shoes, brown stockings, white cotton shirt, and " pat,ent " collar and cuffs. His hair, beard, and mous- tache were turning grey. He had In his possession, besides the revolver, ss. 6d., a pipe, and a knife. Mr. It. Buckton, coroner for the district, held an in- quest. on the body of the deceased. Superintendent Nob- lett watched the inquiry on behalf of the police. Thomas , Roberts, a farm labourer, residing in High-street, Hale, said he was employed on the Manor Farm, Hale. On Tuesday he was reaping in the wheat field when he saw something near the machine. He found it to be the body of a man. Deceased was lying on his left side. The body was very much decomposed.—William J. Crown- shaw, cutler, Dale-st., Liverpool, stated that he scld revolvers. He recognised the bill head produced as one of his. It was given for a revolver on the 4th July, which cost 14s. The name "A. H. Bartley "'which was ' written on the hack of the receipt was not in the same handwriting, and must have been put on afterwards. He remembered a man buying a revolver on the 4th July. He asked for a receipt for the weapon,and he gave him one. It was the first time witness had given a receipt for a revolver. The man appeared to be between forty- five and fifty years of age. He also bought twenty-five cartridges, one of which he fired in the shop to test the I penetrating power of the revolver.—Police-constable Clarke deposed to being called to the body on Tuesday. The deceased held a six-chambered revolver in his right hand. Two of the chambers were empty, two contained the remains of exploded cartridges, and two were loaded. The head ot the deceased was very much shattered, and the body very much decomposed.—The jury returned an open verdict.

div.head: AGRICULTURAL DESTITUTION AND
div.p: AGRICULTURAL DESTITUTION AND
HARVEST FESTIVALS.

Sir,—l rely upon your ever-readiness to help a good cause to allow the above heading, and the few words which follow thereon, to occupy a prominent position at this period of the year in your columns. The grand old promise of patriarchal times—" seed- time and harvest shall not fail "—is just now receiving its annual fulfilment; but, while rejoicing in the perpe- tuity of this Magna Charta of the husbandman for all ages, we cannot close our ears to that °Linz. promise, "The poor ye have always with you, and whensoever ye will ye may do them good." For four years now an endeavour has been made, through the press, to localise that, it is to be feared, rather elastic word "whensoever," and to associate it with a fixed occasion, viz., our Harvest Festival Thanks- giving Services, the idea being that, in the outcome of these rejoicings the number of those who have "lived by the land," but who from various causes—chiefly illness, misfortune, or old age—have gone under" in the vicis- situdes attached to agriculture, more especially of late years, should not be forgotten. . If from a thousand pulpits, during the next few weeks, I could ensure the repetition of those promises I have quoted above, and their practical application to the case of the Royal Agricultutal Benevolent Institution, what a result might we not look forward to ? Let me not be misunderstood. Ido not desire to under- value the assistance which the institution has received of late from ministers of all denomiaations, from the late Archbishop of Canterbury,who" warmly approved of the claims of the institution in connection with the offertories at harvest services," to small village congregations whose offerings partake much of the character of the "widow's mite," and are entitled to the same thankful acknow- ledgment which that offering received. Last year the result of Harvest Festival collections represented an addition to the funds of the institution of £5,570, the largest amount yet received, and ten timesl the amount of ten years ago, thus proving, I think, that I the Press, in lending their assistance—as they have so cheerfully done—have appealed to a sentiment which, • at "Harvest Festival" time, with its bright and happy associations, is uppermost in many minds. At the annual meeting of the institution, which took I place on the 18th June last, under the presidency of the Earl of Northbrook, it was shown that from 2,000 an- nual subscribers in 1860 the number had increased to over 18,000, and that, including the pensioners elected this year, there were 780 persons receiving help at the present time from the institution. From the want of increased funds, however, there remained, after the last election, a list of 286 unsuccessful applicants, to say no- thing of the thousands who are awaiting a chance to lodge their applications. When writing to you at this period last year, I ex- pressed the idea that, in the same way as our Hospital Sunday Services are devoted to furthering a specific object, so I hoped to see the time when our Harvest Festival Services would be held mainly in furtherance of this most deserving charity. I would strongly urge that at a harvest festival there 19 a certain fitness in remem- bering the case of those who, in better times, and in their period of prosperity, could look forward to the gladness of "harvest home" with feelings which now are too often, it is to be feared, overshadowed by cares and anxieties. Any person desiring further. information as to the in- stitution, or wishing to contribute to its funds, should communicate with Mr. C. B. Shaw, 26, Charles-st., St. James's, London, S.W., the secretary of the charity. WALTER GILI3ET. Elsenhato Hall, Essex. August 19th.

PLEURO-PNEITMONIA. AT WARRINGTON.

On Wednesday an outbreak of pleuro-pneumonia was discovered on the premises of Mr. Thomas Ford, Lower Wash Farm, Latchford, in a herd of four cattle— one cow and three calves. These have • since been slaughtered by order of the borough authorities. Mr. Ford had another herd of cattle, numbering twenty-two, which are outside the borough but have been in contact with the infected animals. These will probably be slaughtered by order of the county authorities.

div.head: REVISION AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE REVISION AT WARRINGTON.

Mr. J. T. Foard, revising barrister, will hold a Court at the Warrington Town Mall, early next month, for the purpose of revising the burgess lists, and hearing claims and objections. The Liberal party will make 200 fresh claims, and 197 objections, and they will also make 11 or 12 lodger claims, but no objections to the names of lodgers already on the list. The Conservatives will make 178 occupiers' claims, 182 objections, and 20 lodger claims. Mr. John Clayton, the liberal registration agent, and Mr. Hampson, the conservative registration agent, have for some time been very busy preparing for the re- vision, but it is anticipated that Mr. Foard's work will be mostly of a routine description.and no points of an unusual character are expected to arise.

div.head: ALLEGED ABDUCTION OF TWO
div.p: ALLEGED ABDUCTION OF TWO
GIRLS. EXTRAORDINARY WARRINGTON CASE.

Information reached us last night of an affair which, if all the particulars we hear are authentic, is, to say .the least of it, of a scandalous nature. There is every reason to believe that the informa- tion is founded on fact ; but we are not, at present, at liberty to disclose the names and identity of the parties principally concerned in what looks like a very barefaced abduction of two girls. It appears that a Warrington publican, who is the occupier of a full-licensed house, and who is known as a betting man, has in his service a certain individual, who in July last made the acquaintance of a girl of sixteen years of age, who seems to have been rather fascinated by his attractions. This girl had a companion, who attained her fifteenth year in November last, and she in due course became acquainted with the publican and his assistant. On Monday night, it is alleged, the four came to an arrangement to proceed next morning together to Wolverhampton. By some means or other, the mother of the younger girl got wind of the fact :that her daughter had gone to Wolverhampton in company with the others. She acted in a very prompt way on hearing this, and immediately wired to the police at Wolverhampton to detain the girl, giving at the same time particu- lars by which she might be identified. Acting on the instructions of Major Day, the Chief Constable of Wolverhampton, an officer of the force of that town was in waiting at the station on the arrival of the train from Warringon. He detained the girl, who was taken to the Police Station, and subse- quently brought back to her friends in Warrington. As the police of Wolverhampton, however, had re- ceived no authority from the parents of the older girl enabling them to detain her, she was allowed to go away with the two men. Subsequent inquiries dis- closed that she on the same night occupied a room with the companion of the publican, but she also has since returned home. It is stated that she told her parents that she was going to Accrington in search of a new situation, but, though they knew she was going away, they had no idea that she was going to Wolverhampton, or that she was to be accompanied by a " male friend." The two men, one of whcm is married, are said to have since gone to the races at Scarborough. The Criminal Law Amendment Act of 1885 provides that " any person withdrawing an un- married girl, under the age of 18, from the pos- session of those who have lawful charge of her, and with intent that she should ba unlaw- fully known by any man, is subjected to a maximum penalty of two years' imprison- ment with hard labour. It will be seen from this that both men have been guilty of a serious breach of the law, and have rendered themselves liable to imprisonment. It is for the parents to take action ; and it is to be hoped that they will let it be seen that their households are not to be invaded with impunity. •
WARRINGTON BREWSTER SESSIONS.
THE CHIEF CONSTABLE'S REPORT.

In view of the annual brewster sessions for the borough of Warrington, which are to be held next Tuesday at the Sessions House, Irlam-st., the Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) has prepared his usual report to the magistrates. It reads as follows: "I have the honour to inform you that the Annual Brewster Sessions for this Borough wil Ibe , held at the Sessions House, Warrington, on Tuesday next, the 26th inst. The number of license holders are :-87 licensed victuallers, 48 beerhouse keepers, and 70 shopkeepers, &c. The transfers during the year were :-Nine licensed victuallers, 11 beerhouse keepers, and 11 shopkeepers. Two licensed victu- allers were summoned for offences against their licenses, both being convicted, one fined 20s. and costs, and one 10s. and costs. Three beerhouse keepers were summoned, all being dismissed. Below is a table of drunkenness in the Borough between each Brewster Sessions, during the last ten years. div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

NI IT At• AW.AULT BY A MILITIAMAN. Charles Wynne, a militiaman, was brought Up at the Warrington Police Court on Tuesday, on a charge of having assaulted two young women named Kate Kimblin and Bridget Gorham, in Battersby-lane, on Saturday night. It appeared that the prisoner wanted to claim acquaintance with the girls, and, failing in his object, he struck them. Prisoner was sent to goal for a.month. SENT TO PEISON FOR NEGLECTING HIS CHILDREN. The Warrington magistrates on Monday sent a tan- ner named Joseph Charnock to prison fora month, with hardls.bour, for neglecting to maintain histhree children, who had become chargeable to the common fund of the Union. Mr. Shearer, re;ieving officer, stated that pri- soner had allowed his three children to remain in the Workhouse since March, 1889. The cost of their main- tenance hadteen ...‘2,54.. Prisoner frequently worked, but he was fonder of drink than work. ASSAULT ON A WIDOW. Yesterday, at the Warrington Police Court, Samuel Ball and John Henry Hers, young men, were summoned for having assaulted Alice Burns. a widow, on the 11th August.—Mrs. Burns said that a number of youths were using bad language, and she hit one in consequence. Thereuponshe was knocked to the ground and severely maltreated. She alleged that the two defendants took part in the assault. There was no evidence against Hayes, and he was dismissed. Ball pleaded that com- plainant struck him without provocation. but the magis- trates thought him at fault, and fined him ss. and costs. WIFE ASSAULT IN DIAL-ST. At the 'Warrington Police Court, on Wednesday, a young man natned Smith, a hawker, who lives in Dial- at., was charged in custody with drunkenness, disorder- ly conduct, and a brutal assault on his wife, whose face bore marks of ill-usage. He excused himself on the groundthat the woman, who herself has been brought up 33 times for various offences, had been drinking all the day Wore, and had pawned things out of the house. Until he became acquainted with her he had never been in trouble in his life. Under the circumstances he was only ordered to pay ss. and costs, in addition to being bound over to be of good behaviour. MARRIED MISERY. A wire-worker, named John Ansbury, was brought up at the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Tuesday, on a charge of wife assault. Mrs. Ansbury, whose right eye was black, said that on Friday night her husband kicked her until she was senseless. In answer to Mr. A. Browne, who appeared for the defendant, complainant denied that she was a drunken woman, or that she was always pawning the clothing of the family. The magis- trates thought that a bad assault had been committed, but remarked that perhaps the complainant was to scene extent atfault, as the did not seem to have the sweetest of tempers. The defendant was hound over to keep the Peace, himself in £2O, and one surety in 1.10. CHASTISED BY HIS BROTHER-IN-LAW. At theVarrington Police Court, yesterday morning, a yonngman named John Chadwick, an ironworker, was summoned for :havina. assaulted Edwin Ford, his brother-in-law, and Ford was summoned for as- saulting his wife. Mr. A. Browne appeared for Chadwick. The evidence disclosed that Ford, who is a painter, was brutally ill-treating his wife on the 9th. inst., when Chadwick, her brother, came upon thssecene and gave him a good thrashing. Mr. Browne-said that Mrs. Ford had left her husband six times., in consequence of his ill-treatment. She earned 225. a week, and had to keep her husband, who very seldom did any work. He was conthaually drinking, and thmthims. her. The magistrates dismissed the sum- mons against Chadwick. Ford was fined ss. and costs, and ordered to find a surety for his good behaviour, and the Bench granted an application for a separation order, Ford to pay ss. a week towards the support of his wife and children. ALLFAED STABBING BY A DRITNEEN LABOURER. At theWarrington Police Court, on Monday, before the Mayor (Alderman Francomb) and other magistrates, an Irish labourer named James O'Brien was charged in custody with having been drunk and disorderly in Folley-lane on Sunday afternoon. There was a further charge against him of having unlawfully wounded a fellow labourer named Timothy Connolly. Complainant, however, dill not appear, so that the second charge could riot be gone into. It was allegedthat the prisoner and Connolly quarrelled over some beer, and that the prisoner, after giving his opponent a blow-Which loosened his teeth, drew a knife and stabbed him under the chin. The pace were summoned, and Constables Monaghan and Corcoran apprehended the prisoner. The Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) said that one of the chief Wit- nesses, as well as the complainant himself, -was not to he found. The prisoners, he added, gave the constables a " sweating," as they had to drag and carry him the whole of the way to the Bridewell. A fine of 20s. and costs, or 19 ne month's imprisonment, was imposed upon -the prisoner for the offence of drunkenness and dis- orderly mind

Arley Park went in first,.and scored 74, Ding batting well. Stretton, however, quickly sdored 84, for the loss of three widlrets, for whicti Mr. Dun and the Revs. F. C. Timins a-ncIT. W. Cook showed excellent form. Mt. S. M. CROSFIELD'S ELEVIIN V. STALYBRIDGEI. , Played at Stalybridge, on Saturday. The home team included Chatterton (Derbyshire County), Pointon (Che- shire-county), and Booth (Denton pro.), consequently the Warrington v. Stalybridge fixture was cancelled, and a mateh played as above for the benefit of Earle, the Staly- bridge professional. Mr. Crosfield won the toss, and sent-"J. J. Crosfield and Podmore in on a bad and wet wieket to face the deliveries of Earl ond Chatterton. With only one run scored Podmore was caught, and 2 -runs-later S. M. Crosfield was also out. Lawton retired at%. J. J. CroSfield and Clarke were both sent back at the same total, viz.' 14, when Yonge and Voisey made -the only stand for the eleven. They both played a forc- ing game, and by hard hitting took the total to 45 be- fore-Voisey was out to a well-judged catch In the long 'field. The innings closed for 65. B. Clarkson and Poin- ton were together for half-an-hour before Lawton bowled thaamateur for 21-cut of the 22 scored for the first wic- ket. Chatterton hit nut finely, and after a while Pointon followed suit, and they carried the total to 61, when Bell went on, his first over being a maiden. In his second he 'beat Chatterton, who was bowled off his pads for 29-2 , '£m.7l. Eight runs later Earle was splendidly caught by Pethnore for 7. Pointon was mixt out for 27 clean bowled-4 for 87. MISCELLANEOUS. The popularity of baseball in America is said be very , muchon the decline. The attendance at some of the impor- tant games during recent weeks. ha.s,says the" Illustra- • ted American:' been hardly sufficient to pay the wages of the attendants on the grounds. The cld baseball crowd is thinning out. The crank and the enthusiast are not the familiar figures they were last year. Few people now make a serious attempt to keep up with the per- centages of the rival teams. Few people care who may win the pennant, an event fraught with a national min- portance in years go ti 6 by. New York or Chicago wins or loses without the plaudits or the gibes that formerly made the baseball sheet of the daily newspaper its most , attractive feature. One of the two rival leagues must inevitably kill the other, that is very evident; but the survivor will find that the interest in baseball has also been killed.

The EXscutive Of the County Bowling Association met at the Angel 4ili6tel., Stretford, on Monday evening, for the purpose lreediVing the reports of the semi-finals, fixing the ,finalsottia (Completing arrangements for the individual meiit cortMes6ition. Mr. Coombs, vice presi- dent, was in the chalit, And the following were present : —Mr. Singleton' Newton-le-Willows; Mr. Barnes, With- ington ; Mr. Relsall, Stretford; Mr. Brindle, Wigan ; Mr. Walton, Urmston'; Mr. Oilier, Broughton: and Mr. Hadfield, Didsbury. Regarding the individual merit competition, it was arranged that the last day for enter- ing should be the 30th of August. The county secretary (Mr. R. Evans) reported the issue of the semi-finals as follows :—Newton-le-Willows, 249; Urmston (Croft's Bank), 166; Stretford, 200 Hain, 187 ; Wigan, 229 Liverpool Albert, 198. A debate arose as to playing the finals by full teams, but it was decided to abide by the old arrangement for the present season. It was settled that the finals be played as follows :—Stretford to play at Newton on the 30th of August; Newton to meet Stret- ford on the 6th of September; for the Association prizes, Withington to visit Wigan on the 10th of September, and Wigan to play at the Midland on the 13th of September. The entrance for the individual merit competition was fixed at 55., the contest to be disposed of in one day on a green neutral to all concerned.

THE CHESHIRE MURDER MYSfERY:' SEARCH FOR JAMES JONES. In consequence of information supplied by a corres- pondent, a reporer has for some days past been engaged • in a search for the man James Jones, who is alleged to , have been concerned in the Cheshire murder case at Alpraham some thirty years back. A correspondent stated that about three months after the murder he saw Jones, with whom he was acquainted while in Beeston, at work at Miles Green, Halmerend, and that Jones then admitted that he had just come from Beeston. When news arrived from America that a confession had been made by some person not stated, and varicus papers suggested that the self-accusation had been made by Jones, inquiries were instituted, with the result that on Wednesday a reporter found in Chell Workhouse a man named James Jones, of the same age, and answering the description given above mentioned. The workhouse was visited by the correspondent by whom the matter was first ventilated, and he confidently recognised Jones as the man whom he had met thirty-three years ago at Miles Green, and who was formerly lodging with Blagg in Alpraham. Indeed, this circumstance was admitted by Jones, who confessed that he had lived within a few miles of the place where the murder took place, and had come thence shortly after the crime. When asked to say whether he was an associate of Blagg's he betrayed great reticence. Jones stated that he was born in Wrexham, where he had lived until he was ten years of age. After this he began working on various farms between Wrexham and North Staffordshire. He had laboured at Tilstone-by-Malpas, some eight miles from. Beeston, and also at Shacklock, about the same distance away. He knew the various farmers and landowners in the neighbourhood, but when questioned as to his knowledge of those immediately around Beeston, stated that he had never been in that town notwithstanding the fact that at the time Beeston was die railway station for the district in which he was engaged. When asked directly about the murder, he put on a vacant air, and said he could not remember. Jones ' is a man of medium height, who states that he is nearly seventy years of age, and although his appearance denotes that in his youth he was possessed of consider- able vigour, within the last few years he met with a ) serious accident, of which he bears evidence in various . scars about the face and head.

TIM WARRINGTON VOLUNTEERS.
On Saturday there was a special parade of the members of A and D companies of the Ist Volunteer Battalion South Lancashire Regiment, A company being under the command of Captain J. D. Buckton . .
and lieutenant F. M. Appleton, and D company
under the command of ffeutena.nt J. A. Edelsten-.
This was somewhat of.. an. innovation upon the

ordinary routine, being for the purpose of Perform- ing manceuvres of a more varied and interesting character than usual, and was arranged by the officers of the two companieg independently of the bat- tallion. The two companies full in at the Drill Hall, and having previously received an ample supply of blank ammunition, marched through the town, headed by the new Bugle Band, to a large field at Brodie, kindly lent far the occasion by Mr. William Bennett. There were . present on parade, in addition to the company officers, 2nd Lieutenant Chorlev and Surgeon Adams, together with eleven sergeants, and about 80 men. On arriving at the field, the men were formed up at one end as one company, preparatory to going through the new form of company attack. A small party, under 2nd Lieutenant Chorlev, was detached and posted in the distance as a defending force. As the men had not previously been taught the new attack, it was then explained to them, and carried out fairly well, the volley firing being execu- ted rather too slowly. The men were afterwards re-formed, and went through the attack a second and third time, showing marked improvement on each occasion; in fact, allowing for the limited ground avail- able, the last performance may be described as exceed- ingly creditable. The final charge was made with fixed bayonets, bugles playing and drums beating. The men cheered vociferously, and the officers in front led them. After some firing exercise the men then left the field, throwing out an advance guard along the Manchester road.

They proceeded to the National Schools, in Church-st., where they partook of a substantial tea, provided by the company officers. After tea a number of company prizes were presented. Major Pickmeve and Mr. J. M. Edelsten joined the companies at tea, and afterwards presented the handsome cups which they had respec- tively given to the companies for competition.-Captain Buckton in the course of some remarks reviewed the very satisfactory work of the year now drawing to a close.- Major PICK:UP:RR then addressed the men, and alluded to the original formation of A company, which was at one time the only company in Warrington. Colonel Green- all, Quartermaster Hutchinson, Mr. Edelsten, and him- ,pelf were among those who were enrolled on the first day. ''At a meeting of all the members shortly afterwards, when he (Major Pickmere) was elected to the chair, Colonel Greenall was elected captain, himself lieutenant, and the late Mr. John Shaw ensign. In those days they had to provide themselves with everything except the rifles, which were lent by the Government ; they had no band, and, indeed, in those days bands were very scarce in the neighbourhood. They had rifle green uniforms,of which they were very proud : They used to drill in the old cin- der yard, by Cockhedge Factory, and at first were very timid about showing themselves: but at last hired a band for the occasion and marched through the town to the open space in front of Arpley station, where the guns are now placed On the way a large crowd gathered, which increased until they were fairly blocked at Arpley station: in fact, they could proceed no further. All the people came to their windows to see them pass, and he had been told that many who saw them from the win- dows actually shed tears as they passed, and he believed it was true. He then referred briefly to the subsequent history of the corps, and said that he always regretted having had to leave it. He greatly admired the new uniforms, and said that he thought there was nothing like scarlet and white. He paid a high tribute to the band; and was glad to hear of the good work done dur- ing the past year. He encouraged them to continue, remarking that they would become better Englishmen by doing their duty, and learning to fear God and honour the Queen. It was also a satisfaction to him to know that Colour-Sergeant Jolley, who had for the year won his cup, was such a creditable member of the corps. (Applause).-Colour-Sergeant Jolley then came for- ward and was presented with the cup, amidst loud applause. Major Pickmere then presented the other prizes won in the A Company competition.- Mr. Edelsten briefly addressed the men, and referred to some of his expe:iences in the corps. Colour-sergeant Wood, the winner for the year, was then presented with the cup given to D Company by Mr. Edelsten, who said that as the cup was somewhat smaller than the one just presented, he thought he could not do better than put " something " inside it.-Lieutenant Edelsten next gave out the money prizes, commenting.' especially on the fact ' that three had been won by recruits of this year, a cir- cumstance which,as he pointed out,ought to attract new men to the company. The winners were Sergeant Whit- field, Sergeants Master, Cook, Cliffe, Lance-Corporal Thornton, Privates Stirrup, Flanagan, Scarisbrick, Gar- nett, and Starkey. A vote of thanks to the prize givers was then expressed by long and enthusiastic cheering, and musical honours. The sergeants of A Company were presented by Captain Buckton with the badges to which they were entitled by virtue of that being the best shooting company for the past year, and the members of both companies received the new efficiency badges and service stars which they had earned. The men were then marched back to the Drill Hall to the strains of the bugle band, and there dismissed. The prize list was as follows :-A Company prize list- The Company competition : 1, Colour-Sergeant Jolley, silver cup and 15s. ; 2, Sergeant W. Spencer, 125.; 3, Private J. W. Plinston, 10s. ; 4, Sergeant W. Taylor, Bs.; 5, Bugle-Major D. Plinston, 6s.
