INDEPENDENT ORDER OF RECHABITES.

MEETINGS AT WARRINGTON. On Monday evening a meeting promoted by the local "Tents " of the Independent Order of Recha- bites was held in Wycliffe Hall. There was a moder- ate attendance. The Rev. J. Yonge presided, and, there were also on the platform Bro. H. Sharpies, H.D.R., of Manchester; Bro. J. W. Hall, D.S.; Bro. C. 11. Mills, C.R. : Bro. W. Wright, and Bro. T. Massey CR . .

The Cuainmarz, who was received with applause, said he was always glad if he could do anything to help for- ward the cause of temperance, a caust which, in this town of Warrington, appeared to wait a considerable amount of helping. He hardly liked to suppose—in fact he could not suppose for one moment—that the real tem- . _

perance people 'o'f- Warrington W;l:e—a'sleeio—o-17-a-p;t-h-e-tiC, but certainly there was something or other somewhere which seemed to seriously hinder the progress of temper- ance in the town. (Hear, hear.) He understood there , were two Rechabite tents in Warrington, one known by the name of Charity, and the other by the name of Union. He had no doubt those tents would be all the better for the movement that was being inaugurated that evening. He was pleased to find that the Orier of Rechabites had tents and representatives in all parts of the world, and he had no idea that it was so wealthy as to possess a capital fund of half a million. fie thought there were very considerable advantages connected with the Order and that it held out very great inducements especially to young men who wished to join a friendly society. (Hear, hear and applause.) Bro. J. W. HALL, D.S., mentioned that the Order of Rechabites had had an existence in Warrington for 55 years. The Union tent, in connection with which that meeting was more particularly held, had 56 members and it had a fund of over £4OO. Mr. Hall then referred to the advantages of the Order as a friendly society, and to the small management expenses incurred. Unlike some other sick and benefit societies, the meetings of their tents were held at places where no intoxicating liquors . . . .

are sold, so that vatiilst at their meetings there were no temptations held out to themselves and to the youths who joined them. In the Warrington district there were at present six tents, and they intended if possible t 3 open out other four. Of the six tents already existing there were two in Warrington,one at Ashton-in-Makertield —and that was the best one in the district, having 107 members. There was one at Bry-nn, near Wigan,another at Orrell, and also one at Golborne. Bro. H. SHARPLES, FI.D.R., in his address, said the Order of Rechabites had about 1,600 branches in all parts of the United Kingdom and in colonies under the British crown. Their adult membership was just over i 90,000 while their juvenile membership was betweep 40,000 or 50,000, so that they were a great temperance army and brotherhood. They had their clearance card system, so that a member could go all over the United Kingdom and to the colonies and find himself at home in other branches of the Order. In the colony of Victoria alone they had 10,000 Rechabites, and Mr. Sharpies re- ferred to instances in which valuable help had been given by Australian Rechabites to brethren who had emigrated to that country. A necessary condition to joining the Order was the total abstinence pledge, and they found that out of their 90,000 members not one per cent left through the breaking of the pledge. (Applause.) On the motion of Brother Mims, seconded by Brother WRIGHT, a vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman and Brother Sharpies. The CHAIRMAN, in responding, referred to the coming licensing sessions at Warrington, next Tuesday. He was glad to know that there was a growing feeling that there were already sufficient public houses in Warrington. He hoped the magistrates would again show that they were determined not to increase opportunities for the sale of drink in the town. (Hear, hear). It seemed to him little short of a scandal that the same men with the same applications for the same houses and the same licenses should come year after year to ask for the licences which had, every time asked for, been refused. He thought there ought to be some understanding come to, or spine method discovered and adopted by the Bench, to put a stop to that continual asking for a thing which had, over and over again, been refused. ,(Hear, hear, and applause). , The meeting then terminated. MEETING IN BRICK-STREET.

A second meeting was held in Brick-st. Schoolroom, on Tuesday evening, Councillor H. Roberts occupying the chair. There were also on the platform Bro. Sharpies, Bro. Wright, Tent secretary, Bro. W. Hudson, Bro. Mills, and Bro. Halt, D.S. The.CIIAIRMAN, in his opening remarks, said that if he was net a Rechabite in essence, he was in spirit, and those who knew him were aware that he was a life teetotaller, and that he had so far taken a fair share in the work of temperance in Warrington. There were two things in life which no one could :possibly avoid. One was sickness, and the other death. That being the case, it became incumbent upon every man that he should as far as he possibly could ameliorate those two sad condi- tions by providing for them to the utmost of his ability. It was the duty of all men, particularly of men who were married, to connect themselves with some friendly society, so that when the time came when, through some unfortunate accident, or some disease contracted, they were laid aside from work, they might receive that assistance and benefit from a brotherhood which helped so many families over those difficult times in their history. But before a man joined a friendly society,he should take care what society he connected himself with. It was ridiculous for a man to join a society so badly in debt, or mortgag,ed,that there was no probable chance that he would be abre to get the benefit his contributions entitled him to. He had no hesitation in saying that no man could be wrong in join- ing the Rechabite Society, which was a .sound and wealthy one. It was a very good thing if all the mem- bers of a friendly society were teetotallers, for they were the best" lives" in the country. Several of the best of the insurance companies occasionally offered reduced premiums to teetotal lives to induce them to become members. When they had a society like the Rechabites, composed of teetotallers, at any rate they had a greater chance of having less calls than was the case with any other society. He gave all credit to other societies, but thought it was a misfortune that many clubs and societies held their meetings in public-houses, which must be disadvantageous for them. In some instances, the rent of the room was expended in drink. (Applauee,) Bro. W. WRIGUT then read a report of the working of the Charity Tent, which has been in existence for some- thing like 55 years, and has met all claims for sickness and death during that period. At the annual balance qf this district in 1688 the amount of the funeral fund wak £374 14s. 10id., and the amount of the fund at December, 1889, was £427 15s. 51d. There was also a balance in hand on the management fund. The number of benefit members was 290. Bro. SEEARPLES then spoke at considerable length on the benefits of the Rechabite Order, his remarks being listened to with great attention. Bro. W. HunsoN proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Sharpies for his address, to Councillor H. Roberts for presiding, and to Bro. Hall for taking the chair during the latter portion of the evening. He remarked that if there was a town in England that wanted stirring up as regarded the temperance cause it was Warrington. They were opposed by influences of a gigantic character, and it became the duty of all temperance people to use all the energy they had in endeavouring to prevent the enormous strides that drink was making. Bro. MILLS seconded the proposition, which was car ried and briefly acknowledged by Bro. Sharpies. Bro. Hall, who also replied., said that he was sorry that in Warrington they had not more temperance men in the Town Council. When the proper time the Rechabites must strive to see if they could not be represented on the Council, as well as the drink traffic. The meeting then closed. FURTHER MEETINGS. On Wednesday night a meeting was held in the Tem- perance Hall, Latchford, and presided over by Mr. J. Harrison. Addressss on Rechabitism were given by Bros. Sharpies, T. Hall, and J. W. Hall, and afterwards , a strong desire was expressed for the formation of a tent in Latchford, and, we understand, it is probable that this desire willl be carried out. After the meeting at Latchford, Bro. Sharpies visited the Temperance Mission Lodge of Good Tempiars, in Academy-st., and there delivered another address on be- half of Rechabitism. Mr. Sharpies also presented to one of the members of the lodge—Bro. Charles McCoy—a re- galia, in recognition of his havine, obtained the largest number of members for the lodge during the last three months. rho-number of members obtained by Bro. McCoy is ten.

Meetings in furtherance of Rechabitisru were held at Lowton Common, on Thursday night, and at Golborne last night. At Lowton the chairman was Bro. W. Hud- son, of Warrington, and the speakers were Bros. Sharpies, Pilling, Hulme, and Tunstall. ft is likely that a tent will be formed at Lowton as a consequence of the meet- ing.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ' ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ' ATHLETICS.
CRICKET.

The classificid list of counties has been Issued by the Cricket Coamfil. Sussex is, of course, retained for the present yearin the first class; but her claims will be hotly disputed next year by Warwickshire, Somerset, Leicester, and Derbyshire, who are now placed with Hampshire, 'Essex, Cheshire, and Staffordshire in the second class. Of these contestants it is probable that it will be difficult to choose between Derbyshire, Leicester, and WarwiOkShiro at the close. Somersetshire is playing very wen, andit has in its ranks men who have been well trained inmany hard-fought fields and are worth a place in any connty eleven ; but one of the three midland counties, vl/1,1 expect, supply the successor to unfortu- nate Sussex.

Gloucesterdhire has again done well in defeating a powerful Watts 4jeleven. The western county has scored splendidly in the-championship since Woof re-joined,and his bowling was the main cause of the second, as it was of the first, 'victory over Notts. Shrewsbury was again out of form, %tit Flowers played a fine innings. Dr. Grace, batting °ma soft wicket on Friday, WA a won- derfully differentoperson to the Dr. Grace who failed so badly on a similar wicket on the Oval. Richardson, Sherwin, and Tox-were absent from the Notts team, their places beingetaken by Needham, Daft, and Carlin; whilst Glancesterplayed the strong,est eleven it has put in the field far years.' In the first innings of Notts Woof took seven wickets-for 27 runs, and in the second dis- missed ShrewSbtrry, Barnes, and Butler in one over, 'Gloucestershire have now beaten Yorkshire, Notts (twice), and Sussex ; and time and weather have 'robbed them of victory in other contests.
CYCLING.

Week after wedlethe c-y-c-ling-w—orld has recently been electrified by the doings of R. J. M'Credy, the great Dublin University•tkier, who has now secured all the safety bicycle championships, and who by his successes has so conclusively preyed the superiority of the pneu- matic-tired machines. When M'Credy returns home -almost, every Irish cyclist will be there to do him homage, as he is looked upon in the light of a liational hero. inas- much as the pneumatic tire is an Irish patent which was lat first very coldly received by the cyclists of this , country.

Riding in magnificent form last week on the Padding- ton Recreation tract •M'Credy won the fifty miles championship in 2 hours -29 minutes 55 1-5 seconds. There were no less than Sixteen competitors, and as a welcome relief from the wretched " loafs," some of our championship events Starve beep, the whole crowd rode as for clear life, the race9Deing.a .splendid one, every re- cord from 22 miles beingtrroken. L. Stroud. the Oxford University rider, was second, and A. F. Illsley third, whilst that grand rider, J.ll. Adams was fourth. Thir- teen of the competitors covered rver 21 miles In the hour, Whilst six managed to get onttide 40 miles In two hours—facts which speak eloquently of the capabilities of the riders as a whole.

Cyclists are in favour with the French Ministry of War. It bas made arrangements .to augment their number coutiderably during the autnmn manceuvres both in the reserve and regular army. 'Notice is given to all Resereicts who have machines • to bring them at an early date to their respective depot, where they will be placed in store for them until the rnant,luvres begin. Should the muster be insufficient ;thoDepartment will hire other machines. It is thought desirable to .have a great number of soldiers able to use the iron .horae. Cycling companies are the best adapted to steal mataes on an enemy by reason GC the speed and silence with which tisey may advance.

Mr. P. C. Wilson :writes to the " Daily Graphie " : Mr. M. A. Holbein, of the North-road and ;Catford Cycling Clubs, started on a Whippet safety bicycle from Teter- borough to beat his own record for iiity miles en the road. He was accompanied by myself, ef the Bath Road and Catford Cycling Clubs, and Mr. E. Dangerfield of the mane clubs, on a tandem tricycle. Floibein rode the fifty miles in 2h. 38m. 575„ and we on the tandem tricycle rode the same distance in 2h. 40m. 345. Both machines 'heat the mord. The best previous tandem record was 12h, 36m. 3s, by G. P. Mille and A. J. Wilson, September 22, 1836. Haibein beat the safety, record on August 3,, , 1890 ; time, 2h. 40m. 38s. lie is 29 years of age, was born in Manchester, and holds all the recognised road records. Our start was from feterborough, through Norman Cross, Stilton, Alconbury. Buckden, and Biggieswade, finishing at Hitelrin. "fhe records were timed by F. T. Bidla,ite and A. J. div.head: SUCCESSFUL SWIM ACROSS THE CHAN NEL.
div.p: SUCCESSFUL SWIM ACROSS THE CHAN NEL.

Davis Dalton, the American back-swimmer, started on Sunday evening from Boulogne to swim across the Channel, from the French coast to Folkestone. Dalton has for the last two months been training at Folkestone. He had intended to swim from the English side of the Channel, but, under advice, he determined to select Cape Gristlez as the point from which to begin his undertaking. The distance he had to traverse was about sixty miles. Dalton undertook to swim the whole distance on his back, and by propulsion from his legs only. Owing to the boisterous weather Dalton had been unable to fix any date, and for several days he had awaited the opportunity which presented itself on Sunday morning. Shortly I after three o'clock Dalton left Folkestone in the life boat Ocean wing for Cape Grisnez, with Mr. Dunn as captain and pilot. It was blowing a stiff breeze, but the wind gradually abated, and by night the weather was quite favcurable. Dalton was very ,confident of success. His belief was that by swimming .Dri his back he would have betteropportunities of restin,, himself than in the ordin- ary style of swimming. Dalton landed on Folkestone beach en Monday afternoon. He had been 23 hours in the water.

A Dever correspondent, telegraphing at half-past two on Tuesday morning, says that Dalton, who accom- plished the feat of swimming the Channel, and landed at Folkestone yesterday afternoon, is in a very precarious condition, suffering severely from internal cramp. The distanoehe accomplished was about 50 miles, the tide carrying him to the westward. . .
A'tele'gram, despatched at noon on Tuesday, states that Dalton, the American swimmer, still lies in a pre- cations condition at the Folkestone bathing establish- ment, but has greatly improved.
DID D'ALTON SWIM THE CHANNEL?

Four gentlemen, dating from the yacht Argo, at South- sea, publish a letter in Thursday's Times" stating that they left lloulogne Harbour just ahead of the Ocean King, the craft which accompanied the American swimmer Dalton, and that although they kept a vigilant lookout for a considerable period, they were unable to perceive any man in the water. They pointedly suggest, in fact, that the feat of swimming the Channel was not accom- plished by Dalton. In reply to this an affidavit was sworn by Dalton, or, Thursday, before a Folkestone magistrate. in which the swimmer declared that he swam the w'holeffistance, and announced his intention to take proceedings against the siznatories of the letter..

div.head: FIGHTING IN MOROCCO.
div.p: FIGHTING IN MOROCCO.
80 PRISONERS BEHEADED.

A depatch from Tangier of Wednesday's date says that the Sultan of Moroeeo, while proceeding along the Tadla-road,,changed his course unexpectedly and turned to the North, taking in the rear theZemmour tribe, who lately attacked the camp of the Sultan's son and massacred a number of his troops. The Sultan attacked the Zertunour, and after a battle, in which he was the victor, decapitated eighty of the prisoners. The Sultan's action, adds the despatch, has had a great moral effect upon the 13atbary tribes. TANoma, MURSDAY.—lntelligenee from the Sultan of Morocco's camp states that the Moorish army has de- feated with heavy loss the insurgent Zemmour tribes. There is no truth in reports published by Spanish papers that the Sultan was surrounded by a large army o f the united rebel tribes.

div.head: TERRIBLE RAILWAY DISASTER.
div.p: TERRIBLE RAILWAY DISASTER.
TWENTY PERSONS KILLED AND THIRTY INJURED.

New Yordt, WEDNESDAY.—Seventeen persons have been killed and thirty injured in the accident which be- fell the Woods gall express near Quincy yesterday. It seems that the engine when turning a curve near Quincy suddenly went off the rails, and fell alongside the track. Four of the five cars attached escaped, hut the fifth was smashed, and all who were traveling in it were killed. Many were frightfullyinjured, and several were scalded to death, owing to the car catching the full escape of steam from the engine_ Some repairs were bein made at tke spot, and it is stated that these were so iao• fficient that the rails snapped under the pressuure of she engine antheaused the disaster.

The railway accident near Quincy, reported on Thurs- day,:is said to have been caused by workmen leaving a big jack across the rails. One aged man was found in an attitude indicating that be ,liad screened his wife with his own body against the scalding flood; both were dead. The accident proves to have ,been more disastrous than was at first thought. Twenty persons were killed, and thirty others injured.

div.head: IRISH LEAGUE OF AMERICA.
div.p: THE IRISH LEAGUE OF AMERICA.

NEW YORK, IVESDAY NIGHT. Mr. O'Reilly, the treasurer of the Irish League of America, said at Speed, Milwaukee, on Tuesday, at a picnic for the benefit of the Parnell Fund, that some people had been disposed to ask what became of the vast sums sent to Ireland. The sums had not been so large as many people imagined. During the last ten years they had amounted to only 1,000,000 dollars, an average of 100,000 dollars for each year. The largest sum for any two years was 300,000 dollars, and this was not large compared with the sums raised in Ireland. The attendance at the picnic was large, and several thou- sand dollars were raced for, in aid of the fund.

div.head: OUTRAGES IN ARMENIA.
div.p: THE OUTRAGES IN ARMENIA.

REPORTED MASSACRE AT MOOSE. Mont, TllESDAY.—According to reports received to day the condition of things in Armenia is becoming more and more deplorable. A letter from Erzerouni states • that in the town of Moosh there has been a massacre of Christians. The number of the victims is not yet known. but it is believed to be great. Accounts of murders cf Christians in the villages of the district of Moosh are con- tinually coming in. Zekki Pacha, who was on march - from Erzeroum to Bayazid with two battalions of in- fantry and a battery of artillery, has changed his direc- tion, and taken the road to Moosh. Between Bayazid and Van all communication is interrupted, neither traffic nor travellers passing between the two places' . Thit Governor of Bayazid has called in all the Kurds of his district who were in the mountains with their flocks for the summer, and has assembled them round Bayazid. There are rumours current here that Persian troops are being sent towards the Turkish frontier.
MR. GLADSTONE AT HAWARDEN STIOW.

Mr. Gladstone, speaking on Thursday at the flawar- den and Buckley Horticultural Association, expressed great satisfaction at the improvement in the quality 9f exhibits compared with those of last year. He believed ?f, would be immensely for the benefit of the country' If farmers contrived to introduce a more systematic and per- manent regard to the minor branches of production. It had been said that the English climate was not so gfood f or- fruit farming as that of France. But it was not the climate that stood in the way, and for proof of that le them look to Scotland, one of whose universities had been first selected for the delivery of a lecture on the important subject of fruit farming. In the course of further remarks, Mr. Gladstone referred tc' a book on "Profitable Rabbit-Farming," written 1a.9 Major Morant, the animals raised being tame ones in hutches, and suggested this as a minor branch of Tr' duction connected with the great subject of turniq the land to better account. Towards the close of big remarks Mr. Gladstone also referred encouragineY tO the production of eggs and milk.

div.head: ALARMING FIRE AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: ALARMING FIRE AT ST. HELENS.

-- About a quarter to eight on Sunday night a firer of a most alarming character, was discovered on the extensive premises of Messrs. Pilkington Bros., plate-glass manufacturers, Cowley-hill, St. Helena. The building covered an immense area, and about 2,000 hands are employed therein when the Works are in operation. For the past eleven weeks, hoW" ever, the casting-hall men have been out on strike for all advance of warms, and their absence has necessitated the stoppage of all other workpeople. The dispute stnll remains unsettled, but the conflagration is accounted , or apart from the unfortunate disagreement between the masters and men. The announcement that the Plate- glass works were on fire occasioned a great sensation ill the town, and there were suspicions entertained in sea!) quarters that the outbreak might be due to an inane"' ary. The managers, however, entertained n° such idea, and stated that such fears were groundless. The flames broke out near the pans in which saltcalte liquor is boiled, in a portion of the works known as the saltcake house. In this house several labourers were at work, and it is supposed that by the overheating of one of the pans the adjoining woodwork, including a large wooden fan used for the purpose of driving air into ,tne saltcake, caught fire. Immediately it was observed alarm was raised. The flames, however, spread Nvi)..,,'t' great rapidity, and in a few minutes the whole of t" building was ignited. The works "buzzer "was sounded, and information of the fire was conveyed to the fire" brigade station at the Town Hall. The firebell rang 3.1 people were leaving the various places of worship, an" considerable excitement was occasioned. As quickly as possible the men in the works got out W°,. pipes, and attempted to suppress the flames, 1°.,"„," owing to the unfortunate strike there seemed lack of unity in regard to the operations. The real worked heartily under the circumstances until the arrival of the borcugh brigade with the steam eng,4l.,e; This was taken to the settling pits, near the grinal..t sheds, and soon there was a plentiful supply of water sa. hand. In the meantime the whole of the roof ovr.r the saltcake pans had been destroyed, and as the flamees shot upwards they cast a glare over the neighbourhooa. Tne roof of the saltcake house was also partially deg- troyed, and the efforts of the brigade were directed t° ) preventing further spread. On •:,wo sides of the burn' ing building were valuable property, and fortunatel9 , the men were successful in saving these portions of the ) works. The flames burned fiercely for about an hour before the willing workers got a firm hold upon the fire. The loss amounted to about £1,500, which is, however, . covered by insurance. Among those present superin- tending operations were Captain Thomson (manager), Mr. Jenkinson (chief engineer), and Mr. Preston (fore , man.)

div.p: THE FUNERAL OF CARDINAL NEWMAN. IMPRESSIVE CEREMONY. The mortal remains of Cardinal Newman were, on Tuesday, conveyed to their last resting place at Rednal, Birmingham, with all the grave ceremonies laid down for the burial of a great dignitary of tho Romish Church. From early morning the neighbourhood of the Oratory in Hagley-rd., had been thronged with people, who watched the arrivals of the bishops and peers staying in the neighbourhood, who had also attended the dirge sung by The Fathers on Monday evening. The requiem service was timed to commence at eleven o'clock, but an hour before that the holders of tickets were presenting them to the policemen who in large force guarded the entrance to the cloisters which conduct to the entrance to the • chapel. Inside, although applications for tickets had been made in enormous numbers, only a comfortable attendancethad been permitted. Here the dignity of the occasion began to make itself apparent. The light which . streamed through the circular windows of the thick walls only partially illuminated a sombre scene, where every , - scrap of ecclesiastical decoration was overlaid with black velvet fringed with yellow, so that as the eye wandered to the great apse which forms the chancel it seemed to loose itself in a thick darkness. On a bier in front of the chancel steps was the object to which many eyes •t were turned. The coffin containing the late Cardinal rested there beneath a violet velvet pall, which before the Requiem commenced was removed to show the polished oak coffin underneath. On the foot of the coffin el. Was the red hat of the cardmalate( while the Cardinal's biretta rested on a lower pedestal, the front of which bore the arms of the deceased dignitary. The heraldic symbol consisted simply of three hearts, with the motto " Cor ad Cur loquitur ' (Heart speaketh. unto heart), and the Cardinal's hat as a crest. In compliance with the laws of the Church the body, as it rested in the seal- ed coffin ready for interment, was clothed in full pontifi- +L cal vestments, with plain mitre and crozier. The coffin 111 bore upon its lid a shield with the Cardinal's arms and fv, the following inscription :—" Eminentissimus et Rever- t,. endissimus Joannes Henricus Newman, Cardinalis Diaeonus S. Georgii Velabro, Obiit die xi. Augusti, MDCCCXC. R.1.P." The principal lay members present were the Duke of Norfolk, the Duke of Newcastle, Prince Doria, Viscount. Viscountess, and Miss Southwell, Viscount Feilding . (representing the Earl of Denbigh) Lady Margaret , Howard, Lord Arundel of Wardour, Lord North, Lord 'Braye and the Hon. A. Verney Cave, Lord Dormer, Lord Emly, Lord Coleridge, Captain Lord Edmund • Talbot, Baron and Lady Mary von Hugel, General , -Lord Ralph Kerr, Lady Bateman Scott and Miss Scott, Lady Simcox, Sir Rowland Blennerhassett, Sir Edward Blount, Sir Sherston Baker, the Rev. Sir William Cope and Lady Cope, and Mr. Justice Day. From Oxford University there were the President of "Trinity College and the Provost of Oriel, while the Dean of Durham, the Rev. Canon Furse,the Rev. Canon Paget, and the Rev. J. Keble were among the congregation.. 'The relatives of the deceased Cardinal who attended as chief mourners were Mrs. T. Mozley, Messrs. A. and J. Mozley, J. Fourdriniere, and H. W. Mozley. Amongst the Church dignitaries present were—Dr. Clifford, Bishop of Clifton; Dr. O'Reilly, Bishop of Liverpool; Dr. Hedley, Bishop of Newport; Dr. Bagshawe, Bishop of Notting- • ham ; -Dr. Knight, Bishop of Shrewsbury; Dr. Riddle, Bishop of Northampton; Dr. Virtue, Bishop of Ports- Mouth; Dr. Butt, Bishop of Southwark; Dr. Patterson, . Bishop of Emmaus ; tbellishop of Plymouth ;Dr. Donnelly, Bishop of Canea ; and Dr. O'Dwyer, Bishop of Limerick. • The scene in the Oratory during the Requiem was • brilliant rather than solemn, the unaccustomed figures of Capuchins, Franciscans, Dominicans, Passionists, and Benedictines, in their strange habits as they mingled in the procession; the bright mauve of the bishops' robes and the splendid vestments of the Bishops Celebrant and . the bishops who were to perform the ceremony of absolu- tion making up a striking picture. Bishop Ilsey was the Celebrant of the Requiem, Canon O'Sullivan was assist- ant priest, Canon Longman deacon, and Canon O'Han- lon sub-deacon. The chants were performed by a choir and priests of the town, assisted by members of the choirs of the Oratory Chapel and that of St. Chad's Cathedral. There was no instrumental accompaniment, bet the music was exquisitely rendered. Then Bishop Clifford mounted the pulpit, and delivered the discourse On the life of the just and holy man who had passed away. The remarkable change which had come over England in its attitude to the Catholic religion he ascribed to the success with which Newman had broken down the hairier of mutual dis- trust by the publication of the " Apologia," and as an example of the widespread confidence reposed in him, declared there was scarcely an individual of note who had been received into the Church during the last thirty years who, who during his search after truth, had not received some assistance from Cardinal Newman. He was truly a man of God, always feeling himself to be in the presence of God, and with the duty of serving Him and doing his will foremost in all his thoughts. His love of truth, and his warm sympathising heart were chief among the traits of his character. Devoid of personal ambition, and most unselfish, naturally of a retiring dis- position, and very sensitive,he was a sincere friend,most considerate to others, feeling any slight or injustice Offered to his friends or himself. His writings would be read wherever the English language was spoken, and would continue to do sorlie of the work he had done on earth. With sorrowing hearts, they committed his soul to God.

Then came the ceremony of absolution, which, ordi- narily performed but once, is in the case of high person- . ages several times repeated. The Bishops of Clifton, Northampton, Nottingham, Newport, and the Bishop of ths Diocese officiated. The choir began by singing in harmony the verses written for the funeral of Cardinal Wiseman and each bishop in turn passed round the coffin with holy water and incense, repeating in an undertone the Pater Nester. This was the moment when the scene became most striking. A hundred tapers were held by the clergy round the coffin, the polished lid of Which seemed to be aflame with light. Bishop Ilsley, Wearing cope and mitre, sat at the -foot of the coffin, Whilst the other four bishops in copes and mitres stood around, the bright illumination bringing out every figure in the scene most strongly. The coffin was then Shouldered by six bearers and conveyed to the hearse in Waiting for Rednal, where the body was to be interred. A grand procession of clergy and laity followed it along the cloisters. Only Bishop Clifford, the Duke of Norfolk, Lord Emlv, the Cardinal's relatives, a number of the Fathers of the Oratory and the Birmingham clergy f °flowed to Rednal. Rednal is a breezy country Spot about eight miles from Birmingham, where an Oratorian's retreat was founded by the Cardinal out of the surplus of subscription with which he had de- frayed the cost of the Achilli trial. There is a burying ground in connection with the retreat. The Cardinal Often visited this quiet refuge, which allured him by its seclusion and touched him with its rural beauty. Till* to-day there were but six graves in it, but now the remains of Cardinal Newmann lie side by side with those of his dear friend Ambrose St. John, whose death in 1878, was one of the great griefs which overtook the Cardinal's declining years. Here, with a simplicity which contrasted strikingly with the ' gorgeous ceremonies at the Oratory, the Cardinal was buried. The Rev. Austin Mills, Dean of the Oratory congregation, performed the burial service, the Fathers of the Oratory chanting the " Miserere " as they approached the grave, the Cardinal's body servant following with his biretta, and the relatives corning last. When the body had been laid in the grave and a last look taken, the procession came from the burial ground and returned to Birmingham.. Perhaps the Cardinal's body will not always lie there; it may be that in the years to come his remains will be brought back to the Oratory and re-interred. Of the wreaths sent to the Rednal Retreat, the largest was an enormous one from the Marquis of Ripon, composed of 'tuberoses, stephanotis, white carnations, cream roses, &c. Another floral tribute came from Baroness Burdett Coutts and Mr. Burdett Coutts. On Tuesday masses for the dead, in memory of the late Cardinal Newman, were solemnized in the . different churches and chapels of the two metropolitan dioceses of Westminster and Southwark, and were attended by comparatively large congregations, the attendance being numerous at St. Mary's Moorfields (for many years the pro-Cathedral of the late Cardinal Wiseman), where a solemn requiem pro defunctis was sung by the Right Rey. Monsignor Gilbert, the Vicar-General of the Arch- diocese, and the priests of the Mission. Cardinal Manning, delivering an address on Wednes- day, at a requiem service for the late Cardinal Newman, In the Oratory, South Kensington, said they had lost their greatest witness for the faith, and were all poorer and lower by the loss. It was true, as someone had re- tnarked, that whether Rome canonised him or not, he Would be canonised in the thoughts of pious people of InalaY creeds in England. His writings were in their hands, but beyond the power of all books had been the example of his humble and unworldly life—always the same, in -union with God, and in manifold charity to all Who sought him. "WEEP NOT FOR ME." Mr. Arthur W. Hutton writes to the " Pall Mall Gazette" as follow :—I have been surprised no one has recalled Newman's verses in the " Lyra Apostolica," which I send herewith. The hope expressed in them that after death he might know what was passing among friends left behind is very characteristic. They Were not reprinted in his " Verses on Various Occa- sions"

Weep not for me; Be blithe as wont, nor tinge with gloom The stream of love that circles home, Light hearts and free! Joy in the gifts Heaven's bounty sends; Nor miss my face, dear friends! I still am near. Watching the smiles I prized on earth, Your converse mild,-y@ur blameless mirth; Now, too, I hear Of whispered sounds the tale complete, Low prayers and musings sweet. A sea before The Throne is spread; the pure still glass Pictures all earth scenes as they pass. We on its shore, Share in the boson% of our rest +God's knowledge, and are blest!

div.p: THE LATE CARDINAL NEWMA.N.
LOCAL PULPIT REFERENCES.

The Rev. John Yonge, pastor of Wycliffe Congre- gational Church, Warrington, on Sunday evening ; preached a special sermon in reference to the late Cardinal Newman. There was a large congregation. ' Mr. Yonge selected as his text the 'Words :—" 0, send out Thy light and Thy truth ; Igt them lead me," Psalm xliii. 3, which also appear in the book used by the Congregationalists, over the hymn "Lead, kindly light, amid the encircling gloom," which was written by the late Cardinal Newman, and which was sung before the commencement of , the discourse. In the course of his sermon, which was listened to with marked attention, the rev. gentleman said that on the unanimous testimony of all who knew him,and upon the abounding evidence of his words and works, one of the truest saints of this country and century lay at that hour in the Oratory at Birmingham awaiting his burial. The fact of his death had come upon this country, especially upon all its more cultured and religious classes, as a great national bereavement. Intelligent evangelical protest- ants regretted and mourned the decease of John Henry Newman, Cardinal of the Roman Church as sin- cerely as did Catholics themselves, and it was probable that many pulpits that day, Noncon- formist as well as Anglican and Catholics, would give respectful and sympathetic tribute to his memory. They would do this in recognition of the un- questionably high and holy purpose and spirit of this man. Evangelical Christians, of course, lamented that he forsook the evangelical faith in which he was born and educated. That he should have done so might re- main to many a mysterious problem. But he was a saintly man from the beginning. His aspiration from boyhood was to be pure, true, holy. The Christian life with him was not a profession, but a passion. It was unquestionable that, however far he might have wandered from what we hold as the better and truer faith of his youth, and however incomprehensibly he surrendered his intellect and will at lag to the enthralling teaching and system of Rome, he never let go his spiritual ambition to be excellent, to live near God, and in complete devotion to Jesus Christ. John Henry Newman had lived and died a Saint of God—one of the purestand best of men. Few individual men of our time had exerted so large and permanent an influence upon the religious life of a con- siderable portion of this nation as had the late Cardinal. Most of them who had taken note of religious affairs would know that in recent years in the Church of England things were different from what they were. She had undergone considerable alteration in the drift of her doctrinal teaching, and in the character of her ritual and services. We had become familiar with talk about ritualisin, sacramentalism, and sacerdotalism in the Established Church. The fact had become a matter of general re- gret that, in pulpits of the Establishment, evangelical truth—the doctrine of the simple gospel of Jesus Christ— was to be heard but rarely ; and when heard, as some- times it might be, from the lips of very advanced ritual- ists, it was surrounded by a ceremonialism, and adcom- panied by sacerdotal pretensions which went far to obscure the plain evangelical message, and which intruded the officious intervention of the priest between the sinner and the Saviour. The prevailing doctrines, the widely adopted ritual, were not Protestant. The rising clergy were not evangelical. Whereas once to be a ritualist was to be deemed eccentric and unusual, now to be an evangelical was to be considered old-fashioned and narrow. The Church of England was mainly, if only coldly and formally, evangelical, until John Henry Newman, in alliance with John Kelpie, and the celebrated Dr. Pusey, and others, all of them being mon of great spiritual excellence, and of devoutest purpose, brought out a series of pamphlets which were known as "Tracts of the Times," and so gave the name to the men who wrote, read, and followed them, of Tractarians. Probably the seniors among them might have some recollection of the sensation produced forty or fifty 3, ears ago by this new Oxford movement. It was intended, no doubt, to give new life and earnest- ness to the churches of the Establishment, but it was also meant as a counter-move to the political tendency of the day, which was deemed by some to be operating to the disadvantage of the church as a sacred institution and teacher. Keble claimed for the Church of England that she possessed the true Apostolic suc- cession—" that she, and she alone, was the true Catholic Church, and that Rome had wandered away from the-right path, and foregone the glorious mission which she might have maintained." With this position Newman in that day heartily sympathised, and by his pen and his preaching did more than any other man to maintain and promote it. Ultimately the Bishops, and the heads of the Houses at Oxford, were aroused to action, and as a result the celebrated Tracts were stopped, and Newman was thrust back more than ever upon his own thoughts and studies. Newman now transferred his study from the Scriptures, and plunged into the study of the Fathers. The preacher, having further recounted how the Cardinal was at last led to join the Catholic Church, said that they believed most earnestly that Newman was seriously misled in his thoughts, studies, and reasonings. And they believed, further, that his teachings and example had tended to the serious misleading of many more. The ritualistic and sacerdotal reyival in the Church of England could , only be regarded by them with the greatest distrust and ; dislike. The resurrection of the priest in a so- called Protestant community; was a present-day fact , which boded ill for the church of the nation. They might not as yet admit that the 4 Roman faith had any real chance in this country. It would not have if their free evangelical churches were alive and active throughout the land. But if that faith should find supremacy again it would be due to Newman. , He himself had declared that the "Ritualists are leavening the various English denominations and parties far beyond , their own range with principles and sentiments tending , towards their ultimate absorption into the Catholic ( Church." Against this they needed to be on their guard. Their young people especially needed to be careful lest any attraction of a musical service, a pretty ceremonial, or a respectable social influence, should lead them to take up with a church that was tending towards Rome. That , night they could think of Newman emancipated from the ' hallucinations, sophistries, and superstitions of his later faith; made free in the clear light of the land of glory, rejoicing in the vision of God. The Rev. Father Larkin, preaching at St. Alban's (8.C.) Church, on Sunday evening, dealt with the same subject. He said that the only Catholic influence that ever Cardinal Newman could remember in his youth was the fact that he was once taken by his father into one of the London chapels, and he lived to be a man of 44 years of age before he came again near any direct influence such as that. In 1839, during the Long Vacation, he re- mained at Oxford and went into a long course of reading with regard to the ancient heresy. After an unsuccess- ful attempt to harmonize the teaching of the Protestant Church in England with the teaching of that one church which has spread through all the world, the light came to him on the 9th April, 1845 11, was baptized, and made his confession, thereby becoming a Catholic. He entered thoroughly into the spirit of the church, and entered so humbly that he who was the pontiff in one religion became an acolyte in another, living to the age of ninety years and dying a cardinal of the holy Roman Church. At the conclusion of the service, the organist (Mr. J. B. Caldwell), played the Dead March.

div.head: CHARGE OF ROBBING SIR CHARLES
div.p: THE CHARGE OF ROBBING SIR CHARLES

DILKE. At Westminster Police Court, on Monday. Albert Griffith, aged nineteen years, well dressed, and described as a billiard marker, was charged on a warrant with being concerned with another man, named Edward Bryer, now in custody, in stealing a cashbox, containing LW in gold, and £4O in notes, a receipt for £l,OOO, and other documents, from 76, Sloane-st., the residence of Sir C. Dilke. Suer, who was charged last week, was second footman at Charles's, and it was stated that be raised an alarm that the house had been broken into. Subsequently Miss Abraham, who is Lady Duke's pri- vate secretary, found a desk which she had left locked 'broken open, and the cash box was missed. Part of the I missing property was found in Bryer's drawer, and he then confessed that he and Griffith had planned the rob- bery, and divided the money.—Prisoner was remanded in custody for a week.

THE ACCIDENT AT THE CHEMICAL WOrKS,

div.head: SANKEY BRIDGES.
div.p: SANKEY BRIDGES.

- Sir,—The report in your paper last Saturday, of the accident to Frederick Roberts, is inaccurate. He did not fall into a tank of acid. Either from disobedience or ignorance, he disregarded the order given him to get three gallons of acid from certain bottles, and put it into a tank containing liquid. Instead of doing so, he went to a carboy near at hand, and took three gallons of another sort of acid, and put it into the liquid in the I tank. Immediately an explosion occurred, blowing some of the liquid over him, and burning him in places rather severely. Happily the wind was blowing strongly, driving the spray of acid from him, or the result might have been, if not fatal,•very serious. The insertion of this correction will much oblige. Yours respectfully, JEFFREY • HA RDMAN. Warrington Chemical Works, Sankey Bridges, August 18th, 1890.

EQUITABLE LOCAL RATING. Sir,—At this time, when so many tradesmen and householders are smarting under the scourge of the increased assessment, it will not be out of place to dis- cuss the important question whether,in order to secure a more equitable distribution of rating, the local rates and taxes ought to be levied continuously upon ei house and shop property, that is to say, whether let or unlet. If this were done I contend :—(1) That thereby no in- justice would ensue to landlords. (2) That serious pre- sent injustice to tenants, arising from houses and shops being kept unlet until an exorbitant rent can be obtained (leaving the sum total of the rates to be made up by the tenants of occupied houses and shops) would be removed. (3) That not only by this plan would the tenants derive benefit from a great reduction in their quarterly rates. but landlords also would gain by the restraint thus put upon the speculative builder, who would no longer erect (I should say" run up ") by the hundreds if he knew that when they were finished he would have to pay the local rates for them as well as the ground rent. 4. That it is no more unfair to demand payment of rates when the house is unlet than payment of ground rent the landlord being considered as the occupier of his In 'et property. I would further suggest to your readers that side by side with this important question of continuous rating should be considered :- 1. The justice of rating at an assessment of 4 per cent. on the selling value all land within a certain radius of the centre of London. 2. The rating at 4 per cent. on cost of const. action all private mansions throughout the country. 3. Whether it would not be far more equitable than the present system that a national rate should be levied for poor rate, School Board rate, police, roads and bridges, and sanitation. I need scarcely add that, as far as my time will per- mit, I am prepared to defend these suggestions either in the Press or at public meetings.—Yours faithfully, J. HAYSMAN. Finchley-rd., London, N.W.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

A STEAMER FOR THE SHIP CANAL. There was launched at Port Glasgow on Wednesday for Messrs. Ifillgomf and Co., of Manchester, a twin- screw steel steamer named The Satellite, of 1,400 tons register. Her dimensions are—Length, 2601 t. : breadth, 34ft. 9in. : depth, 1911. Two sets of triple expansion engines will be supplied by the builders of the vessel, Messrs. Blackwood and Gordon, and she is expected to attain a high rate of speed. FATAL ACCIDENTS. On Tuesday afternoon Mr. 11. Churton held an inquest at Ellesmere Port on the body of a man named Standish Lea, who accidentaly fell off a plank into the Ship Canal Dock at Eastham, and died at Ellesmere Port Hospital. Also on Edward Williams, aged twenty-three, residing on Frodshatn Marsh, who, while engaged remov- ing an empty wagon from s steam navvy, was knocked down and run over by a wagon, owing to his horse bolt- ing. He sustained fatal injuries. Verdicts of " Acci- dental death" were returned. A verdict of accidental death was returned by a jury on Thursday at an inquest held in the Ship Canal Hospital, Barton-on-Irwell, on the body of an excavator on the canal, named Joseph Bingham, 29 years of age, who was knocked dawn by a wagon on Wednesday and died from his injuries.

div.head: LY MM.
div.p: LY MM.

Music AT THE Caoss.—The Lymm Church of England Brass Band played a selection of miscellaneous music at the Cross, Lymm, on Saturday evening. There was a large attendance. Mr. T. Gregson conducted. Tug PARISH CHURCH.—The new roof of the Parish Church is not yet finished, and the windows have still to be put in. The builders and stone masons have,however. departed, and manv of them have found employment on the Ship Canal at Thelwall. A handsome new clock has been presented by Miss Fox, of Brookfield, Lymm, to place in the church tower when completed. Nothing definite has yet been decided with reference to the bells. To replace the old bells about £BOO will be required. THE REMOVAL OF A BODY mom' THE BT7I2IAL GROUND.— On Thursday, the Rev. G. %V. Guest, rector of Lymm, was served with a faculty by Mrs. Cash, wife of. and at the instance of,Mr. John Cash, of Acorn Villa, Gee Cross. near Hyde, in the name of the Rev. Thomas Espinell Espin, vicar-general and official principal of the Lord Bishop of Chester, for the "decent and reverent " dis- interment of the body of Brute Cash, the young man who hanged himself, last Tuesday week, in the Long Butts. The faculty ordered that the body be removed ton vault in the new parish of St. George's, Hyde. Dur- ing the afternoon the body was raised, and measure- ments taken for a new coffin, he having been buried in a "town's coffin," being unknown at the time of burial. We believe this to bc the first removal from Lymm burial ground. The parents of the lad were anxious he should lie alongside his brother, who put an end to himself some twelve months ago. NEW STAINED WINDOW.—It will be remembered that the old west window in the churchtower contained three stained lights, and was in memory of "Rector Legh." This window was taken out before the raising of the, tower, and as the architect designed the new window to have four lights instead of three, the stained windows have had to undergo entire reconstruction. This un- dertaking was completed on Thursday morning by Mr. W. Knowles, of 23, Stoneg,ate, York. The old lights were embellished by the figures of S. John, S. Mary, and S. Peter, to which is now added the figure of S. Elizabeth. The glass of the old figures has been re-burnt and encased in new lead, and surrounded by new settings which are exceedingly rich in colouring. Capt. Legh, of High Legh, has contributed £5O towards the cost of enlargement, the remainder being defrayed out of the tower fund. The following are the inscrip- tions :—"ln memory of the Rev. Peter Legh, second son of Egerton Legh, Esq., of High Legh, rector of the first modiety of Lymm, died March 10th, 1851. Also in memory of the first wife of the Rev. Peter Legh, died -July 19th, 1819, and of Jane. second wife of the Rev. tPeter, died November 7th, 1853." Accmenv AT LYMM BRIDOE.—Ort Wednesday afternoon what might have been a serious accident took place on Lymm Bridge. As a lorry laden with aerated waters was coming over the bridge a box of " empties "e On top of one of the horses' backs, which caused him to give a sudden swerve, breaking the pole. AS the heavily loaded lurry had got considerable way on it, the utmost power of the driver was exercised to hold the horses, which were being pushed down the hill sideways by the lurry. 'rho excitement was intense for a few minutes while a trap and horse were being run out .the way, and which bad been standing half way

up the bridge. It was also expected that every minute the horses would be thrown or dashed into one or other of the shops. The driver, who was plucky and courageous in a marked degree, stuck to the reins and crossed the horses' heads, dragging their sides up to resist the impetus of the lurry. Although there were many people about, the driver brought his charge to the bottom of the hill unassisted, at which time the horses became very excited, and would have inevitably rushed off, but for the timely interference of Mr. Thomas Hodge- son, who at very considerable risk caught them by the heads and assisted the driver te bring them to a stand- still. The horses and luny are the property of the Aerated Water Company (Leigh's, of Salford).

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

ESSAY ON " PERssvEnANot." Last evening week an essay was given at the Young Men's Christian Association, by Mr. W. J. Holden, on "Perseverance." There was a good at- tendance of members and friends. The essayist commenced with illustrations, from the lives of ordinary people, and then endeavoured to show how the exhibition of the superior talents of brilliant minds roused the ambition of their less gifted brethren,and served as an impetus to attain to nob- ler things. An interesting discussion followed, and the subject not being exhaugted when the meeting closed, it was decided to take it up again on some future occasion.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF MISS MARY JOHNSON
div.p: MARRIAGE OF MISS MARY JOHNSON
OF 'WARRINGTON. "

The marriage of Miss Mary Johnson, daughter of the late Mr. Ralph Johnson, of Wa.zington, with Mr. R. Lucas.son of Mr. J. Lucas,man.iging director of the Shelton Coal and Iron Company, took place on Wednesday afternoon at Wolstanton Church. A large congregation was present, including many relations and friends of the bride and bridegroom. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. S. Nunn, rector of Lawton assisted by the Rev. L. C. A. Edgeworth, of Wolstatiton church, and the Rev. G. Armitage, vicar of Silverdale. The bride, who was given away by her brother, Mr. F. L. Johnson, was attired in a dre-is of whit, ber -.aline, trimmed with orange blossoms, and veil and canied a massive bouquet of stephanotis. the gift of the bridegroom. The bridesmaids were Miss E. Johnson, sister of the bride and Miss Marjorie Broome, niece of the bridegroom, who wore dresses of white and heliotrope surah silk, and hats trimmed with white feathers. They a!so wore gold, diamond and pearl menythought brooches and can :ed bouquets of gloire de Dijon roses, both the g:fts of the bridegroom. Captain W. H. Grindley acted as best man. The organist played the wedding march and other appropriate musical selec- tions. The honeymoon ,a ill be spent in Ireland. The presents to the bride were handso.ne and numerous.

div.head: PARR'S BANKING COMPANY.
div.p: PARR'S BANKING COMPANY.

A special meeting of the shareholders of this Company was held at the bank premises, Winwick- st., Wareington, yesterday afternoon, for the pm pose of confirming resolutions of the directors proposing an increase of the capital of the Compr ny. The chair was taken by Mr. J. C. Pr le, chairman of the Board of Directors, and there was a frir attendance of directors and shareholders. The first esolution proposed that the nominal c_ it& of ta., C pi y should be increased from £2,F30,0C its present amount, to .C 3,000,000 by the creatic,, of 2,000 new shares of £lOO each, such shares to be issued at the price of .£5O per share. The Chairman moved that the shares be issued, £2O per share to be paid as capital and £3O per share as premium. This was seconded by Mr. N. Eckersley, and cairied without discussion. This issue, at a price so much below the market value of the shares, will be equivalent to a substantial bonus to the shareholders. It will add .£40,000 to the paid up capital, making it £OOO,C. ; and ..CBO,OOO to the reserve fund, making it £360,( The increased business of the bank enables the directors to find employment for the addition to the working capital. The second resolution, which was adopted on the propos itionof the chairman, seconded by Mr. Eckersley,was to the effect that the qualifica- tion of a director should be the holding of 30 shares in his own right, instead of 100 shares, as hereto- fore.

div.head: WARRINGTON WATER WORKS COMPANY.
div.p: WARRINGTON WATER WORKS COMPANY.
HALF YEARLY MEETING.

The ordinary half-yearly meeting of the share- holders of this Company was held on Wednesday afternoon, at the Offices of the Company in Cairo- st. In the absence of Lord Winmarleigh, the chair- man, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., M.P., the deputy- chairman, presided. There were also present Messrs. J. C. Parr, Peter Stubbs, James Marson, John Geddes, T. Barham, Foster (Manchester), T. W. Mellor (Ashton-under-Lvne), Henry Neild, William Fairhurst, W. Mawdsley (Garston), J. Wright Booth E. J. Nicholson (law clerk), and John Ross, seere-

tary. The Directors submitted the following report : "The Revenue Account shows a balance, including £1,045 55. brought from the previous half-year, of £4,922 4s. 3d. The dividend on the £40,000 preference stock amcunts to £9OO leaving a balance of £4,022 4s. 3d., out of which the directors recommend that there be paid for the half-year a dividend at the rate of seven percent. per annum on the £30,000 ordinary seven per cent, share capital; a dividend at the rate of seven-and- a-half per cent, per annum on the £15,000 ordinary seven-and-a-half per cent. share capital; and a dividend at the rate of eight per cent. per annum on the £30,000 ordinary ten per cent, share capital. The balance to be carried forward is the sum of £1209 14s. 3c1., as against £1,043 10s. id. carried forward at the end of the corresponding half-year of 1889, for which half-year a dividend was at the rate of six-and-a-half per cent. per ' annum upon the three classes of ordinary share capital. The reserve fund amounts to the sum of £3,743 10s. The Warrington (Extension and Water) Bill, 1890, which pro- vides, amongother matters, for the transfer of the Com- pany's undertaking to the Corporation of Warrington, on terms which were approved by the shareholders at an extraordinary general meeting held on the 18th June last, has passed through the House of Commons, and been introduced into the House of Lords. The Bill, as amended in the House of Commons, was approved at a special general, or " Wharncliffe," meeting of the Com- pany, held on the 23rd July instant, and the directors anticipate that it will receive the Royal assent before the closo of the present Session of Parliament." The report, on the motion of the Cuarremax, seconded by Mr. J. CHARLTON PARR, was unanimously adopted, and dividends according to the recommendations of the directors were declared. The meeting terminated with a cordial vote of thanks to the Chairman, for presiding, proposed by Mr. J. CHARLTON PARR, and seconded by Mr. JOUN GERDY&

div.head: MA.RRIAGE OF THE REV. E. F JACKSON.
div.p: MA.RRIAGE OF THE REV. E. F JACKSON.

The Rev. E. H. Jackson, who has for the past three years been stationed in Warrington as one of the ministers of the local Wesleyan circuit, has been appointed to the Sheffield circuit. On Sunday morning he preached his farewell sermon at Bold- st. Wesleyan Chapel, and on Tuesday afternoon he was united in matrimony to Miss Sarah Stelfox, of The Firs, Moore.
THE FAREWELL SERMON.

During his farewell discourse, which was addressed to a large congregation, Mr. Jackson remarked that he had seen many great changes in the congregation during his sojourn in Warrington. Divers of them had come from afar, the hair of many had grown gray, but if they con- tinued to live right they would be able to say, "Though I walk through the valley of death, I will fear no evil, for Thou art with me." It had been a pleasure to him to stand up in that grand old pulpit, which was one of the finest in the Connexion. For three years their ways had lain parallel,but now they were going to divert; but he hoped not for ever. He prayed that they might meet in heaven. Whilst it had been a pleasure to be among the Warrington Wesleyans. it had often been a terrible ordeal to him to preach to them, an ordeal so great that no one who was not a preacher could imagine. Many of them were much older than he, and were preachers and teachers themselves, but so far as shnpli- , city and sincerity were concerned, he could look up to God before them and say, "I have tried to do my duty." With regard to his successor, he hoped they would accord him a hearty welcome. He was a most evangelical man, a man whose heart was right with God. If they were as kind to his successor as they had been to him, then he would be all right.

TES MARRIAGE CEREMONY. The marriage was solemnised at the Wesleyan Chapel, Moore. The time appoiated for the oeremony to com- mence being half-past two. Long before that time, how,- ever,the little ehapel was well filled. The officiating min- isters were the Rev. John Gunnell (superintendent of the circuit) and the Rev. William Brookes. The bride was attired in a brown check silk, trimmed with velvet. She was given away by Mr. John Fairc4ough. T.P. There were no bridesmaids. Miss B. Dutton, a friend of the bride, played Meiadelmbn's "Wedding March" as the newly-married couple left the building. On their way from the door to the carriage which was waiting, they were subjected to a heavy shower of rice, and many wishes were expressed that the union upon which they had entered would not only be a long but a happy one. The honeynoon will be spent in Scotland. Norrierous presents had been received, one being to the bride from her Late 'Sunday sebool clam at Moore.

WYCLIFFE CHURCH. To-morrow (Sunday) evening the Rev. J. Yonge will preach in Wycliffe Church on" The sole priest- hood of Christ."
WARRINGTON HIGHWAY BOARD. A meeting of this Board was to have teen held on Wednesday but as only two members pat in an appearance, no business was transacted.
THE MUZZLING ORDER.

Presiding on Wednesday morning, at the War- rington Police Court, Alderman Holmes asked the Chief Constable if there had of late been any cases of rabies in the town, as he noticed that in some places the restrictions as to the muzzling of dogs were being withdrawn. Mr. Hunt, the Chief Constable, said that there had not been any cases, and informed the magistrate that the Town Clerk had also been inquiring about the matter, which he had now in hand.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

LATEST CRICKET. Yorkshire IEB for five wickets ; and Gloucester 123 for nine. PORTUGAL AND THE CONVENTION. A "Times" Lisbon telegram of yesterday says that all the Ministerial journals approve of the basis of the Anglo-Portuguese Convention. PASSENGERS FROM THE STIL` NDED STEAMER. Lloyd's New York telegram reports that the passengers from the stranded Hamburg-American steamer David have been landed at New York. THE BRADFORD MURDERER. The execution of James Harrison is fixed for next Tuesday. Efforts are being made to obtain a reprieve on the ground that he received provocation. FATAL COLLISION AT SEA.. Lloyd's agent at Strazaire telegraphs that the Redbrook and the Amerique have been in collision, and that the former vessel sank. Three of the crew were lost. The Redbrook was from Newport. THE CONWAY BOATING DISASTER. Yesterday, Mr. Roberts, the coroner for Carnarvon- shire, held the inquest at Conway, on the bodies of Misses Fanny and Beatrice Yarcoe, Dr. Greene, and William Evans, four of the eight victims of Wednesday's boating disaster, which is reported on page three. The verdict was, "Accidentally drowned." THE TILBURY DOCK STRIKE. All the men returned to work at the Tilbury Docks, yesterday, although they express dissatisfaction at being compelled by the London Executive of the Dockers' Union to do so. They declare they will leave the Dock- ers' Union and join the London Southern Counties Labour League. SHOEBURYNESS MEETING. The 3rd Middlesex, Ist detachment, have taken the first prize of £lO for the highest aggregate in the two 40- pounder competitions, with 78 points. The 7th detach- ment of the Ist Essex won the first prize challenge cup and badges for the highest marks in shooting and reposi- tory combined, by 169 points. The Bth detachment of the same corps was second. THE REPORTED CASE OF ASIATIC CHOLERA. On inquiries being made at Poplar Hospital, the sea- man, Robert Teigh, was reported to be better, having taken a considerable quantity of fluid nourishment. The state of collapse is passing off. The captain of the Duke of Argyll ridicules the idea that Teigh is suffering from Asiatic cholera, and declares that the attack is no- thing but an attack of painters' cholic. He says that a good deal of painting was recently done on board the vessel. ALLEGED MANSLAUGHTER BY A MOTHER. Mr. Diplock held an inquiry at Willesden Vestry Hall, yesterday, regarding the death of a six weeks' old infant, whose mother was charged at Marylebone Police Court, on WCdnesday, with neglecting it. It was stated that the mother systematically neglected and left the child and had been heard to say, " 'Twould be a good job if 'twas dead." The jury returned a verdict of manslaughter against the mother—Ellen Power—who is already in cus- tody pending police court proceedings. TERRIBLE EXPLOSION AT I GOVERNMENT ' FACTORY. TWO WORKMEN BLOWN TO ATOMS. A terrible explosion occurred at twenty minutes to seven yesterday morning at the Government gun- powder factories at Waltham Abbey. The men had not long been at work. The sound of the explosion was heard over a large area, and its force broke windows miles away. The" Central News" telegraphs that great alarm wai occaSioned in Waltham and neighbourhood yesterday morning by a violent and destructive 'explosion at the Royal gunpower factory. The full result of the disaster is not known, but two workmen were blown to atoms, portions of their bodies having been found greatly dis- coloured, at long distances from the scene of the acci- dent. A third man was severely injured, but it is hoped that no further loss of life or personal injury was sus- tained. Search is, however, being made. The explo- sion occurred in one of the granulating houses, the building and machinery being demolished. Such disas- ters seldom occur in these houses, and the cause in this case is quite unknown. The report of the explosion was heard for miles around. Many windows in Waltham were shattered, and some walls fell. A later account says that the two men killed were the only persons in the factory when the explosion occurred. The injured man was in an adjoining shed, preparing to go into the factory, when he was knocked down. He is likely to recover. Only a comparatively small quantity of gunpowder exploded, but it did considerable damage. The inquest is to be held on Monday. The explosion is supposed tc have been due to an accident. There has not been an explosion at these works for 20 years. THE NEW BRIGHTON TRAGEDY. EXECUTION OF SPICER. Felix Spicer, who was convicted at the last Chester Assizes for the murder of his two illegitimate children, William and Henry Palin, at New Brighton, on Whit Sunday, the 25th May, was executed yesterday morning within the precincts of Knutsford Gaol. The prepara- tions for carrying out the last sentence of the law had been made some days previously by the Acting Under- Sheriff of the county. the governor of Knutsford Gaol and other officials. All hope of a reprieve was dissi- pated on Wednesday night when a reply was received from the Home Secretary, that, having fully considered the statements placed before him as to Spicer being of unsound mind when the murder was commmitted, he saw no reason to interfere with the law taking its course. This sad news was communicated to the culprit by t he chaplain, who, during the time since culprit's convic- tion, has been most assiduous in affording him religious consolation and preparing him for the terrible fate that awaited him. The short distance from the cell to the place of execu- tion was traversed very rapidly, and the prisoner was then hurried on to the drop. While Berry was arrang- ing him and placing the white cap on his head, the wretched man said :—" I am dying. I was mad if I perpetrated that crime on the poor, dear children. May God bless and keep me. Have mercy on me, a poor miserable sinner ; have mercy upon me. Oh, dear Christ, have mercy upon me." As the clock was about to strike sight Spicer exclaimed, "Go id morning, gentlemen," and Berry, stepping quickly back, pulled the fatal lever. Death was instantaneous, and beyond the usual contrac- tion of the muscles there was not a quiver of the body. The executioner, performed his task with remarkable dexterity. Spicer, who had hardly varied in weight since his incarceration, weighed list 101 b., and measured 5 feet 5 inches, and was given a drop of 5 feet 5 inches. TUB INQUEST. The inquest was held before by Mr. H. C. Yates, coroner, within the precincts of the prison. The gentle- men summoned on the jury are: John Fairhurst, Thomas Yarwood, Frederick Lee, George Lee, Thomas Warbur- ton, William Wildgoose, Robert Lee, Edward Briddall, Edwin Jackson, John Norbury, Alfred Edwards, and William Williamson. THE DECEASED AND PALIN.--STARTLING DISCLOSURES. Immediately after the inquest a rather important fact came to light, having an important bearing on the prisoner's conduct towards Palin in not marrying her, which had been so generally condemned. The real fact now appears that Spicer was a married man, and that he was born in London sixty years ago, being the son of a wine merchant in Tower-st. Early in life he married a woman in the county of Kent, but, according to his statement, finding her unfaithful he separated from her, i and had been living apart ever since. Towards the close ) of the final interview with the chaplain this morning he 3 said, "I forgive Mary Ann Palin, and hope that she and 3 the children will prosper." Spicer also complained of 8 2 Palin's harsh treatment of him, which he said had goaded 2 him to madness, in repulsing him when he wanted to o make up the last quarrel. It is now believed confidently 0 that his Kentish wife is dead. 0
THE AMERICAN STORMS.

WASHINGTON, THURSDAY.—Severe storms are general. Several cyclones, causing great damage to houses,farms, and other property, have passed over portions of the country. At Philadelphia a stable was destroyed and several tramcars were Smashed by the storm. Four per- sons were killed, and ethers received injuries which are likely to prove fatal.

div.head: FATAL FALL AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: FATAL FALL AT WARRINGTON.

On Thursday, at the White Hart Hotel, Sankey- st., Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy-coroner, held an inquiry regarding the death of a woman named Mary Riordan, 48 years of age, the wife of a pen- sioner who lives in Blackhurst-st, She left her bedroom about midnight on Wednesday, and acci- dentally fell downbtairs. The woman was picked up by her husband and conveyed to the Infirmary, the injuries to her head being very severe. Death resulted the same day. Evidence having been taken,the Corone, referred to Vie dangerous stairs in many of the Warrington houses. He had; one, or twice before held inquests on deaths arising from falls downstairs, and he thought it was a pity that in such a prosperous town as Warrington there should be houses where people should be exposed to such dangers for the want of a few extra shillings. It seemed to him that the time was long passed for building houses in such a state.—lnspector Cox, of the Borough Police Force, said the houses were built before the Act came into force.—The Coroner : Then the Town Council ought to condemn them.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

THE AMERICAN RAILWAY STRIKE. "FIGHTING TO THE BITTER END." NEW YORK, TEURSDAY.—The conference between Mr. Powderly and the other officials of the Knights of Labour and the officers of the New York Central Railway has failed to bring about a settlement. :Mr. Powderly will to-day issue an appeal to all the Knights in the employ of the New York and Vanderbilt /connecting lines. stating that it is the intention of the association to fight the rail- way company to the bitter end.

div.head: LICENSING CHANGES.
div.p: LICENSING CHANGES.

At the Borough-P-Olice -CORI-rt.:Oil Monday, the , following transfers of public-house licenses were granted:—Green Dragon' Bridge-st., from James Taylor to Peter Baguley ; The Alexandra, Scotland- rd., from John Armstrong to James Taylor; Rope and Anchor, Buttermarket-st., from Henry Summer- scales to John Woodward Powell. THIS BIRTH AND DRATH RATH OF WARRINGTON. For the week ending Saturday, August 16th, 1890.—The mean temperature was 58.7 Fahrenheit, and therefore 2.65 degrees colder than the pre- ceding week. The maximum temperature 71 Fahrenheit, was recorded on the 12th inst, and the minimum temperature, 46 Fahrenheit, on the 13th inst. The rainfall measured HO in. The general direction of the wind wa. S.W. During the week, which was the 33rd of the current year, 14 births and 19 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 19 76 per thousand, against 16.12, the average of the previous four weeks, and against 226 the corresponding week of last year. The deaths included 1 from typhoid fever; 3 from diarrhcea ; 2 from brain disease; 3 from lung dis- ease; 1 from liver disease; 5 from debility. One case of scarlatina and one of typhoid fever were reported under the requirements of the Act of Parliament.—Jomi H. GouistALL, Medical Officer of Health.

div.head: SWINE FEVER AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: SWINE FEVER AT WARRINGTON.

An outbreak of swine fever took place yesterday on the premises of Robert Edward Burgess, 71, Wellington-st. One animal was found dead in the sty and it certified to have died ot swine fever. With regard to another pig which was with the dead animal it has not yet been ascertained whether it is suffering from the disease or not.

div.head: WARRINGTONIANS AT HAWARDEN.
div.p: WARRINGTONIANS AT HAWARDEN.

On Thursday a small and select party of War- ringtonians visited Ilawarden, for the ostensible purpose of viewing the delights of the flower show held on that day, but yesterday it was freely rumoured in the town that their real objct was to catch a glimpse of the great statesman whose name is so intimately connected with the village of Hawarden. The party was in no sense a political one, but it is worthy of mention that one of the mem- bers, who is a very pronounced Conservative, was quite charmed with the reception that Mr. Gladstone gave to the large number of visitors to the exhibition. Yesterday he described to an " Examiner " reporter bow delighted he was to see the homely feeling that characterised the actions of Mr. Gladstone and other members of his family who were present, and who seemed to do their very best to make everybody at home with them. If this particular gentleman,who is a very honest and straightforward Conservative, were to make one or two more journeys to Haward en, the probability is that he would at last return to his native heath in a better state of mind, politically, speaking. Mr. Gladstone's geniality pleased every- one, and it is not at all surprising that Conserva- tives even Warrington Conservatives left Hawarden delighted with their experience.

div.head: MARKETS.
div.p: MARKETS.

MANCHESTER TRADE, FRIDAY.— There is not much trade (loin to-day in any department, and cotton is again tame, with an estimate of only 6,000 bales for the day's busi- ness. This is the sixth day in succession when sales have been estimated at that figUre, and the oldest member of the Exchange hardly remembers a similar occurrence. These con- tinued small sales are making matters very unpleasant for the •• bulls" yet they have not lost all hope of recovery. The Immediate futhre of prices depends largely on the action of spinners. Yarns ate very slow, and little offering either in twist or weft. Bundles are also quiet. but merchants have some business in hand if prices were tempting. Cloth market very dull and producers would be glad if some angel could come down and trouble the waters for many of them need help.
