div.head: ANNIVERSARY SERMONS.
div.p: ANNIVERSARY SERMONS.

On Sunday the anniversary sermons in connec- tion with the Brick-street and Friars'-green Sunday school were preached in Friars'-green chapel by Mr. ' R. B. Woods, of Pendleton. Each of the three ser- vices was largely attended, especially those held in the afternoon and evening. A service of song illustrative of the life of Gideon was ably ren- dered by the choir at the afternoon service. The collections, which were in aid of the school funds, realized .£2O us. 4d. FLOWER SERVICES AT PADGATII CHURCH._

A flower service mas held in Padgate Church on Sunday, and was well attended. During the sing- ing of the hymn "0 gather the flowers together," the children went up in order and presented their offerings of flowers and fruit to the Vicar, the Rev. J. J. Longhorn, by whom they were placed upon the steps of the altar. An able address was then delivered by the Rev. C. E. Jackson, curate of St. Elphin's, from the text "Consider the lillies." The flowers were subsequently sent to the Warrington Infirmary.

LAWN TENNIS. Latchford v. Warrington. Played at Warrington, on the ground at Arpley, on Tuesday evening, with the following result—Messrs. A. H. Crostield and E. Draper (Warrington), beat Messrs. A. Dun and J. A. Edelsten (Latchford), 3 sets to 2; Messrs. E. Willis and Bullivant,(Latchford), beat Messrs. Jas. Dun and J. F. Jackson (Warrington), 3 sets to 1 ; and Messrs T. and G. R. Williamson (Latchford), beat Messrs. W.S. Haddock and E. A. White (Warrington). 3 sets . .
to love,Latchford winning the Match by two events to one, 8 sets to four. PRESENTATION TO A WARRINGTON ORGANIST..

An interesting presentation has been made to Mr. J. J. Lythgoe, organist of St. Paul's Church, by the choristers, on the occasion of Hs marriage. The Vicar (the Rev. S. Wilkinson), in presenting a silver tea service, spc ke of the good feeling which existed between the organist and the choir, and wished Mr. Lythgoe along, happy, and useful life. Messrs. Potter, Fryer, and Lawless also spoke in compli- mentary terms of the services rendered to the choir by the organist : and a vote of thanks having been accorded to the Vicar and Mr. John Parkinson (assistant organist), the proceedings terminated. MI7SIC IN TUE PARK. -

_ The band of the Ist Volunteer Battalion (Prince of Wales Volunteers), South Lancashire Regiment, will play the following programme in the Park on Sunday commencing at 3.15 p.m. :—March ,by desire) "The Conqueror," I. Stirk ; Anthem "Lord of all power," Mason ; Selection "Mass in C," Beet- hoven ; Selection "Mass in G," Weber; Cornet solo "There is a green hill," Go:mod ; Selection " Seme • ramide," Rossini ; Clarionet solo "A Dream," Delafosse ; Chorus "Hallelujah to the Father, " Bee t- hoven ; "God save the Queen." As a mark of respect to the memory of the late Mr. James Stirk, the band will at the close of the progtamme play the "Dead March in Saul."

div.head: LICENSED VICTITA.LLERS' TRIP.
div.p: LICENSED VICTITA.LLERS' TRIP.

On Thursday the annual excursion of the members and friends of the Licensed Victuallers Association took place, Llandudno being chosen as the destina- tion. The party, numbering about 70 persons, left Warrington Central station at 8.50 in the morning, and went from Liverpool to Llandudno by the St. Tudno. They reached Llandudno at about one o'clock, having had a p' ,asant sail. Dinner was served in first-class sty.t at the Grosveno , in Mostyn-st.. Mr. Sumner, the proprietor, proving a very capable caterer. The weather during the afternoon was showery, but notwithstanding this the outing was an enjoyable one. The return journey was commenced at 4.30

div.head: TIIE TOTAL ABSTINIINCE MISSION.
div.p: TIIE TOTAL ABSTINIINCE MISSION.

On &Imlay there were three meetings in connec- tion with the Warrington Workingmen's Open Air Mission, on the enclosed ground off Bewsey-st. In the afternoon Mr. T. Frain (vice-president) was in the chair, and Messrs. J. Price. G. Sanbrook, J. Drury, and Taylor (St. Helens) gave encouraging addresses. In the evening Mr. T. Frain presided, and was supported by Messrs. J. Price, J. O'Reilly, C. H. Mills, and F. Dixon. The first meeting at Bridge Foot was held in connection with this mis- sion, Mr. J. Kilduff presiding, and addresses were given by Messrs. G. Wild, J. O'Reilly, and J. Kilduff Several of Mr. Sankey's solos were sung. There was a very large attendance at each meeting.

div.head: DEATH OF A CHILD,
div.p: DEATH OF A CHILD,

On Wednesd—a-Y,--Dir.--VET7-11U;band, deputy- coroner, held an inquest in the parade room, at the Bridewe4, as to the death of an infant, three months old, named Thomas Patrick Connor. The mother, Mary Ann Connor, said her husband was a forge labourer, living at 19 Back Dolman's-lane. On Sunday morning she found the child lying be- side her in bed quite dead. The deceased was one of twins and had been delicate since birth. Both she and her husband were quite sober when they went to bed on Saturday night. Bridget McNamee, a neighbour of the last witness, spoke to having seen the child soon after it was found dead, and it appeared to her to have died in a fit. A verdict of , death from natural causes was returned.

div.head: BREWERY EXCITESION.
div.p: BREWERY EXCITESION.

On Saturday, the office staff belonging to the firm of Messrs. P. Walker and Son, Limited, Warrington, and Burton, had their annual trip, the destination this year being Chatsworth, Haddon Hall, and Matlock Bath. The party, which was made up of representatives from Liverpool, Warrington, Birkenhead, Chester, Manchester, travelled by saloon carriage, Bakewell being reached shortly after eleven. Here wagon- ettes were in waiting, and after luncheon at the Rutland Arms a start was made for Chatsworth. Haddon Hall was next visited, and then the party drove to Matlock Bath, where dinner was in readi- ness at the New Bath Hotel. After dinner had been served, and a few loyal toasts proposed, a vote of thanks to the Chairman and directors of the firm for affording another enjoyable day was passed with acclamation. The return journey was com- menced shortly after seven. PRIMROSE LEAGUE FESTIVAL AT GRAPPENIIALL. The annual demonstration in connection with the Grappenhall Habitation (No. 1573) of the Primrose League was held at Grappenhall Heyes on Saturday, by permission of Mr. J. Charlton Parr. There were between 400 and 500 persons present. Among those present were—Mr. Parr, Mrs. Parr (Ruling Coun- cillor), Mrs. Edward Greenall (treasurer), Mr. Lister-Kaye (secretary); the wardens— Messrs. Hankey, Thomas Mulkey, Wallace. Ashcroft, ,Long- shaw, Spence, Mitch, and Roughsedge ; Mrs. Stubs, the Misses Stabs, Mrs. Stanton, Mr. and Mrs. Marson, Mr. Charles Marson, Mr. and Mrs. Wynne Jones, Mr. John White, Mrs. Gilbert Greenall, Mr. Alfred Greenall, Mr. Frank Greenall, Mr. and Mrs. Thomas Fletcher, the Misses Fletcher, Mrs. Greaves, ' Miss Greaves, Miss Kidd, and the Misses Smith. The members of the habitation and their friends were allowed to fish in the different ponds on the estate; others rambled about the park and gardens, and not a few witnessed a cricket match between a team from the Warrington Post Office and oue from Grappenhall. St. Paul's Band was in attendance, and played selections of music. In the evening the band played for dancing. roe, was provided in a large tent on the lawn in front of the house, the caterer being Mr. Speakman, of the Saracen's Head Hotel, Wilderspool. Shortly after. six o'clock, Mr. Parr addressed a number of those present in front of the Hall. He said he was very happy to congratulate the members upon the success and the growth of the Primrose , League, and of that Habitation in particular. It had considerably increased since they last had the plea- sure of meeting in that place, and if its success con- tinued in the same ratio, the prophecy in which he indulged last year would soon be fulfilled, and they , would be able to say that nothing flourished in that neighbourhood like the Primrose. (Hear, hear, and laughter). He afterwards proposed "that this meet- ing desires to record its unabated conndence in the Government of Lord Salisbury, and its special ap- preciation and admiration of his firm and success- ful foreign policy." Mr. R. Cappock se,conded the motion, which was carried unanimously. The band then played for dancing.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

TEMPORARY THAN/MM.—The license of the Legh Arms Hotel, Golborne, was on Wednesday, at the Warrington County Sessions, temporarily transferred to Joseph Nicholls. DRUIDS' DINNER AT LOWTON.—The annual dinner in connection with the Independent Order of Druids was held at the Jolly Carter Inn, Lowton, on Saturday. About 100 sat down to dinner, and afterwards the men adjourned to the bowling green and indulged in a game elf bowls. EDGE GREEN PRIMITIVE METHODISTS.—The annual tea party and field day in connection with the Edge Green Primitive Methodist School took place on Saturday, when a procession was formed, and, headed by the Rey. J. Dudley, paraded the principal streets. The party re- turned to the school and partook of a well-catered tea, after which they adjourned to a field where various games were indulged in. SERVICE Or SONG.—On Sunday, special sermons and a service of song took place in the Wesleyan Chapel, Gol- borne. In the morning and evening Mr. J. Wibberley, Warrington, preached before large congregations. In the afternoon the service of song, entitled—" Red Dave, or trust in God," was rendered, the connective readings being given by Mr. J. Williamson. The choir were under the leadership of Mr. Wm. Mather. COLLIERY FATALITY.—On Friday night a fatal accident occurred at the Edge-green Collieries, of Messrs. Ric- hard Evans lk Co. A matt named Thomas Tott, aged 43, residing at Legh-street, Golborne, was engaged as a shot- lighter, and rammed a shot which, however, failed to go off in the expected time. Contrary to rules, he then at- tempted to prepare a second shot, with the result that the first shot exploded and brought down a large quantity of coal upon him. It is stated that deceased had been warned a few hours previous to the accident of the danger arising from such a course. PRESCOT.
other

WESLEYAN CLIAPEL.—The Sable Singers held an Evan- gelical service, consisting of Bible reading, addresses, and sacred melodies, on Sunday evening, in the Wes- leyan Schools. There was a good attendance. A VIOLENT PRISONER. —At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, John Corner, a rough looking man was charged with being drunk and disorderly and with assaulting Sergeant Milne on the previous night. The prisoner was very disorderly and kicked the sergeant several times on the legs and body. Prisoner was fined 10s. and costs in each case. ALLEGED CRUELTY TO A DON/M.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, John William Sugden, a marine store dealer, High-st., Prescot, was summoned for ill- treating a donkey by causing it to be worked in an uafit state. Constable Gill stated that he saw a boy in charge of the animal at Knowsley. He found a raw wound about the size of a crown piece on its body.—Defendant said the wound was caused by the saddle and harness having slipped forward.—The Bench took his view of the case and dismissed the summons, advising the defendant to look well after his donkey in future. CAPTURE OF SUSPICIOUS CILARACTERS.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday, William Winstanley and John Evans, colliers, Thatto Heath, were summoned for an offence under the Poaching Prevention Act by being in unlawful possession of game. Neither of the dcfendants appeared.—Sergeant M-Xracken deposed that about a quarter-past five on the morning of last Saturday week he met the defendants and two other men in Talbot's- lane, Rainhill. Two of the men ran away but witness and another officer who was with him stopped the de- fendants. On searching them they found upon Win- stanley five rabbits and one net, and on Evans they found one net and threa rabbits. They had also got three bags in which they foura, four pheasants and 17 rabbits- They ascertained the na mes and addresses of the men and let them go.—lt appeared that Winsta.nley had been several times previously convicted for similar offences and he was fined £5 and costs.—Evans, whose first convic- tion it was, was fined 10s. and costs. ANNUAL FIELD DAY—The scholars, numbering over 400, of the British Kindergarten School (Miss Evans'), Prescot, had their annual outing, on Thursday afternoon, in the park adjoining Hurst House. The children assembled at the school at 12.30, and were conveyed from thence in 16 large waggonettes o their destination, where the usual outdoor games N lc largely indulged in. The pleasure of the afternoon was somewhat marred by the rain which fell heavily whilst ' the children were partaking of a very rribstantial tea, under cover. The tea was supplied by Mrs. Taylor, of Church-st.' and gave universal satisfaction. After tea, the sun made his appearance, and the short time remaining, was spent in a very enjoyable manner, and passed away all too quickly. The children re- assembled at 7.45, each scholar receiving a bun. Three very hearty cheers were then given for Miss Evans, the generous donor of this enjoyable treat. Mr. Orchard (head master), Mrs. Garner (head mistress), Miss Walker (infant mistress), with the other teachers, Misses Peacop, Watson, Houghton, etc., were untiring in their efforts to entertain the children. Special mention should be made of the fact, that the Rev. A. N. Gilmore rendered very able assistance in arranging and carrying out, the above programme.

div.head: REV. C. F. AKED'S DEPARTURE.
div.p: THE REV. C. F. AKED'S DEPARTURE.

EARLESTOPirN BAPTISTS CONDEMNED. On Monday night a public tea meeting was held in Park-road Baptist Chapel, St. Helens, in connection with the departure of the pastor, the Rev. C. F. Aked, who has accepted a call to the pastorate of Pembroke Baptist:Chapel, Liverpool. The Rev. C. Aked has officiated as the pastor of Park-road and Earlestown Baptist Churches for the past two years,and it is generally admitted that his ministerial labours have been rewarded with success. No definite steps have yet been taken in regard to the appointment of a successor, but, it is stated that there will be a final severance of the church connection between the St. Helens and ' Earlestown Baptists. The proceedings on Monday even- ing commenced with a tea party, at which about 200 persons were present. The tables were presided over by Mrs. Aked, Mrs. Gaskell, Mrs. Jenkinson, Mrs. Bewley, Mrs. Cameron,and Mrs. Farnworth, assisted by ladies of the congregation. At a subsequent meeting there was a very large attendance. The chair was occupied by Mr. J. Gaskell, deacon, who was supported by the Revs. C. F. Aked, G. Hammond (Wesleyan), F. Smith, (Primitive Methodist), and J. Cottam (Baptist).—The Chairman expressed the regret of the congregation at losing Mr. Aked's services.—Mr. F. Smith afterwards spoke, and commended the departing minister's spirit of progress in all his actions. He said that during Mr. Aked' s stay amongst them his work Had resulted in a growth of spiritual life, and they wished him God speed in his new sphere of labour —Mr. Bewley (secretary) read several letters of apology for non-attendance, including one from Mr. S. Woods, the labour candidate for the Ince Division, who wrote wishing Mr. Aked a very suc- cessful and prosperous pastorate at Liverpool. In his new department he would be brought in close contact with the working-men of Liverpool, and he was per-, suaded the effect and influence of his personality and labour ^would be far-reaching.—The Rev. G. Hammond, Rev. J. Cottam, Mr. Jenkinson (deacon), and other speakers followed, and there was a general regret ex- pressed that Mr. Aked was leaving St. Helens. The Rev. C. F. Aked was received with warm ap- plause, and in his farewell address thanked them , for the encouragement he had always received. and for the perfect freedom and confidence they had always reposed in him. In leav- ing them, he was opening out for success or failures vast career. The Pembroke Church had a historical' pulpit, rich with traditions, and he went to succeed a heroic and inspired ancestry—to do a great and magnifi- cent work, or fail in doing it. He remarked that what, he said about them did not apply to Earlestown. He had not one kind thing to say about the people of Earles- town. There could be a splendid church built up at Earlestown, given one single thing, and that was, if two or three people who were now supposed to be leaders in the church, were hanged, drawn, and quartered. (Laughter.) If they thought that would not be enough, they could take them into the near- est field, try them by court martial, and have them instantly shot. If they could only suc- ceed in bundling them out bag and baggage, lock.stock and barrel,then they might have a good church there. He concluded by expressing his heartfelt thanks to the peeple at Park-road, and said anything that lay in his power to help them he should do. He prayed that a full prosperity and abounding success would rest upon them, and him. (Applause.) The meeting then termin- ated with singing and prayer.

div.head: ST. HELENS HIGHWAY COMMITTEE.
div.p: ST. HELENS HIGHWAY COMMITTEE.

The monthly meeting of the Paving Highway and', Sewering Committee was held at the Town Hall. on Wednesday afternoon, when there were present Councillor E. Johnson (eh airrn an), Councillors Green- ough, Jones, Morgan, Brown, Foote, Hatton, Fisher, and Green, Messrs. W. J. Jeeves (deputy-town I clerk), and G. J. C. Broom (borough surveyor). The , Deputy Town Clerk reported that with regard to ' the suggested improvement of New-street, Sutton,' the minute passed at the last meeting had been referred ' back by the Council. It was thought that money should not be borrowed for the purchase of land except on the report of the Parliamentary and Lands Committee, but at a meeting of that Committee it was decided to leave the matter to the Paving Committee. The Parliamen- tary Committee had also given instructions for a ;list to be prepared showing the duties of the respective Committees.—Councillor Brown said he thought the duties of the Committees ought to be clearly defined. That Committee had been made the scapegoat for other Committees.—lt was ulti- mately agreed that the improvement of New- street as agreed upon at the last meeting should be pro- ceeded : with.—The Deputy Town Clerk stated that when the Committee made their annual inspection of the highways the Town Clerk was instructed to write to the owner of some property near Hanging Bridge with regard
new

to the building of a new wall or the erection of a - line of fencing. The owner had written stating that he was prepared to build the wall it the Committes would agree to a fresh line. The Committee decided to reque,st the owner to fence the land.—The Deputy Town Clerk also reported that the Health Committee had resolved. to sewer the streets of Sutton, and as the work was being done from the drainage of the streets they decided to ssig the Paving Committee to carry out the work. Ile sug- gested that the Surveyor be instructed to prepare planS and an estimate of the cost of the scheme. This sok ger'. tion was adopted.—The Committee granted an appilea" tion by the London and Manchester Plate Glass Com- pany for their consent to alterations in front of the o!d. Oak Inn, Gerards-lane. The Surveyor intimated that it was his intention to alter the names of Victoria-St. South-st., and York-st. East to Ross-st.—CGuncillor Jones asked what was being done in regard to Church-st., Sutton.—The Surveyor replied that they could not inter- fere with it as it was not a public street.—This was all , the business.

div.p: EARLESTOWN.

CROW LANE CATHOLIC CHAPEL. A solemn requiem mass was offered for the II" Cardinal Newman on Sunday, at the Roman Catho- lic Church, Crow-lane. The preacher was the R2V. Father Gregory, who, in the course of his serniorit,t referred to the loss the Catholic Church through°, the world had swtained by the Cardinal's deaty At the close of the evening service, the organ" played the Dead March in "Saul."

NEWTON HORTICULTURAL SHOW. A. Frost (sec.) and. the committee of menagde; ment. Some excellent arrangements have been not for the gathering, including the attendance of the, Earlestown Brass Band. With fine weather til° exhibition should be a great success.

COUNTY PA.LATI: NE OF LANCASTER. CONTAGIOUS DISEASE: ; (ANIMALS) ACTS 1878 TO 1 886. SWINE FEVER.. THE Exec:itive Cattle .Plague Committee of the County Council for the Uoucty Palatinwof Lancaster as the Local Authority of the Administrative County of Lancas- ter (hereinafter referred to as the said Local Authority), in exercise of the powers conferred by the shave Acts and the Animals Order of IEB6, Da hereby. with theview of preventing the introduction of Swine Feve:r into the District of the said, Local Authority, make the folio wing Regulations ,for the pro- hibiting and regulating the ntovement of Swine into their District From and after the 21st day August, WdS, 'until further directions in this behalf. IT IS ORDERMID THAT r- -I.—lt shall not be lawful to move Swine Into the District of the said Local Authoriity from the District of any other Local Authority in England, Wales or-Scotland, until a License for the nmvement of such Swine into the District of the said Loctl Authority shallthave been granted by an Inspector mmointed by the -said Local Authority. 2.—A Movement License will only be granted on Declaration by the Owner of the Swine or gals agent being handed to an Inspector of the said Local Author- ity, and such Declaration shall specify the 'number and description of the Swine proposed to be moved, and shall show that such Swine (ft) Are not affected with riwine Fever; (b) Have not been exposed: to the infection of Swine Fever. 3.—The movement of Swine Into the District of the said Local Authoriry in contravention of this Regulation is prohibited. 4.—A movement Licence shall continue in force for Seven days from the date thereof., artd no longer; and shall be delivered. together with the Declaration on which it was granted. to a Pollee Constable or other Offoser of the Police of the said Loral Authority forthwith after being made use of or after its expiration. S.—Provided that the foregoing Regulations shall not re- strict the movement of Swine through the District of the said Local Authority by railway without untruck-, Jog. By Order of the sald Local Authority. FRED. C. HULTON, ; Clerk of the Lancashire County Council. ' Preston. 7th August, 1890. NOTE.—Licences and Forms of Declaration can be oh-' tamed frov. the Police, at any.of the County Police Stations. in Lancashire, free of cost. CAUTION. If any Swine be moved incontravention of the above Regu- lations' the Owner and the person foe the time being in chargetheneof, and the person causing, directing, or permit- ting the movement, and the person mooing or conveying the animal. andlhe consignee or other person receiving or keep- ing it, are liable on prosecution to fine and imprisonment. A person snaking a Declaration false in any material parti- cular is liable:to fine and imprisonment.

PERMISSION To SELL—Luke nolmes, auctioneer, was granted permission to seR tat the Holyhead Harbour beerhouse, High-st., receritly kept by M. Kelly. BREACHES Os THE EipecsrioN Am—The Halton School Attendance Committee summoned several parents for not sending their children regularly to school, and the usual fine of ss. VMS imposed in each case. THE GREEN-EVS.D MoNsrint.—Henry Atherton was charged with assaulting Thomas Ellison, a boatman. The complainant said when he came home on Saturday evening, the ninth inst., his wife was out. He went to the Royal Hotel and found her there sitting besides the defendant and two other women. He had been a teeto- taller for 19 years, and he asked his wife what she was doing there. She replied, "I did not come in with him, I came in with the two women." He struck her, and then the defendant struck him on the face with his fist. —The defendant said he went into the Hotel alone, and while he was sitting there the complainant came in and took a running kick at his wife, and was doing so again when he went between them. He never struck the com- plainant. Thomas Ailditch confirmed the statement and the summons was dismissed. DRUNKENNESS.—For this offence a fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon John Lewis, Fred Orme, Mary Orme, Rose Ann Whitby, and Catherine Hagan.—A fine of 2s. 6d. was imposed upon James McTurk, Walter Wilson, Samuel Guest, John Wilson, and Mary Ann Wakefield. TuErr OF A HAM.—Richard'Condon, a rough-looking navvy, was charged with having stolen a ham, belong- ing to Mr. George Wharton, grocer, Church-st. The ham, which -vas hanging at.the shop door, was missed on Friday night, and information was given to the police Next morning, P.C. Woodrow found the ham cut into two pieces in a lodging house, and he ascertained that it had been brought there by the prisoner, who had sold I half to a " mate." The constable, therefore, apprehended the prisoner who was remanded for a week, so that in- quiries mieht be made aslo his antecedents. WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THISIRSDAY.—Before Messrs. F. H. Gossage, H. W. Deacon, andLieut.-Colonel Gaskell.
